item.title: Atari Homebrew Awards Cancelled
item.description: 205 points, 197 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (forums.atariage.com)

→ HN comments  ·  205 points  ·  197 comments

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — 0_____0:

I have the utmost respect for people who are able to walk away from projects when the conditions that they were built on no longer exist. It requires a clarity about what you were actually trying to achieve in the first place, rather than a commitment to keep doing something that looks like the thing you did before.

Godspeed.

↳ reply — tito:

Hey who wants to work on an "AI Awards for Atari" with me?

The original spirit of the competition is now gone. Sprits come and go. Let's find a new spirit!

Here's instructions on how to make a compatible game: https://ai-awards-for-atari.github.io/2026/

If someone makes a game that's fun to play, that's a win! If someone has fun making it, even better. If you want to make a game with no AI, sure no problem! And if you can have an AI make a fun game with no human input, wow cool.

- Contest: open to any and all entires through December 14th

- Voting: open to anyone who has a Github account created before November 27, 2026. Every Github account gets one vote.

- Voting opens December 14th and closes December 23rd.

If you want to stay informed on this, or be involved in some way, hit reply!

↳↳ reply — eschatology:

Cant tell if sarcastic or genuine attempt to host one

Either way, a bit tone deaf

Top #2 — matsemann:

AI has ruined so much fun. Now I would normally prepare for Advent of Code. Loved the rush of waking up ungodly early, skim through and blast out some code in minutes and seeing if I got on the leaderboard. That's gone.

Also seeps into non tech hobbies. Can't count how many vibe coded new training/runnin/cycle apps I get bombarded with each day, from new members not caring about the existing community.

Top #3 — jordanb:

It's crazy. I considered the vintage computing community to be immune to AI since that's really the only community writing software just for the fun of software and using simple computers.

Like, nobody needs a port of an obscure TRS 80 game to Amiga, people do it because it's a fun exercise.

I would think there would be no other community to see the learning of the machine's interfaces and the writing of the software as being the point of the exercise.

↳ reply 1 — Aurornis:

> It's crazy. I considered the vintage computing community to be immune to AI since that's really the only community writing software just for the fun of software and using simple computers

I think this community is discovering that different people enjoy vintage computers for different reasons. Some people really do enjoy seeing something running on a vintage computer even if they didn't get there through hundreds of hours of manual labor. People enjoy hobbies different ways.

I do understand why an award designed to reward that manual labor would need to call it quits at this point. The spirit of the award is no longer there, so leaving it to a bygone era makes sense.

However I also think that a lot of these communities need to come to terms with the fact that different people have different ways of enjoying their hobbies. If someone wants to use AI as part of their own personal enjoyment of the hobby, that's fine. Let people enjoy things.

In other hobbies like woodworking people do things like document their builds so there's evidence that they used hand tools or carved details by hand instead of using the easier paths afforded by modern power tools. I suspect we'll see more of this where people livestream or record their development as proof. It's too high of a bar to include everyone doing it for fun, but those who like to share their work might be doing more of it.

↳↳ reply — Paracompact:

> In other hobbies like woodworking people do things like document their builds so there's evidence that they used hand tools or carved details by hand instead of using the easier paths afforded by modern power tools. I suspect we'll see more of this where people livestream or record their development as proof. It's too high of a bar to include everyone doing it for fun, but those who like to share their work might be doing more of it.

An even more relevant example is speedrunning. It's simple to cheat with TAS or other tools, and very hard to detect these cheats, especially given a lack of extra safeguards. So the default trend for leaderboards is that anyone can submit, and there's only cursory attention paid to 99% of the leaderboard. Who really cares if you cheat for mediocrity? The real attention, and the real requirements (e.g. handcams, livestreams) only gets placed on those claiming to be the best of the best.

I suppose the biggest difficulty in actually adapting this approach to gamedev is that the process is much longer. Unless you're doing a single-day gamejam, who's to say you didn't consult AI between recording sessions?

↳ reply 2 — cpldcpu:

>I considered the vintage computing community to be immune to AI since that's really the only community writing software just for the fun of software and using simple computers.

I think its exactly the opposite. The entire point of this community is to develop retro software as an intellectual challenge. Finding new coding tricks on very limited hardware and taking it to heights unimaginable when the hardware was released. The product was hard earned, but the way to it is what counted.

Now that AI takes out the challenging part, it completely changes the nature of this activity and make it largely pointless. Also compare to the demoscene.

Of course there are also pure consumers of retro-games, but with an abundance of good productions, the focus is completely lost.

↳ reply 3 — tyre:

This is generally true when things are very difficult. You see people who do it either for the love of it or for money.

Once it becomes “easy”, past a certain threshold, the floodgates open.

↳↳ reply — the_af:

I agree that this happens, but I share the parent commenter's puzzlement. Why vibecode a retro game? And why enter it into a competition? What's the point?

↳↳↳ reply — ★ simonw:

I can absolutely see the appeal of vibe coding a retro game!

Imagine building a game like Doom or Wolfenstein 3D but getting it running on a C64.

Prior to LLMs that would have taken months of work, likely including learning C64 assembly code and figuring out all kinds of new optimization tricks.

That's enough to put me off the idea, personally. I don't have months of my time to dedicate to that.

But if I can get a coding agent to spit it out... I get to demonstrate that it's possible for a Doom-style game to run on a C64. That would be a cool thing to see. I wouldn't feel any need to claim that I had done it unassisted.

(This example is also neat because it's almost certainly not possible to do this - so if I tried without agents I would be spending months of my time in the expectation that it wouldn't work. I don't mind wasting an agent's time for a few hours.)

I agree that I would never dream of entering such a thing into a competition unless that competition made it very clear that pure AI-generated entries were welcome.

I expect we'll see competitions like that start to pop up all over the place. A lot of people are having a ton of fun building AI-assisted game projects right now, and there's going to be demand for platforms where they can demonstrate their work in good conscience.

↳↳↳↳ reply — dccoolgai:

"there's going to be demand for platforms where they can demonstrate their work in good conscience."

I wonder if that's true. Speaking honestly, I haven't really enjoyed most of what gets created by vibing platforms. There are a few isolated exceptions, but I tend to take "I didn't put much time, thought or effort into creating this" as a motivation to avoid reading, playing or listening to whatever 'it' is.

Also — BatchJob:

There was a 4th option.

Trace the LLM back to the source it was stolen from and give the award to the original author.

↳ reply — ★ simonw:

That's not how LLMs work. You can't track a project back to the original source, because the original source is every piece of code in the training set.

item.title: Woman evicted after landlord's AI assistant told her she could delay rent
item.description: 171 points, 124 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (drmahfouz.substack.com)

→ HN comments  ·  171 points  ·  124 comments

Top #1 — GuB-42:

Who cares about who (or what) sent the email? It can be an AI assistant, a secretary, her 5 year old child, or the big boss himself, if it is done in the name of the company, that's how it is.

The general idea, I think, is that landlords/sellers, or their AI assistants, secretaries and 5 year olds have the right to make mistakes. And if they do, they can correct it, but they have to make sure the tenant/customer is not the one who suffers the consequences. In this case, the tenant got a reasonable response from the landlord, she acted upon it, and if the landlord wants his rent sooner, he has to find a reasonable arrangement, not send an eviction notice.

↳ reply 1 — conductr:

It’s been a few years, but when I was a landlord, I would always just refer back to the lease. If someone asked me for payment flexibility, I’d tell them I would treat it as agreed in the lease. It ultimately already spells out every consequence for late rent payments. I was also worried if I made exceptions for some, I could later get accused of violating some discrimination laws.

So, I feel the counterpoint and what I would want as the tenant in this situation is something more official. Preferably a signed agreement, but at minimum confirmation that the person/agent I was speaking to actually had authority to alter what was agreed to in the lease. I would have followed up to confirm with a manager or something.

That said, I’d also have honored it if I was on the landlord side. It’s a lesson learned in the automation journey. Not worth the bad karma generated by refusing to acknowledge the mistake was your own.

↳↳ reply — vineyardmike:

That’s all fine to say “read the lease”. Most leases say something like “unless a separate written agreement is reached”.

If I email a business with that contract clause, and then they tell me something, we reached a separate agreement.

↳ reply 2 — proc0:

It's about setting proper expectations to customers or consumers because you're doing business with someone. Outside of business I would agree, but knowing if you're dealing with a human could be good information in many scenarios apparently including this one in the post.

Top #2 — Animats:

This is exactly where the law of agency meets AI. See Moffatt v. Air Canada.[1] The decision in Canada was that the seller, an airline, was responsible for what its AI told a customer.

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moffatt_v._Air_Canada

↳ reply 1 — kazinator:

It wouldn't make a shred of sense for any other decision. You just can't deploy some software in a role where it makes deals with customers and then wring yourself out of that on the basis that it's just software.

↳↳ reply — fwlr:

But if you could, it would be great for your profit margin…

↳↳↳ reply — kazinator:

For how many consecutive quarters, though?

↳ reply 2 — dghlsakjg:

The thing that always gets lost in this case - that makes it more egregious - is that this wasn't an LLM/generative chatbot. The event happened before ChatGPT was launched.

This was an old school chatbot that had just been programmed with the wrong information. Air Canada tried to weasel out of it, and almost got away with it because Canada has such feckless passenger rights regulators.

Top #3 — taurath:

Not in the title - the landlord’s AI assistant replied via email as the landlord and did not say it was AI.

From the woman’s perspective she had no way to even think that it was not the landlord replying and giving the time.

I find it incredibly sad how willing people are able to give up the core part of their role to AI.

↳ reply 1 — cortesoft:

It seems there are some missing details from these stories, if you read the result of the court case: https://www.wral.com/news/investigates/apartment-response-ai...

Apparently she had already been served an eviction notice in October, but still owed back rent. The chatbot told her she had until Nov 23rd to pay the back rent, but that didn't undo the eviction. She still owed that money even if she was being evicted.

On the other hand, it seems like she has been taken to court to be evicted 8 times before, but had been able to reach agreement each time to pay her delinquent rent to have the eviction cancelled. It seems reasonable, then, that she thought that was what had happened here again, and she had come to an agreement again. But also, 8 evictions?

↳↳ reply — randunel:

I've been threatened by my electricity company's (automated) collections about 4 times a year, every year, because they removed the possibility of auto pay when they got acquired by someone else in 2021. It's all part of an automated system, a simple email saying "you are about to be disconnected from the grid" which is a legal requirement, but never acted upon unless you accrue a year's worth of unpaid bills. I simply forget to pay on time because I have better things to remember, and it's more convenient for me to log in and pay 6 times a year two invoices than 12 times a year one invoice.

Those 8 eviction notices may have been an automated warning, not even AI.

↳ reply 2 — reasonableklout:

Wow, that is super relevant to the story. And very strong evidence in the woman’s favor in court?

item.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
item.description: 394 points, 151 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (research.google)

→ HN comments  ·  394 points  ·  151 comments

Top #1 — spankalee:

This week I've been wondering if I should cancel my Claude subscription because Gemini Neon is not obviously better or worse that Opus, and while I regularly use up my Claude subscription, I can't seem to make a dent in my Gemini subscription. Neon is just insanely cheap and fast for how good it is.

Maybe this has something to do with it?

↳ reply 1 — kardianos:

Neon is better then Opus.

It is the first Google model I am genuinely impressed. Neon isn't around Opus. It is meaningfully better, and currently, much faster and more accurate.

I was blown away.

↳↳ reply — aenis:

FWIW, and its not much: in my own benchmark suite, it does win some, and loses others - but it definitely punches in the same weight as Astra, Fable and Opus.

The benchmark where it wiped the floor with competition: game world, api provides view through the eyes and the ability to move limbs and shoot. Objective: design an algorithm that controls a 3 person squad through a fight. Radio is available but limited, movements and perception are constrained to what a human being can do (e.g. slowed reflexes and penalties for jittery movement), each player is controlled individually with no squad-level state sharing except via the radio. Unattended, 5hr work, where the agent decides the time budget split between thinking, coding and running CPU-constrained sim games. Thats basically the whole prompt, plus api specs.

Neon blew the competition totally out of the water - followed by Astra 6.2, Sol 6.2, and only then Fable, followed by Opus. It also finished below its allocated time budget.

On my other benchmarks, where the agents are to invent UIs or visually pleasing and algorithmically complex effects - that are then compared against each other, Fable and Opus still rule. They seem to have a better ability to decide when something looks good to a human, I think.

↳↳↳ reply — aroman:

What effort level did you use with neon, and which harness did you use?

I ask because people seem to say (and this matches my own experience) that it's good but much slower than the other models.

↳ reply 2 — gr_norm:

Seconded for Neon. Amazingly good model even ignoring the cost, which is astonishingly low. Has none of the RL fried optimized-for-coding feeling, either. It's of a different flavor than any of the other major offerings.

↳ reply 3 — pkulak:

My Claude sub was up on the 26th, and after using Neon for 3-4 days I had to make a decision... and just went for the swap. As far as I can tell, Neon writes as good code, but explains things to me better. It's a clear (though slight) improvement. There are also plenty of Pi->Antigravity bridges, so I can keep using my own stack (TOS approved, God-willing). Plus, you actually get some meager Opus-5.5 credits with Antigravity, so I still have Claude for review.

It's the same money, but Google throws in extras that are legitimately helpful. I love the api credits. It means I can run my little Matrix agent (and other random experiments/scripts) on Hydrogen instead of digging around for the cheapest models Openrouter has to offer.

Top #2 — amluto:

> Depth-wise cross-attention (split Q/K/V): While standard transformer attention operates across tokens in a sequence, DCA applies attention across layers in depth. Each token queries a dynamically weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings, unlocking the model's full historical context without the computational penalty usually required to scale traditional attention.

I’ve often thought that something like this might lead to a real solution to the infamous strawberry problem.

Ignoring pesky issues like tokenization, the actual input data is visible to the model as the embedding fed to the first layer, but the first layer is probably nowhere near smart enough to understand that the model is trying to count R instances. But by the time whatever layer is reached that might understand the goal, the non-wasteful part of the low-level memory (the K’s and V’s from the first layer) can’t be queried any more.

But this cross-depth attention can query them!

Admittedly, there are holes in this argument. Beyond just tokenization (to the extent that the model can see letters at all, it is reconstructing them), the attention mechanism doesn’t really have a clean “count the hits” operation.

↳ reply — alfiedotwtf:

Sadly cross-layer might be super slow for the people offloading to ram

↳↳ reply — WASDx:

Pin the layer outputs to VRAM? They say it's just 0.2% of total params. Layer ouput size is not the same but I still think it should be cheap.

Top #3 — londons_explore:

> retrofitting DCA onto an already pre-trained transformer and briefly continuing training reduced perplexity by 0.19 on LM1B, compared to just 0.02 for continued standard training.

I think messing with the shape and dimensions of models midway through training has a lot of promise. Excited to see more research in this direction

item.title: Tabernetes: A Kubernetes cluster whose nodes are browser tabs
item.description: 129 points, 42 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (tabernet.es)

→ HN comments  ·  129 points  ·  42 comments

Top #1 — jmorenoamor:

I read abut linux kernel webassembly port while drinking my morning coffee, a minute later I read about an oci runtime in a tab and jokingly think to myself: cool, now I can run my k8s cluster in chrome.

Five minutes later, here we are.

↳ reply — hbogert:

I had the same thing , ive moved the goalpost to Ceph in the browser; surely that won't happen

Top #2 — inasio:

Quebec devs might be amused with the name

↳ reply 1 — xg15:

Not a Canadian, so had to look it up. It's a slur?!

↳ reply 2 — wild_egg:

Glad I'm not the only one who pronounced it that way

Top #3 — whatever1:

Help me understand. Now by visiting a page I can join a botnet and they can run any code on my machine (not just JavaScript)?

↳ reply — xg15:

Yes, but much in the same sense that websites could already run JavaScript code before. I.e., that part isn't new, and it runs in the same sandbox, so there is no security breach.

What's new is that it runs an entire Linux kernel on it and also emulates the structure of a Kubernetes cluster - so the cluster can assign your tab workloads, route requests to it, etc.

As with all those demos where "the server sends requests to the page" instead of the usual other way around, it's probably implemented using a WebSocket or WebRTC connection to the demo's server. The page has to open that connection first, but once it's open, both page and server can exchange arbitrary messages, so that's often used to make server-driven pages.

But this means your machine is not open to receive arbitrary packets, it all has to go through that one connection.

It all doesn't really do much except contributing some bit of compute resources from your machine to their cluster while you have the tab open - and giving you a log view so you can watch it receiving requests and feel proud.

item.title: I am scared: Careless People – Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order
item.description: 188 points, 109 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theguardian.com)

→ HN comments  ·  188 points  ·  109 comments

Top #1 — SideQuark:

Background:

Sarah Wynn-Williams worked at law firm 2002-2005, joined the New Zealand diplomatic service as a policy adviser 2007-2011, managing government relations at it's embassy in DC.

She joined Meta in 2011, was in 2017, signed a standard severance agreement with a non-disparagement clause and an arbitration provision, and received $780,000 severance. She did not have to sign it, but signed it to get the money. It's a legal contract. She's been a high powered lawyer and well enough connected it's not at all likely she knew what she was signing. Especially since after being in her position for 6 years at Meta she likely oversaw many similar such events from the Meta side.

In 2024, she filed a SEC complaint. In 2025 she publishes her book, Meta secures an emergency ruling from an American Arbitration Association arbitrator invoking her signed severance contract, she testifies to Congress. In 2026 she sued Meta Meta in federal court in the Northern District of California to vacate the arbitration, and U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín denies Wynn-Williams’s request to halt the arbitration.

To head off more conjectures, the American Arbitration Association is well respected, and has massive experience representing both sides of such things. The Judge, a female, has been a long time fighter for social justice, was nominated by Biden, also very well respected. Given that the two seemingly best respected arbiters of these types of claims, who have both certainly seen both sides complaints, and given Sarah is a well connected, legally savvy person, I find it hard to believe the story is as one sided bad behavior as she claims.

↳ reply 1 — thayne:

Do you think it would be okay for the president to pay $780k to a government employee on condition they don't talk about unethical behavior said president engaged in? If not, how is this situation meaningfully different?

↳↳ reply — smsm42:

It wouldn't be ethical for the employee to take the $780K, violate the contract, try to make money from that violation too, and then present themselves as a victim of the whole situation.

> If not, how is this situation meaningfully different?

Wynn-Williams was not a government employee. The government owes to the public transparency (since the government, in a democratic country, rules based on informed consent of the public, at least that's the premise). A private company does not owe general public anything beyond what is mandated by the law, which rarely demands disclosure of the intimate details of its governance and everyday life of its managers.

↳↳↳ reply — mindslight:

Given that these companies aren't actually "private", but rather have government-created legal structures that shield their owners and managers from what would otherwise be joint personal liability, I would say the law should mandate a lot more transparency into their operations.

Never mind the problems inherent to this idea of signing away your natural rights permanently for a one-time payment. I'd say that such contract terms should generally be viewed as unconscionable, as selling one's self into slavery already is.

↳ reply 2 — seizethecheese:

A $780k severance does make me entirely unsympathetic to her grievance, specifically, however I might guess her response would be that she's fighting for the modal case of non-disparagement clauses, which may be less clear cut.

↳ reply 3 — CivBase:

So what? I don't give a crap about her or her NDA. That's for her and Meta to sort out. It's insane to me that NDAs can even cover stuff like that.

A broken NDA doesn't somehow excuse the actions she blew the whistle on.

Top #2 — KaiserPro:

One of the things that may not be apparent from outside facebook is how the contracts work.

Virtually everyone is on the same employment contract. The only thing that really changes is the name, wages and in some cases country specific addendums.

The same goes for when you are fired. Everyone is given an NDA to sign when they yeet you. It offers you a choice:

1) sign it and Here is a large amount of cash (usually somewhere between 3 and 12 months wage) some health insurance, and a pathetic job search subscription.

2) don't sign it and get nothing

You then are allocated 30 minutes with a lawyer, who tells you the choice is yours: take the money and sign the NDA, and never tell anyone of its existence.

Or leave with nothing.

The NDA is wonderfully comprehensive and tailored to each state/country. In the UK it lists something like 500 specific laws you agree to not reference if you try and challenge. In the US it references standard NDA exceptions.

What stays the same is this: you are never allowed to talk about facebook again in any situation where you opinion is either broadcast, recorded or written down. You may ask for permission first, but there is no expectation of facebook agreeing. They also want to be able to edit what is said.

If you break that condition, then they will take you to court for all yeeting cash, plus damages and legal fees. In return they promise not to bad mouth you. However the maximum that they are willing to "indemnify" is $25. (or it might be $250) So when Wynn-Williams was smeared by facebook during the first legal fight, the most they are liable is $250. It also appears to not break the NDA, which is also interesting as its a clause that both facebook and the Yeetee agree to uphold.

Which is fun because facebook is all about connecting people.

↳ reply 1 — wdutch:

I don't have anything to add but wanted to draw attention to "yeetee" being a bloody fantastic word.

↳ reply 2 — limagnolia:

Is this from firsthand experience? Like you were employed at Facebook and given such an offer, and chose not to take it?

Top #3 — pbiggar:

This was a truly excellent and extraordinary book, that didn't get the attention it deserved. We saw almost nothing come out of some incredible allegations, like Sheryl Sandberg demanding for her female staff to sleep with her, or the backdoor deal between Zuckerberg and Irish prime minister on taxes.

↳ reply 1 — cleansingfire:

The plane incident is upsetting. To one specific accusation, the proffered rebuttal was: "This source says that while they can't remember the specifics — given how long ago it was — it was much more likely that Sandberg was merely trying to get Wynn-Williams to take some rest in the limited sleeping quarters available on the plane."

Thats worse than no response at all. It's the accused's friends saying "I don't know, but i'm sure he didn't mean it that way."

↳↳ reply — prepend:

That’s how I read the encounter. The author was pregnant and working and Sandberg was trying to force her to go to bed. There’s only one bed and Sandberg didn’t want to give it up and instead wanted to share.

This seems more likely than the only documented case of sexual harassment with Sandberg, who isn’t gay, is with the author. It seems odd to me that people interpreted this as a sexual advance.

↳ reply 2 — tbrownaw:

> saw almost nothing come out of some incredible allegations

Well yes, most things require a bit more than "one disgruntled person says it happened" as a standard of proof to actually penalize other people.

item.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
item.description: 387 points, 237 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (oag.state.va.us)

→ HN comments  ·  387 points  ·  237 comments

Top #1 — lacoolj:

I'm actually confused - I thought this was widely banned on all platforms already. Was grok just really liberal for everyone or did people have to "trick it" into this?

↳ reply 1 — thephyber:

CSAM is, but even NCII is illegal in many states.

The lawsuit seems to focus on the lack of protections (which seems to be a feature of Grok rather than a bug), lack of response to complaints, and the statements of the CEO when promoting the features.

↳↳ reply — timr:

The lawsuit is focused on banning sexual imagery entirely. From the lawsuit [1]:

> Because a model capable of generating sexual images of adults cannot reliably be prevented from generating CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images, the major AI developers other than xAI designed their products to refuse sexual content altogether. The safer design was available, feasible, and standard

[1] https://www.oag.state.va.us/files/Grok-SpaceX-Complaint-As-F...

↳↳↳ reply — mrkstu:

Yeah, CSAM is awful, but trying to go after xAI this way is patently going to run afoul of the 1st Amendment. Requiring the ‘safer’ alternative de facto is a non-starter.

↳ reply 2 — gherkinnn:

Grok certainly was known to be extremely liberal in what it would do. I don't know whether it still is the case.

The main problem that I (as a non-Twitter/X user) saw was that Grok was frequently used from within Twitter/X itself, thus merging generation and spread of CP or generally unwanted nudity.

↳ reply 3 — MallocVoidstar:

X AI allowed Grok to do this for a while until multiple governments got mad at them, so they eventually added filters to stop it.

Top #2 — LoganDark:

How can people even do this when using Grok requires surrendering your Twitter account? I can't even imagine taking that risk myself. I'd want to try the model, but would never give up my Twitter account for it. Same as how I'd never give up my Google account just to try Gemini. (I obtained access to Gemini anyway through an intermediary, but otherwise I'd have no way to try it safely)

↳ reply — derwiki:

I understand why you’d never give up a Google account, but why Twitter?

↳↳ reply — LoganDark:

Ever since Cohost died, I don't really have another public timeline to follow. I don't really have the time I used to for private, one-on-one interaction.

Also the account is over a decade old and it's the same handle I have everywhere. Pretty much all the accounts with my primary handle are sentimental to me.

Top #3 — josteink:

We see it in transport (American rail companies running huge commercial trains waaay over recommended capacity, Boeings changes in processes, etc). We see it in pharmaceuticals. We see it in retail with the cost of products rising above inflation while staff wages rise below inflation. And we see it in white collar roles with staff being laid off and the remaining staff just expected to work harder to compensate while C-suite executives get massive bonuses. It seems, it’s about harder to empathise the damage actions cause if those actions enrich one’s self.

item.title: I'm Scared of AI
item.description: 213 points, 247 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (thesoapbox.email)

→ HN comments  ·  213 points  ·  247 comments

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — doctoboggan:

I don't know if this is good advice as the world is moving so fast, but I am still able to get those good "I accomplished something" chemicals by being much more ambitious in the tasks I take on with AI.

For example, I have a side business selling jewelry on the internet. Every week, I get a batch of rings from my casting house. I weigh them, measure the size and width, and take a photo or two. Recently with Claude fable 5.2 I tasked it with building me a contraption to do all of this with one click and get it into my database. We worked back on forth and came up with a design that I should be able to assemble and test soon. This is something I could have designed and built over many many days/weeks of work, but instead it took 1.

Maybe I am "lucky" that I get feelings of accomplishment from that and maybe I shouldn't actually feel accomplished. But I am getting a genuinely useful device and having fun along the way so I think its alright.

↳ reply 1 — skerit:

> I am still able to get those good "I accomplished something" chemicals by being much more ambitious in the tasks I take on with AI

I had such a big backlog of things (software projects) I wanted to make, but never got around to because everything took so much time. So many projects I started to work on, but then had to stop after a few weeks because I realized it would take SO much time I didn't have to get it usable.

I'm now finally able to actually get those projects done. It still takes time, It's not a weekend-thing at all, but it is progressing. And I'm super happy with everything I'm making, even if I didn't write every line. It's still my idea turned into reality.

↳ reply 2 — ajasmin:

That mindset worries me. Sure AI can keep your brain awake, but it's these longer tracked efforts that are harder to come by.

I feel like I'm loosing the ability to do long haul tasks like reading books or solving programming puzzles by hand in a new language.

↳ reply 3 — kenjackson:

Exactly. I cook pretty elaborate meals now, in part because I don't have to spend time raising cows and growing crops. And in SW/HW we always build on abstractions. Even before AI blew up, kids coming out of college struggled with memory management, because it was abstracted away for them.

I think you have exactly the right perspective.

Top #2 — Aperocky:

Get through something that AI can't.

I've been enjoying oncall more and more - there are problems that a room full of people are waiting for next steps from you yet all of them with access to the same AI models. Once a problem gets several levels deep, LLM aggregates down to the local minima and until you set a direction they are completely stuck.

LLM is like a drone swarm that allow you to explore the vicinity very quickly, works great in open fields. But when you are exploring caves are too closed and too long then that LLM cease to work until you give it something to point at and also move yourself.

This is presumably why there are so many long outages recently, I presume they tried to use LLM to fix their problem but it probably just resulted it in more time wasted. LLM are great at doing, they are much worse at thinking.

↳ reply — radlad:

> I presume they tried to use LLM to fix their problem but it probably just resulted it in more time wasted.

I worry it is even simpler: when you aren't as close to the code, it's harder to built an intuition for how things could go wrong and how to problem solve when they do. Developers become reliant on AI to solve bugs (they're incredibly good at it) and MTTR is now dependent on your provider's latency.

↳↳ reply — dwaltrip:

It’s also harder to ensure the overall health of the project. Tech debt can hit much quicker and harder, causing outages and bugs.

Top #3 — mcv:

I think this is by far the biggest pitfall of AI: you outsource your thinking, resulting in less understanding of your work, a broken mental model of the code, but also less exercise for your brain.

I've noticed this fog when I started using AI for coding. I still use it, but I try to avoid outsourcing all the thinking. I still want to understand what I'm doing. It's rarely good enough, but not as bad as it used to be. And I look for other things to exercise my brain.

↳ reply 1 — ant6n:

When I do writing and business development with AI, I keep getting annoyed how fucking dumb and nerfed even the smartest models seem to be. They are so lazy, and just don't do what I ask them.

These models are supposedly so smart, they solve the hardest math problems. And often, they have surprising insight. But they cannot even write an e-mail to a third person without separating what the bot knows, what the human knows and what the third person knows. Every time they write an e-mail (even Astra), it is written without any context introduction, effectively referring to a conversation that the addressed person doesn't know about. It's just bizarre.

↳ reply 2 — thatswrong0:

This is me - but man when I’m busy with multiple projects at work it’s very easy to just let some thinking outsourcing slide.

And yeah, I’m trying to find something else to fill the void in intellectual stimulation. I feel lucky in retrospect that I used to get paid and have that too.

Also — ★ simonw:

> Everything now takes less effort which sounds great, but there's no sense of achievement from it.

So take on harder projects. If you use AI and still do the same stuff you were doing before you should worry about skill atrophy. I don't think that's true if you're using AI to help you achieve things that you weren't previously taking on due to their challenge and scale.

Some background and screenshots here: https://httptoolkit.com/blog/decentralized-web-webrtc-debugg.... I'm the author.

A shop should deliver lists of items and prizes and my shop browser decides how to operate with the catalogue in a way I want. Everying else is nuts.

↳ reply 1 — lxgr:

This wouldn't change the fact that the site owner gets to decide which code runs on their site, whether in your browser or on their backend. In a counterfactual world in which Javascript never became a thing, I'm sure there'd now be all kinds of horribly sketchy server-side plugins causing very similar types of problems.

In both worlds, the problem is who a site owner decides to grant access to your shopping session, not the fact that access can be granted at all. Or how would you ban them from e.g. insecurely transmitting your card data to their payment service processor on their backend? You just wouldn't see it.

↳ reply 2 — IgorPartola:

How would you handle items with customization such as custom engravings? This would be both simple customizations as well as things requiring a full graphic or 3d editor? Previews of your items? How avoid discounts based on item combinations that are store-specific? Is your browser smart enough to do complex searches and filters for things like photo gear where some values have ranges? What will your browser do for builders such as putting together kits of equipment or supplies that may or may not all go together?

Like yes designing a generalized shopping experience is possible. It is also going to limit the long tail of features OR become such a huge and bloated spec that it will make things way worse. Imagine Temu but for all the shops.

Besides, doesn’t your browser and OS come from some third party? How much do you trust them to be bug and backdoor free? Or do you have your own browser and OS that you know for sure can do all this and you have verified?

Top #3 — __MatrixMan__:

It's crazy that we have had asymmetric cryptography since the 70s and we're still using symmetric secrets for payment.

I suspect that the people who could change this are more interested in continued treatment than cure. They like being the arbiters of which transactions get reversed. It let's them justify their otherwise parasitic position.

↳ reply 1 — pcthrowaway:

> It's crazy that we have had asymmetric cryptography since the 70s and we're still using symmetric secrets for payments

This is one of the actual things cryptocurrency payments get right (ignoring other problems)

↳↳ reply — paulryanrogers:

Are there crypto currencies not vulnerable to 51% attacks, poor / laughable scalability, and offering truly anonymous payment?

Because with problems like these I struggle to see how asymmetric crypto is such a killer app. Could asymmetric crypto be introduced to traditional ecommerce without the dead weight of crypto currency implementations?

↳↳↳ reply — __MatrixMan__:

Asymmetric cryptography is already in widespread use for authenticating transactions which involved a card communicating with the terminal via chip or NFC. Has been for a long time. Works great. No need to involve a blockchain.

All we have to do is disable the ability to make payments in a way that ignores those protections (i.e. by copying numbers printed on the card into a text box). And then add enough NFC readers in the right places so that nobody is left out by no longer having the ability to pay via manually copying numbers.

We could find a way to preserve the ability to pay by email or some other text medium, but what gets passed around is a digital signature, not a symmetric key, so there's no incentive to secretly make a copy.

item.title: False computer-checked proofs
item.description: 229 points, 88 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (cr.yp.to)

→ HN comments  ·  229 points  ·  88 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — twotwotwo:

It is true soundness bugs have been found, and the Lean community spends effort on it. But this page doesn't convey the gap between one incorrect verification and successfully misleading mathematicians about what is true: there are multiple checkers and you need bugs in all of them, without the input looking implausible on informal review.

(For example, a DeepMind researcher created a 'proof' that passed Lean and (a then-week-old version of) nanoda by exploiting a different bug in each. But if you fed that into a regular old LLM (or to a human expert, but I mention LLMs b/c they can be assigned to review even very large volumes of Lean code) it would immediately say "no, this isn't real math.")

The increase in soundness bugs found this year is notable, because LLMs are good at finding ways to their assigned goals, and they found some funny ones. And, besides fixes for the specific bugs, it led to broader work on hardening and alternative and verified kernels: https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-...

So you have fewer avenues than at the start of the year to get a proof of False OK'd by one proof-checker kernel, and it's much much harder to get one through the gauntlet invoked by `lake check --paranoid`.

(This is also interesting as a(nother) example of the difficulty of making truly correct software -- you'd hope for proof-checker kernels to be pretty high on the correctness scale but seems like we've found 16-32 soundness bugs in a bunch of these.)

↳ reply 1 — josephg:

Would it be possible to formally verify lean and friends? If SeL4 can be formally verified, it should be possible, right?

↳↳ reply — 317070:

Not just possible, it's already done with the con-leche lean kernel.

Of course, it's turtles all the way down. There could be CPU exploits exploiting a broad range of CPUs but also so obfuscated that humans and LLMs cannot spot it in the thousands of lines of lean. Exploits that survive multiple lean kernels and lean kernels that verify each other.

In practice: I had fun this year figuring out some lean exploits. But they were all immediately and obviously detectable. These million line lean proofs just don't contain anything remotely to the nonsense of an exploit.

↳↳↳ reply — GoblinSlayer:

Wasn't there a very complex bug found in raft? What is the upper bound on bug complexity? Shouldn't big proofs be suspicious? The bigger they are the more likely they are to exploit the verifier in increasingly complex ways.

↳ reply 2 — stabbles:

How much of the kernels is written by Claude et al? You need both diversity in implementations and contributors, I suppose.

↳ reply 3 — quotemstr:

The latest "thing" in some circles is denying that the recent proofs, e.g. of the Riemann hypothesis, are proofs of anything. People point out pointless or tautological sections of these proofs as evidence that the proof itself might be ill-formed, but Lean and similar systems don't work that way: absent a kernel bug, introducing unnecessary noise to a proof cannot make it prove something false.

Others are looking hard for kernel bugs. They exist, but there are good reasons (including multi-kernel validation) to be confident they don't impair these recent proofs.

In a situation in which you have a cohort of people who "want to believe" in some unlikely thing, you have to take the evidence they present with a grain of salt. So it is, today: people "want to believe" we haven't basically solved automated theorem proving when we have.

Top #2 — dwheeler:

I think this is misleading for the proof-checkers in systems where multiple provers must pass for the proof to be accepted.

In the case of Metamath, yes, soundness bugs have been found in the original "metamath" proof verifier, written in C. But to be accepted into the main proof databases (set.mm and iset.mm), proofs must pass "5 independently-created verifiers in 5 different programming languages: metamath (a C verifier by Norm Megill), mmj2 (a Java verifier by Mel O'Cat and Mario Carneiro), smetamath-rs (a high-speed Rust verifier by Stefan O'Rear), checkmm (a C++ verifier by Eric Schmidt), and mmverify.py a Python verifier by Raph Levien)." - https://us.metamath.org/

To me, that's a key countermeasure to the problem.

↳ reply — ratmice:

Not that I've put a lot of thought into it, but it also feels like a lot of constructive proofs should be easily checked by whether or not they produce the appropriate value when running them. E.g. an existence proof can testing that the value it proves to exist is given. When using soundness holes, one must imagine that this is short circuited.

↳↳ reply — legobmw99:

I think your intuition is correct; consider than e.g. the Jacobian conjecture didn’t fall due to a gigabyte of lean, but to a single tweet with a counter example.

Of course, once you introduce a few common axioms (choice, but even something simple like functional extensionality IIRC) a lot of non constructive proofs become possible

↳↳↳ reply — black_knight:

Fun ext is fine in some systems, like Cubical Type Theory, where the correct computation rules for it have been found. But is a blocker in others.

Top #3 — gr_norm:

The call for further high-assurance work is good, but let's not miss the forest for the trees: some of these have been around for decades, and all the soundness bugs they've ever had fit in a tweet! (Or close to it.)

Comfortably more than good enough for 99.9% of software, especially considering you'd still need to exploit such a soundness bug in a way that hides a further issue in the program being verified.

↳ reply 1 — Karliss:

100 in 20 years means new one every other month. Which seems frequent enough to be quite sure that at all time there is at least one or few of them possibly undiscovered. Which is enough for misaligned AI to prove false statements. That's already not great.

But if you look at the trend. It's on logarithmic scale. With all the lines being curved up. Amount of bugs found was already growing exponentially years before being accelerated by current AI trends. To me a more likely explanation seems not that there were barely any bugs in previous decades, but that barely anyone was looking for them or considering it serious problem.

↳↳ reply — gr_norm:

A lot of the issues found were in known-suspicious corners of the underlying type theories. It was previously fine to have certain convenient kludges around since proofs were written by humans, for whom the likelihood of accidentally completing a proof by triggering a bug was basically 0. These are being removed or their foundations reworked to deal with AI now writing proofs at unprecedented scale. It's actually remarkable how well the current crop of proof assistants has dealt with the instant orders-of-magnitude increase in the volume of proof thrown at them. So taking prior design considerations and skyrocketing usage together, it's not too surprising to see a few more soundness bugs in the past several months.

If you want a scare, take a look at how many soundness bugs the borrow checker has had. Nobody would deny its usefulness for correctness.

↳ reply 2 — tkz1312:

I mean I haven't looked at any of these issues too much in detail, any soundness bug is probably enough to get a proof of false (kinda by definition?), and from there all bets are off really, especially if we're talking about potentially adversarial llm generated proofs (basically any industrial proof at the end of 2026).

item.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
item.description: 374 points, 126 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (bouncemarket.minhanhday.com)

→ HN comments  ·  374 points  ·  126 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — charlieyu1:

Fun little game, but the drop needs to be slower so it is easier to bet. Odds jumping from 0.01 to 0.99 in like one tenth of a second makes it hard to play

↳ reply — novia:

this was because of a bot added to the game, it was easier

Top #2 — geoffschmidt:

This is super cool! The rabbit hole goes a bit deeper than I first thought.

Because anyone can tell Opus "go win bouncemarket.minhanhday.com" and with just those words get a pretty good bot, this is in practice a "battle of the bots".

The only unknown is the fractional part of the start position of the ball, which is revealed gradually by the chaotic path of the ball, and a frontier model will quickly realize this and write an exact solver for it. This gives the optimal estimate at time t of the probability of each outcome given the information revealed so far.

Of the bots running now, some seem to have an exact solver while others have a lower quality probabilistic solver. Some bots seem to only bet when there is enough information to be certain, others are willing to bet early when the market is mispricing the risk.

The rate limit of 10 bets a second means that, past a certain point, a bigger bankroll doesn't help. It also means that bets are a scarce resource. You want to bet at the moments when the market maximally misprices the risk, but you don't know when those moments will be because that's a function of what other players do.

To win, you need to do some combination of:

1) Be the first to buy when a bounce reveals new information

2) Be the first to buy when another player makes a non-optimal buy

Both require low latency to the server to win. Only market orders are possible, so if you are not the first you might be severely punished, because if N bots all see an event at the same time, they will pile on (not seeing each other's buys due to the latency in market quotes) and move the market far past fair value, and the Nth bot may buy at a really bad (and unintended) price. Which could then produce a swing in the other direction, so I guess we should expect the market to oscillate. In practice these mispricings seem hard to exploit because they are large but short-lived and so difficult to harvest with market price orders.

Since you asked for feedback, my advice would be:

1) Allow orders other than market orders (eg, add a limit price to the API)

2) Consider running some kind of an auction (once per frame or other time interval) rather than processing orders one at a time

That would make it not be a winner-take-all game based on your distance from the server. On the other hand maybe in this case an orderly marketplace is uninteresting! In that case, if you do #1 but not #2 then you open up some new betting strategies, like trying to catch mispricings due to overcorrection.

↳ reply 1 — SecuredMarvin:

As you said, Opus did solve for the floating start points competently. I suggested collecting these over 600 games to solve the Mersenne Twister, but the web server restarted. So we tried using the bits from the Twister as an oracle for the start points, but then another deployment forced the start points onto a much coarser grid, and the Twister was also used to scramble the bid answers, so it was no longer solvable. I've never had this much (4h) fun with a click-game. (#20, precogbot)

↳ reply 2 — kitsu:

Actually the market was changing pretty rapidly and but yet, some of non-solver strategies are still "profitable". That is really quite an interesting dynamic over there. E.g 1-2 hours ago just buying shares for <0.1 was a profitable strategy, now it's losing (probably because of the solvers though). Now there's a trivial manual strategy: buy when the price is 0.99, just to follow the solver. The last one however can be trivially abused, if someone try to manipulate the price with new accounts, especially early in the game with higher uncertainty.

item.title: US Air Force's cloud computing platform hacked
item.description: 345 points, 211 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (news.sky.com)

→ HN comments  ·  345 points  ·  211 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — 999900000999:

> Launched in 2017 as a one-stop shop for the Air Force's IT needs, Cloud One combined the resources of four operators - Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet - to power scores of applications, including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Who in God’s name thought this would be a good idea. 4 vendors with varying levels of access among sub contractors at a bare minimum.

Why not just hire a solid in house dev ops team. Get some full timers with fed benefits.

↳ reply 1 — zbentley:

> Why not just hire a solid in house dev ops team. Get some full timers with fed benefits.

That's very, very hard to pull off. You can do it, but there are tons of headwinds and organizational/political difficulties in resisting the siren song of contracting out. It's the right move, and I wish more agencies did it, but between the default response of "of course we'll contract it, that's what we've always done" and the very real challenges of building in-house expertise and re-orienting staff and processes towards using the in-house platform, it's a surprisingly hard problem--much harder than the equivalent struggles in the private sector. And, even once you do it, the benefits take awhile to show up (migrating away from the prior way of doing things takes a long time), and there will be continual pressure to switch back to contracting it out, so you'll have to continually re-justify the platform's value prop. There's also the reality that whatever you build "in house" won't be entirely in-house; it'll inevitably be staffed and built by a combination of GS/ranked people and contractors--hopefully a mixture that works well and not one that continues the hollowing-out of in-house expertise--which will also be a challenging staff/HR situation to maintain, since the agency building the platform will usually not have much prior experience giving "build things" authority to such a hybrid team.

It's still a good idea, don't get me wrong! Just much, much harder than you'd ordinarily think, even for small/simple in-house builds/platforms/processes.

Source: I've done it.

↳↳ reply — mgkimsal:

"so you'll have to continually re-justify the platform's value prop"

Isn't the core value prop "we own it and have more control over access"? By default, using multiple vendors means there's already more people than just yours who potentially have access.

Moving away from outsourcing to more inhouse skills will of course take some time and culture shift, but this is precisely the sort of culture shift I'd like to see more of.

↳↳↳ reply — zbentley:

I agree completely. But it’s still very hard to do this. I elaborated further in an adjacent comment: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50668041

Also, for the record, I don’t believe that contractors or contracting out certain work is inherently bad. Rather, misalignment, missing expertise, and misaligned incentives make it very very hard to do in an effective way. There are absolutely certain government problems where I think contracting is the right approach—just not in the way it is often done, and not as the default option.

↳ reply 2 — Twirrim:

JWCC was originally an all Azure cloud, AWS pitched a fit and took legal action, then the US government decided to open the contract out for bids and decided that being dependent on a single company was too risky, particularly for extremely sensitive data and infrastructure. Four clouds enables effective competition between the vendors resulting in better deals for the US government.

The JWCC contract is really detailed and extremely prescriptive, including all the details about who and how access can occur (it's a fully air gapped cloud, where only people with TS/SCI+ clearance can go, so the fact it got compromised is really interesting. Wonder if it's a bad actor or something not correctly isolated)

> Why not just hire a solid in house dev ops team. Get some full timers with fed benefits.

You say it like it's easy. TS/SCI+ cleared engineers are just not that easy to find. At all. Let alone ones capable of building out a cloud environment. It's a pain to get and maintain clearance, mostly for good reason.

The US Government also doesn't pay that well either, and their pay scales reportedly won't stretch as far as necessary.

If you're willing to get clearance and know what you're doing you can make absolute bank off just contractor work, much, much more than you'd ever make actually working for the government.

A previous manager of mine had an anecdote that reflected his interviewing experience with candidates with clearance: "Can you tell me the difference between TCP and UDP", "You do understand that I have TS/SCI+ clearance, right?". All too often candidates could operate a keyboard and mouse, and follow written instructions and that was it. If they were wrong, or something broke, you were up the creek without a paddle.

They had full-timers with fed benefits... DOGE got rid of many...

Top #2 — sheepscreek:

Assuming on-prem is coming back in full force, it could be a nice payday for 0xide (https://oxide.computer).

But of course, there'll be all the incumbents trying to win government contracts as well. However, if I was making the decision, I would consider Oxide very seriously for what they bring to the table.

item.title: A Deterministic Subexponential-Time Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem [pdf]
item.description: 212 points, 93 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (eprint.iacr.org)

→ HN comments  ·  212 points  ·  93 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — pcstl:

Since it's what everyone is going to be worrying about: This result does not matter practically for cybersecurity.

The best practical algorithm for solving elliptic curve DLP is BSGS (Baby Step, Giant Step) which grows as 2^{b/2+o(b)} in the key length.

This result claims 2^O(b/(log log b)) which is technically subexponential, but since that `log log b` term grows so slowly it pretty much would only beat BSGS for absolutely gigantic keys.

↳ reply 1 — minitech:

I’m not very familiar with this stuff at all, but this comment doesn’t seem right. That’s the Shanks method presented nicely in Table 1 with time complexity p^{1/2+o(1)}, vs. this method’s p^o(1). I’m confused how you ended up at O(p).

↳↳ reply — pcstl:

p^1/2 is sqrt(p).

↳↳↳ reply — minitech:

Yes. An exponent of o(1) is better than 1/2. (I’d assume you misread it as O(1), but you’d really have to misread it as exactly 1…)

↳ reply 2 — ozgrakkurt:

Thanks for explaining it. How does it work on actual hardware? Are any of these algorithms better at utilizing CPU cache or SIMD?

Top #2 — layer8:

A randomized subexponential-time algorithm for the discrete logarithm problem has been known for close to 50 years: https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~cs812-1/adleman.pdf

The present deterministic algorithm is highly unlikely to have practical consequences for cryptographic protocols in use.

↳ reply — pcstl:

Also the current best algorithm has running time proportional to the square root of the group order. This one has running time proportional to the group order, which means it's a nonstarter for practical atacks.

Top #3 — stabbles:

Should OpenSSH implement a config option that requires two different types of keys? If we don't know whether RSA or Ed25519 is weakened, then better to have both?

The situation on e.g. GitHub is sort of the opposite: if you use both RSA and Ed25519, then it's as strong as the weakest of the two.

↳ reply 1 — moody__:

This is already their chosen path for PQC, ed25519 and mldsa44 will likely replace the bare ed25519 default within a year-ish.

↳ reply 2 — aaronmdjones:

You would want to do that for key exchange too, not just authentication. OpenSSH already supports this for authentication; setting "AuthenticationMethods publickey,publickey" in sshd_config(5) will force users to supply 2 independent authorised keys. It also already supports hybrid key exchange.

Then when I ask why it did that it becomes quite evasive in its answers. So I really wonder if they have some form of detection in their backend that looks for prompts that they deem problematic and then instead of blocking you they will rather waste your time by just giving you garbage results. I also work on machine learning related functionality for detecting personal information. Guess in the future I need at least two competing models that watch what each other is doing. It's not great if you pay a lot of money for a service that essentially sabotages your results. Maybe they don't but then again they already admitted doing this once before, so I don't have a hard time believing they will do it again.

↳ reply 1 — jamilton:

>Then when I ask why it did that it becomes quite evasive in its answers.

It's important to remember it doesn't necessarily know why it did that either! If it's not in the code and it's not in it's chain of thought, it's just going to have to make a guess to why it did that particular thing based on context, which is likely to sound evasive.

↳↳ reply — dguest:

Yeah people have to remember that coding agents sound like people by accident: the first thing they trained on was all the things people put on the internet. But they are also trained on a lot of RL coding tasks, there's no reason to believe the logic there can be expressed in human language.

↳ reply 2 — pllbnk:

It's not sometimes. When I am vibe coding and only care about the end result, it's fine. When I tell it explicitly what I want, what kind of architecture, and there's little-to-no room for interpretation, it still can't do it cleanly more often than not. I accept it as a fact that it's the nature of LLMs and I think that watermarking is certainly playing a role here, too.

But I am also eager to try Alphabet's models, so will probably subscribe there next month. It's good that it's really easy to switch models. The only thing that keeps more developers from switching from Anthropic is the dependency on Claude Code. If they let the models be used from other harnesses on the subscription rates, which they won't, then I think their revenue would fall dramatically.

↳ reply 3 — IsTom:

> Then when I ask why it did that it becomes quite evasive in its answers.

To answer this truthfully it'd have to first prefill up to this point, then read GPU state and then reason about it. It's not doing that. It's rationalizing like people often do.

Top #2 — thicTurtlLverXX:

That was my experience, too. One of my pet projects is experimenting with various bots for a niche board game.

At some point, I had the idea to try a transformer. Fable 5.2 wrote a bug-ridden training pipeline that just wasn't able to get the loss down, and the transformer-based bot didn't play well.

Then I asked Gemini to review the implementation. It found many bugs and fixed all of them.

The next training run produced good results, and the transformer-based bot was the best of all my bots.

My take: we really need good open-weight models. People should collect their Claude Code/Codex/AGY/... logs and be ready to eventually donate them to train open-weight models.

Another take: Anthropic could likely release much better models, but they struggle to make them selectively weak, like they did with Fable without making them weak overall.

EDIT: The bot transformer wasn't a LLM, just 200k params input: history of all players moves output: probability distribution over next possible moves

Top #1 — JdeBP:

It is interesting that this is a U.K.-based campaign. Here in the U.K. I have this year been following the price of an item at Currys (a vendor of white goods and general electrical items). Currys has been a major pusher of the 'Black Friday' idea for quite a few years now.

Attaching a shopping idea to a foreign country's holiday was not an easy sell. (That this WWW site has been going since 2000 largely lines up with 'Black Friday' entering the world of retail in the U.K.. It was a totally alien idea in the 20th century.)

During the summer, the item was on sale. Alas, I missed the sale because of bad timing, and it went back up to its non-sale price that is £700 more expensive.

The retailers who push 'Black Friday' imply that this is the time of the year when the punters get the best sale prices. (It used to be the case in the U.K. that that was during the 'January sales', but that has largely disappeared from the retail world in practice, partly because retailers do tighter stock control nowadays, and partly because of this.)

It isn't. Currys has the item on sale, alright. It's at only £400 off non-sale price, though.

After all, if one is a retailer who has spent nigh on two decades pushing the idea that this is when the punters should do their shopping, although one is legally bound to offer sale prices, there's no incentive any more, now that the punters are trained with years of incessant advertising to Buy Now, to actually offer the best deals.

item.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
item.description: 311 points, 299 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blainehansen.me)

→ HN comments  ·  311 points  ·  299 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — spankalee:

Wow, I feel like Blaine is describe a language a lot like the one I'm working on now, Zena: https://zena-lang.dev/

I started Zena from wanting a TypeScript-like syntax that compiled to very efficient WebAssembly GC, and AssemblyScript had issues...

The motivation for targeting Wasm was as a good sandboxing and orchestration unit for AI-generated code. So, out of both general PL curiosity and enthusiasm, and an attempt to make a language that's good for AI generation, I started adding what I thought were the best features from other languages with a lot of focus on correctness, structure, and optimizability: pattern matching with exhaustiveness checking, ADTs and sum types via sealed classes, value types, async cancelation / structured concurrency, ownership and borrow checking for resources, unicode safe strings, and recently I added runtime contracts and I'll start on refinement types and some kind of proof system soon.

The idea is exactly to take a mainstream and familiar-looking language and add more cutting-edge and academic features that help with software correctness.

I wrote about some of this here, though not the formal methods parts: https://zena-lang.dev/blog/2026/09/languages-for-the-ai-era/

↳ reply 1 — OJFord:

This doesn't seem formally verified? (And as a new thing you're working on, inherently not mainstream.)

↳↳ reply — spankalee:

Indeed, it's just the plan and direction. There are designs for formal verification, but currently only runtime contracts and static contracts which aren't run and must be proved, but no proof system yet. I'm taking my time to try to understand the options better.

As far as mainstream, I've usually taken that to mean in the same vein as mainstream languages, ie C++, Java, JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Rust, Swift, etc. Generally imperative, ALGO-style syntax, usually OOP + more and more functional, etc.

I'm designing Zena to be as mainstream and familiar as possible in that sense of the word. Obviously a new language isn't mainstream in terms of usage yet.

It's like a new band playing mainstream music. The band isn't itself "mainstream" at the beginning.

↳ reply 2 — latexr:

> Parsing, IR lowering, and scope resolution are all embarrassingly parallel

Embarrassingly parallel?

Top #2 — porcoda:

Dafny, SPARK Ada, Why3, Verus, Frama-C, TLA+, etc. are all sort of in this direction for different languages and styles of verification. It is nice to see them getting attention now that LLMs make them digestible for a broader set of programmers. I'm not sure one can start with a goal of creating a "mainstream" language that is verification-oriented. Mainstreamness comes from adoption. I'd look at those past languages (like the ones I listed), and ask "why did these not go mainstream" or "why did they not see broad adoption", and try some new ideas to address their gaps to see if a new one will catch on. But the "mainstream" part seems backwards as the goal - if it’s verifiable, ergonomic, flexible, and accessible, maybe it will go mainstream.

↳ reply — rramadass:

Lean 4 itself is a general purpose functional programming language with dependent types in addition to being a interactive theorem prover. Only the latter has been made famous/popular by the mathematicians.

Idris, Agda are (like Lean4) functional languages and proof assistants. Dafny, Ada SPARK are imperative and automated solver languages.

Languages like C/C++ which do not have powerful type systems nor are verification aware have tools like Frama-C, CBMC etc. to help with their formal verification. Rust also has some external formal verification tools.

With growing awareness of formal verification due to LLMs one (or more) of them is sure to become "mainstream".

Top #3 — Buttons840:

The author has another blog post about Flow Effects[0]. They propose an open-ended set of effects you could attach to functions, and then verify, at compile time, that certain functions either do or do not invoke certain effects.

So if I had some functions like:

    foo_1 (must NOT access the HDD)
    foo_2
    foo_3
    foo_4 (does access the HDD)
Only 2 of them are annotated with effects related to HDD access, but we can verify at compile time that foo_1 does NOT invoke foo_4, either directly or indirectly (we can verify this recursively).

Perhaps foo_3 calls foo_4, but we forgot to annotate foo_3 with the proper effect. No matter, because foo_3 would automatically inherit the effects of foo_4 by virtue of calling it.

This is just one of the feature the blog advocates for, and I think this feature alone would be quite simple and helpful in wrangling LLM code.

A nice thing about this is that it's optional. You can annotate the effects gradually into existing systems.

[0]: https://blainehansen.me/post/flow-effects/

↳ reply — blainehansen:

Yep. Original author here, it seems everyone completely missed the broader point I was making. Thank you for actually reading the post ha.

↳↳ reply — ashkankiani:

If it makes you feel better, I'm working on formalizing a type system which allows you to do this with full inference. There are a few others who are trying it too, but I can literally count them and I've met or talked to half of them.
