item.title: Citroën Hydraulic System
item.description: 133 points, 45 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (citroenet.org.uk)

→ HN comments  ·  133 points  ·  45 comments

Top #1 — jacquesm:

I've owned 1x2cV, 3xDS/ID (one a donor car), 2x Xantia and 1 XM. All of them had something that very few modern cars have, which is that they were quirky but interesting, both technology wise and to drive. If you knew them well you could do just about anything with them.

Anyway, about that hydraulic system: a friend of mine who lived in IJmuiden was improving his house. To do so he had bought a load of concrete tiles in Amsterdam on an impulse (really, really good deal). So he called me up and asked if I could come and help shift them to IJmuiden. When I got there there was this absolutely massive pile and I figured this is not going to end well. I had dropped the rear seat (which you could pull out fairly easily, but the back cushions stayed in place) so there was quite a bit of room and two tiles fit side by side. So we stacked them pretty much to the ceiling and miraculously, the car just kept on adjusting ride height and never gave any sign that it couldn't handle the load. All of the tiles fit. Then we drove to IJmuiden. It all went well until we hit the overpass over the road between Amsterdam and Haarlem on A9. The car took a bit of a dive into the dip and then came back out and came back out further than it went in. And did it again. Before long it was bouncing like a ball with the rear (which was pretty heavy) coming off the ground. I lost some speed and finally got the car to sit by the side of the road, still bouncing. Engine off, let the whole thing come to rest, engine back on, everything fine. We drove the last bit really slow, just in case.

So, that's what an undampened servo oscillation looks like in a hydraulic system. After unloading the backseat went back in and it was just like before. DE-70-72, whoever has it now, that car is as solid as they come (it is still registered, this was more than 20 years ago, the car is from 1968 and it has been off the road for a long time).

The hydraulic computer sits behind the left front wheel well behind a separate shield and it is super complicated, if you have to fix it you better know what you're doing.

↳ reply — user_7832:

Thanks for that anecdote, I've seen you around the site a fair bit but never knew you liked such cars.

I learnt about this suspension system myself after seeing an (unfortunately not very well maintained) Citroen somewhere near Rijswik. (Back home in India we really don't have a lot of old Citroens.)

By an interesting coincidence, while walking past the car park today I was wishing for a more exciting car - one that is "properly" engineered - and was thinking of this suspension setup.

Ladder frames, or even tubed space chassis, for that matter, can be far more robust. Layering 2 suspensions in a vehicle could probably reduce vibration and improve comfort a significant bit. I wonder why GT cars never appeared to do this.

Even standalone, this suspension is in my opinion an absolute engineering marvel, and I really wish more companies beyond just Rolls Royce would care to use it today.

But I suppose the finance guys and bean counters end up winning.

↳↳ reply — jacquesm:

If it was long ago, that most likely was my car. I used to live on Beatrixlaan in Rijswijk, then we moved to IJmuiden. It didn't look like much on the outside but underneath it was as good as new. Blue car with a white roof, red interior. If more recent then someone else.

My current car is very much like that as well, it is a '97, totally restored underneath and tech wise but the skin was left as I found it.

Top #2 — Svip:

Generally goes unnoticed (though not unmentioned), but until after the Xantia, the suspension system also included the brakes and the steering (which would technically not be permitted under modern EU car standards); which meant a leak would eventually not just cause a loss of suspension, but also a loss of steering and braking.

Why incorporate the braking and the suspension? The mechanical height regulator could "feel" how much fluid it needed to fill the suspension with, in order to obtain the desired ride height; which meant it "knew" how heavy the vehicle was loaded, and thus apply the brakes accordingly. This is why in a proper Citroën hydraulic car, the brake pedal feels "weird", in that it doesn't go far down (and quickly becomes hard to press) (the DS tried to make this less confusion by making the pedal a "mushroom" button instead); because the idea is that you should apply gentle braking, and the car will figure out the necessary amount of braking force required (unlike just hitting the pedal like in a normal car, which would result in an almost hard stop).

Why the steering then? I think that's more of a convenience thing, mechanically speaking, as it was already there to provide a form of power steering; though it is funny feeling it getting pumped up (steering was always the last portion to receive fluid during the pumping). At least, as far as I can tell, it has little bearing on the suspension or braking. I know the SM and CX tried the DIRAVI steering, which completely made the steering one way (so you couldn't feel the road); though it was fun to see the steering wheel self-righting even when parked.

Full disclosure: I own a 1974 Citroën DS 23 and a 1998 Citroën Xantia Activa V6.

↳ reply — speedgoose:

I'm very curious, is the Xantia Activa V6 truly the goat of its time or a tiny bit overrated?

I have understood that its famous high speed pass on moose test couldn't be replicated by some, despite modern tires.

My father had a no-turbo diesel Xantia at some point in the 90s. I remember that the car could go up and down, very slowly. It was good for handbrake turns I guess. I remember requesting handbrake turns as a kid.

↳↳ reply — jacquesm:

Short answer: Yes. Slightly longer: I had the privilege of sitting in one on Zandvoort circuit (thanks, Roger) and it was amazing. It took the banks like it was on rails.

Top #3 — frereubu:

When I win the lottery I'm buying a Citroën SM: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citro%C3%ABn_SM Such a beautiful car.

item.title: Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
item.description: 510 points, 437 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (blog.ktz.me)

→ HN comments  ·  510 points  ·  437 comments

Top #1 — loeg:

Author assumes price cartels, but this can be completely explained by supply and demand. Hyperscalars are buying all the storage they can get their hands on; that's it. Manufacturers are loath to ramp up supply (high CapEx), because they'll be underwater if the AI demand evaporates.

↳ reply 1 — miki123211:

I've recently seen an interview with an Anthropic SWE (on Gergely Orosz's X I believe) where she was complaining about how they were having to rewrite from Python to Rust because the hyperscalers weren't giving them the CPU they needed and letting them scale up.

The supply chain issues have gotten so bad that even the frontier labs are suffering from this.

↳↳ reply — dist-epoch:

Would you rather use CPUs to serve HTTP requests in Python or for RL envs for your post-training?

Pretty easy call, even if more CPUs were available.

↳ reply 2 — DanielHB:

Don't explain with cartels what can easily be explained with game theory, all of the manufacturers lose profit margins if any of them ramp up supply significantly.

Sure you could increase the revenue by investing in new production, but you can keep your risks low and increase profit margin instead by investing nothing.

It is the same thing with memory makers.

↳ reply 3 — Cthulhu_:

Arguably this price increase isn't nearly as bad as that of memory, and / or the price of storage has been dropping for years now so this feels more like a correction. I'd argue that without increasing supply / ramping up production, the market will correct eventually as demand stabilizes and drops. (especially when the market crashes, which I still expect to happen - I expect that many of the hundreds/thousands of planned datacenter projects will be cancelled due to various reasons)

Top #2 — joshstrange:

Yep, at the start of the year I bought a 8-bay UNAS before the HD price increases had fully “set” in my brain. It still sits empty because I can’t afford to put drives in it.

I have my hard drive purchase info back a little over a decade and for the past few years (before 2025) I was settling into ~$14/TB. Now it’s _well_ over double that. The only Seagate Exos 20TB (not refurb) on Amazon I can find is $999, ~$50/TB.

It’s a hard time to be homelab-er. I’m eternally grateful that my main server is only like 4-5 years old. I have friends that were forced to upgrade and the RAM costs alone made me sick. In one case they bought half the RAM my server has and paid twice what I paid (aka 4x increase). That said, I’ve never been happier with self-hosting but that makes this harder since I’d love to expand my home lab.

↳ reply — QuiEgo:

It’s a weird time to self host. All of the AI-driven exploits make me super nervous about being an amateur sysadmin with very little time to keep up with this stuff. It used to be fun now it feels like a chore / risk.

↳↳ reply — coldbrewed:

If your self hosted services are behind a VPN, network segmentation gating access to secure trusted devices, workload isolation between your services, and an optional auth proxy gating access, your self hosted env can have functionally no surface area for exploitation.

At a minimum keeping your services behind a VPN drops your surface area to a very reasonable level.

↳↳↳ reply — noident:

That's all good until you want to bring your non-technical friends with you. I would love to get everybody behind wireguard or client certificate authn but it sounds like a nightmare to support everybody's varying choices of browser, OS, mobile, etc.

Happy to take suggestions from anyone who has solved this problem in a self hosted way (meaning "use tailscale" isn't the answer I'm looking for)

Top #3 — WheelsAtLarge:

Memory, both chips and HDs, eventually collapses in price; that’s been the cycle for decades. The boom-and-bust cycle is what has driven the number of manufacturers down. My suspicion is that, in a few years, the price per gig will collapse again. AI is memory-hungry, and PC manufacturers will be pushing self-hosted AI models, which will require lots of memory. I bet we’ll see an increase in density per unit, which will bring down the price per gig. I give it five years at most. At that time, we will be seeing PC's capable of hosting a full AI model for the equivalen of less that $1000 today. It's how tech has worked for decades. There's no reason to think things have changed.

↳ reply 1 — stingraycharles:

"At that time, we will be seeing PC's capable of hosting a full AI model for the equivalen of less that $1000 today."

This is already possible; it's just not state-of-the-art, which will also be true in 5 years. The goalpost keeps moving.

↳↳ reply — kennywinker:

Maybe. Personally, i suspect we’ve hit diminishing returns already. If state of the art development hits a wall, then the local models can catch up. Especially if the bigger-is-smarter ideology is confirmed to be false, and specialized models (one model for RAG, another for coding, for medicine, for legal, etc) turns out to be the right move.

↳↳↳ reply — bitexploder:

I am doubtful… local models will get better. And they are very good. But distillation probably has limits. I am a huge fan of Qwen Flash Next and it is incredibly good. Not sure how far 100-200B parameters can get. Guess we will see.

↳ reply 2 — mceachen:

I'm not so sure. Agents turn this on its head.

The largest compute-hungry tech giants a decade ago had a soft ceiling on what compute resources they needed.

We now have handfuls of companies with trillions to spend on compute, and some even have profitable business models.

They're not going to get *less* hungry for compute over time when there's ever more money to be made.

So many years later... Me doomscrolling, depressingly bored, in a waiting room somewhere.

↳ reply 2 — alienbaby:

Built k8s cluster on 3 rpi4s, setup ingress via reverse proxy NATed to home router, waf, deploy all the things, setup cicd pipelines, upgrade the cluster etc etc.

And then I've just been building anything I can think of. To deploy or just messa round with. Games, web apps, manage data and train models remotely, desktop games, simulations, alife experiments, some websites to sell things, some to show things, lots of failures, etc etc lol anything that falls out of my head.

I've been a developer or sysadmin or DevOps or SRE or doing storage admin or code migration, all sorts, for 33 years at various times and places. It helps me drive these automatons quite well.

And to be honest, I used to love lovingly crafting everything, but I'm getting old! And it is lovely and comfy to just have things spring together on a whim or a moments inspiration.

In the realm of my own personal space, that's fine by me. Go wild, make stuff. At work, it's a powerful tool that must be used responsibly.

↳ reply 3 — raxxorraxor:

I nuked containers and all that shit. I don't need it for medium scale any more. I yolo servers through ansible and they are far better maintained than before. Every service gets its own account, every service creates its key pair to auth against a self hosted id provider, every rotation of key pairs and certificates is automated. Every service restart is logged and interpreted by a local AI that also surveys every log of every server of every app and contacts me if something is fishy.

But the main advantage is in the ease of any CI pipeline, which gets annoying with too much containerisation. Sure, requirement is that alls hosted apps/services follow certain rulesets...

Top #2 — jjcm:

In some ways it's better, in some ways it's worse.

It's certainly easier than ever to spin up a VPS/cloudflare proxy and deploy. Agents can pretty much do that end to end.

The bigger issue is you're then accountable for keeping up with security. Previously that meant using fail2ban and running a system update every few months. Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping, which is happening at an accelerated rate.

It got so bad during October I made https://firefighter.sh/ as a joke (a root-permissioned agent that continuously monitors for CVEs and patches your system live as soon as they drop - it's a security nightmare given the nondeterministic aspect of AI), but I'm actually starting to come around to the idea for my non-critical servers.

↳ reply 1 — cromka:

> Previously that meant using fail2ban and running a system update every few months. Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping,

Honestly, most of those issues can be mitigated by NOT exposing your services to the web and instead relying on Wireguard — and I am not mentioning other VPNs here because they, too, are vulnerable with their vast attack surfaces, like OpenVPN.

In fact I believe all this will lead to better VPN integration in our devices. I REALLY hope Wireguard gets widely adopted to the point every major platform finally adds support for it.

↳↳ reply — BOOSTERHIDROGEN:

I know Netbird or Pangolin use WireGuard, but what do you think of this tools ?

↳ reply 2 — usui:

> Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping

I know security by obscurity is not a good defense, but if the internet were on IPv6, it would be a lot harder for bots to find hosts by scanning the whole IP space, whereas when I open a port on IPv4 I can always see activity on it almost immediately. I've been watching traffic to IPv6-only hosts despite connecting to them from outside the local network and it's been completely silent from strangers. This would buy extra time for any critical CVE that needs patching.

Top #3 — velo_aprx:

With AI, the problem-solving aspect of my interest in computers is gone. And with it, much of my interest in computers.

The fact that AI can do pretty much anything is amazing, but using it feels about as rewarding as using cheat codes in your favorite game as a kid.

It's great fun for a while, until you realize you've ruined the game for yourself.

↳ reply 1 — sham1:

I've reached a similar conclusion, which is why I refrain from using AI for hobby things. My homelab is for me to experiment with stuff and maybe to learn something, not to let the robot do all the thinking and work for me.

I understand that some people like the idea of opportunity cost having gone down with the ability to just throw a problem to the robot and have it solve it, but I dunno. My hobby is computers, not AI, so I'd rather do the hobby instead of automating it away. It's like with art, I like the human aspects even if the AI can also do all the things for me.

↳ reply 2 — esond:

I have likened it to playing Guitar Hero. Yes it’s fun, yes I can do it for hours. But no, it is not the same feeling as playing the music for real on a real instrument.

item.description: 481 points, 121 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (worksinprogress.co)

→ HN comments  ·  481 points  ·  121 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — sfjailbird:

As a Westerner, I've been to Lahore, and the historical architecture is indeed fascinating. There are palaces and public buildings from the mughal period that would have been wonders of the world, had they still been standing. Only thing is, they are ruins, and you have to extrapolate from the few surviving pieces to the ruined whole to get an idea about the original splendor.

Besides that, even though people there are very sweet, Lahore is not an international tourist city, so I don't know that I would recommend going, unless you know what you're getting into.

↳ reply 1 — hnlmorg:

This might be a dumb question, but are you able to expand on what you mean for the last paragraph?

If the people are welcoming then what are the risks to tourists?

↳↳ reply — sfjailbird:

I mostly meant that it is not really set up to serve international tourists (natural given that there are so few of them), so some of the facilities that tourists depend on, like easy travel to certain places, easy access to information, guides, standardized terms for lodging, etc. You practically need someone local to be able to access the most interesting stuff.

On the flip side English is an official second language, so signage is very often in English, unlike a lot of places in the region and around the world.

I think the advice about going out at night and avoiding certain areas is given out of an abundance of caution. There are probably areas to avoid, but in the places I went (deep into the ant hill that is the city's interior) I never felt unsafe, also at night (which is bustling). I even had a driver return with my phone that I left in his car, and other experiences like that.

I think what is meant is that there is no 'night life' as in bars, partying and such. Still lots of restaurants (local food is amazing).

↳ reply 2 — abdussamit:

Hey, I'm from Lahore! Been here for the last 25 years.

Thanks for appreciating the good of Lahore.

I agree with you, that a Lahore visit is great if you plan very carefully e.g. don't go out after evenings, speak to a local about where to stay (prefer the 4-5 star hotels if you can afford), and travel during day time wherever you want to.

And as is true for every place, don't go in tight closed streets and don't be adventurous.

I mean, I've travelled and I wouldn't do the above even in any country. So it's business as normal.

Rest is just the noise of Lahore, I have been here and it's a lovely place to visit.

item.title: CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud
item.description: 323 points, 157 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (krebsonsecurity.com)

→ HN comments  ·  323 points  ·  157 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — wongarsu:

That's an interesting case. It's not immediately clear to me that this even is wire fraud. There is material deception (they claim "We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients", while paying ransom). But is there intent to defraud here? The customer does get what they asked for after all: they get their data back, at the price they were willing to pay

That that price was substantially higher than what the ransomware groups were charging RansomwareHelp seems inconsequential, every business has markups. And RansomwareHelp might have been able to get substantial discounts by being a trusted repeat customer for those ransomware groups

↳ reply 1 — gtowey:

The fraud part is they bill the client with made up items. If you tell someone that the price is based on a dozen engineers working for hundreds of hours, or that it's for time used on some sophisticated compute resources, but none of it ever happened, then that's fraud.

On the other hand, if they just told clients the price was based on negotiating with the hackers and adding a arbitrary mark-up, then there would be no crime here. But then I doubt they would have any customers, because the victims could do that themselves.

↳↳ reply — kobalsky:

> if they just told clients the price was based on negotiating with the hackers ..., then there would be no crime here

isn't it illegal to pay hackers in many places? I thought that's why companies were using these services, so they get a neat and tidy invoice they can pay with fiat.

↳↳↳ reply — jongjong:

Yeah, the company may not actually care how they got the result and they probably know better, in fact. They are pretending to believe because they want a result but also want their asses covered legally.

It seems more that they defrauded the government rather than the customers themselves... And maybe some clients were partially in on the fraud; pretending that they didn't know how he delivered results. The customer simply wanted everyone to believe that they refused to pay ransom. So the customer wasn't defrauded; they got exactly what they paid for...

Now with this indictment, they all get to act surprised... I can imagine some top corporate CTO who has a PhD in cryptography and in charge of security "Oh my, I'm shocked that this Ransomwarehelp business we used turned out to be a fraud! I had no idea that they couldn't actually crack 256-bit AES with Sha-512 key derivation!"

↳ reply 2 — granfalloon:

I was looking at reviews for a company like this a while back, and there were a bunch saying stuff like "This was expensive, but I was not willing to pay the criminals and am so grateful I was able to fight back." I know that I would be pissed off and feel I was defrauded.

↳ reply 3 — technion:

I'm not suggesting it should be legal or that he should get away with it, but I feel like this has always been a very open secret. Companies know they can only get data if they pay a ransom, and they know politically it's better if they pay someone who can make it go away for just above the ransom cost using wink wink secret skills.

↳ reply 4 — ★ tptacek:

These are the elements of a fraud case: material deception, relied on by the victim, for the profit of the offender. Add telecommunications, its wire fraud.

Top #2 — avodonosov:

Initially he only included a 2% margin - $260 over the around $13,000 requested by the fake ransomware group as the lowest possible price. And that $260 might have been just to account for bitcoin volatility.

Only after this was comminicated to the fake victim, the fake ransomware group agreed to reduce the price. What should have he done, tell the customer that his yesterday's quote was a mistake?

As for the initial $2,750 diagnostic fee, why can't he charge that, he did perform some initial study of the case.

> The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.

> The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.

↳ reply 1 — tsimionescu:

Here is what the company charges you for:

> “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”

So even if his quote were entirely reasonable, or even if he paid 20k dollars while charging 16k, this would still be, pretty clearly, fraud.

↳↳ reply — stingraycharles:

Yes but companies aren’t allowed to pay hackers ransoms so this allows them to have plausible deniability. That’s what the whole setup is about.

↳ reply 2 — Aurornis:

> What should have he done, tell the customer that his yesterday's quote was a mistake?

If you broker a deal for a client, you have to be honest about what they’re paying for. If you tell them that it costs $13,000 but it actually costs $4,000 and you pocket the difference, that’s fraud.

It would be different to say “I will solve your problem for $16K, leave the details to me”. That’s fair.

Charging someone a $2,750 fee and then billing them a line item for $13,000 for what’s supposed to be a pass-through payment is fraud if you only actually pass through $4,000.

It feels like a fine line but it’s actually not once you consider what contracts and invoices would look like.

Top #3 — lordnacho:

I wonder if you could write the contracts so it isn't fraud? Just put "let us do whatever we need to do, including paying the ransom" in the contracts, and tell people that's just a break-glass that will not normally be needed.

Because the way it's described, it definitely seems like fraud to market the thing as "won't pay the ransom" when you actually just do that.

↳ reply — cwillu:

I believe there are security firms that will do just that; it's the misrepresentation that makes this fraud.

item.title: YouTube Ad Punisher – Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays
item.description: 503 points, 603 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  503 points  ·  603 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

Top #1 — noitpmeder:

Is this actually an issue? Using uBlock Origin on firefox I don't think I have seen a youtube-forced ad in YEARS. And then adding in the SponsorBlock extension gets me around anything embedded into the video itself.

SponsorBlock is actually awesome, and for those that like to see internet numbers go up, it tells you how much your own submissions have saved other users over the years (the 11 snippets I've added have helped others skip 20d of ads).

↳ reply 1 — wilkystyle:

Jumping on this to add an additional warning: Just because an extension starts out safe does not mean it will always remain that way. This has been mentioned numerous times before on hacker news, but maintainers of any mildly to moderately popular browser extension are routinely offered tantalizingly high sums of money to either sell the extension to a less scrupulous third-party or to add data collection code for said third-party.

You are never 100% safe, but dramatically limiting the scope of what you trust is a great step in the right direction. I use two and only two browser extensions (uBlock Origin and Bitwarden) everywhere I go, and I have zero issues with ads on YouTube (or anywhere else, really).

Edit: I should also clarify that I am not speaking negative of this particular extension at all, nor the work that has gone into it.

↳↳ reply — Grimburger:

On firefox as a trusted extension this is audited by mozilla from what I know

Also it's one of the most downloaded extensions on the planet, really think they are going to be trying that and not getting noticed instantly?

Raymond Hill has been an outspoken critic of all the attempts to stop adblocking but conceded with manifestv3 changes and made one that works with chrome now, think the guy has very much proven himself and would never trash his legacy like that.

↳↳↳ reply — dns_snek:

Those trusted/recommended/featured badges in extension stores don't offer a strong guarantee, they're not manually and thoroughly reviewing every update like you might assume.

> After receiving Recommended status, safety standards are maintained through automated checks, monitoring, and periodic technical reviews.

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/recommended-extensions-...

Speaking of which, browsers should really start implementing "minimum release age" mechanisms for extension updates.

↳ reply 2 — dns_snek:

Yes, in a sense. Youtube seems to do a lot of A/B testing over very long time frames so your experience could be completely different than other people's. I've never had an ad get past the ad blocker but I've had a lot of fake-buffering and videos refusing to play that makes the site unusable over the past 1-2 years.

I remember people telling me about this for months and I had no idea what they were talking about until one day they targeted my account as well.

↳ reply 3 — cagey:

I run exactly same Firefox w/uBlock Origin and SponsorBlock on Linux, and aside from reliably getting "Experiencing Interruptions?" popups (which I assume are caused by the extensions doing their good work) I too have been watching YT ad-free for years.

Also a shout-out to the "Backstage Play" Firefox extension (on Android) which lets me listen to YT-sourced audio without the YT-playing Firefox tab having focus.

Top #2 — jillesvangurp:

Firefox + ublock origin works fine. And not just on Youtube, I use it with Amazon prime as well. I have that for package deliveries and you get the video subscription included. I've not opted to pay them extra for ad free video delivery because it seems ublock origin just removes the ads for me. So, no need. They have a decent movie selection and the occasional series I enjoy watching.

It seems people are conflicted between wanting to use Chrome (made by Google) while not wanting to see ads, the distribution of which is Google's core business and main source of income. While trying to work around all the clever ways that Google is coming up with to ensure ad blockers/removers don't work on Chrome.

Youtube works just fine on other browsers. There are three mainstream alternative browser engines at this point: Firefox, Safari, and Ladybird. Of those, Firefox is so far the easiest to configure to your liking when it comes to ad blocking and a 100% ad free experience on Youtube. I'm sure Ladybird will catch up rapidly as well. The more people use alternatives, the more Google and others will be forced to deal with minimizing how obnoxious and disruptive they allow ads to be.

MS lost the browser market to Firefox and later Chrome because it didn't do that. Google can lose that market just as easily. Internet Explorer once seemed to be too big to imagine it would ever go away. And now it's just a bad memory. I hear people complain about ads on Chrome and all I think is "Stockholm syndrome". The problem is Chrome, not ads.

Top #3 — jonplackett:

I’m all for ad blockers in most places but I have completely caved in on YouTube.

My reasons are

1. YouTube seems to pay creators reasonably

2. Being able to use the YT app without the crippling of things like background playback and downloads is very useful.

3. YouTube seems get YouTube music free, so cancelled Spotify with more or less paid for it.

I know I’ve given in. And I accept it

↳ reply 1 — TeMPOraL:

> and downloads

Note: "Make Available Offline" or whatever the current name all streaming services settled on is not downloading. Downloading something means getting the data in a self-contained form (e.g. file or files) whose existence and lifetime does not depend on the source app/website. Without that, all you have is a glorified button for extending cache TTL - you still don't get direct access to data, and you still can't control when the app decides to delete it.

It's important to maintain a clear distinction in language here. Confusing these two things usually leads to a nasty surprise when said cache wipes itself clean just as you board a 12 hour flight or train ride with no Internet, or worse.

↳↳ reply — zeroonetwothree:

Well sure it’s not exactly the same but I still consider it downloading if it’s available offline.

↳↳↳ reply — IshKebab:

What if it disappears the files when it detects you've gone on holiday?

↳ reply 2 — npteljes:

I don't think you've given in. You realized that the service gives you good value. There is no shame in that, especially since the payment is month to month.

item.title: First images of the impact of DART asteroid deflection experiment
item.description: 184 points, 55 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (arstechnica.com)

→ HN comments  ·  184 points  ·  55 comments

Top #1 — teekert:

“These types of bodies, because of their low gravity, have a very counterintuitive behavior,” Michel said. “Each time we interact with them, whether to take a sample or to make an impact, the response of the surface was not the one we predicted, simply because our intuition relies on what we experience every day on Earth. Even if the rules of physics are the same in the Universe, they express very differently depending on local attraction.”

I don't really get this, we can simulate the formation of entire star systems and galaxies, but here they rely on intuition? All masses and forces are known right? What's so counter "intuitive" (expectation) about this?

↳ reply 1 — mhurron:

You are putting way to much meaning into that statement. They don't mean they threw out math and winged it based on feelings, they mean that their assumptions of the coherence of these objects was very wrong.

They thought, based on their experience on earth and the way we model everything, they were dealing with a large rock that had been created by gravity gathering smaller rocks forming a single body with a surface. Basically, like everything else we've landed on.

What was found on Bennu was a loose conglomeration of pebbles and boulders with the coherence of a McDonalds playground ball pit. That sort of changes how you plan landings because the thrusters and impact is more than enough to overcome the force of gravity 'holding' the surface together.

https://news.arizona.edu/employee-news/five-lessons-osiris-r...

↳↳ reply — JumpCrisscross:

> based on their experience on earth and the way we model everything

To simplify this, we choose which model to use based, usually, on intuition. Nobody bothers to verify that the cars in a crash-test model aren't antimatter because that's intuitively nonsense.

↳ reply 2 — gus_massa:

Solids are difficult. How hard and sticky and deformable is a material is difficult to guess, specially if it's super cold at a few kelvin and without air and water to round it and add mud in between the cracks.

Galaxies are easy, you only have stars that follow the newton laws, and a few invisible black holes, and clouds of hydrogen, and dark matter, and ... well, perhaps they are not so easy, but still easier than solids. From https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardness

> Hardness can be measured in different ways, such as scratch hardness, indentation hardness, and rebound hardness. Hardness is dependent on ductility, elastic stiffness, plasticity, strain, strength, toughness, viscoelasticity, and viscosity.

item.title: Tracking Diseases Cured by AI
item.description: 315 points, 191 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (diseasescuredbyai.com)

→ HN comments  ·  315 points  ·  191 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

Top #1 — jollymonATX:

The criteria of phase 3 passed is a very long process. You have 0 as a statement of capabilities, in this context it is not that alone. The current zero read is a function of time to pass a phase 3 clinical trial which is not plausible currently. It takes 6-10 years from stage 1 to a passing stage 3. 10 years ago was 2016, 6 years ago was 2020. If that is 0 in 2030 then it might be interesting.

↳ reply — theptip:

Generally, I think the OP isn’t sensitive to the signal we’d expect to see if AI is having an impact; the bull hypothesis for AI would be: trend break with lots more new drugs since ~2020, and that rate accelerating YoY. Secondary hypothesis being an increase in success rates per stage (since AI should eventually be better at picking winners for expensive slow steps). You would explicitly not expect to see phase 3 trials completed in the 5 year window where AI has been going crazy. And especially not if AI is just learning to get good at biology in the last year or two.

To test these hypotheses I put together a quick dive looking at ClinicalTrials.gov data:

https://claude.ai/artifact/GpCUurD85LyR5vkXnBmBYc

I don’t see a clear trend break around the GPT era (~2020).

Interesting observations are that total number of drugs entering trials more than doubled 2014-2022, but this has leveled off (opposite of the “ai acceleration” hypothesis). Number of drugs entering phase 2 also increased during this time (but we don’t seem to have data on the more recent cohorts to see if this will level off as the new-drug entrants did).

Top #2 — corry:

(1) Totally respect holding people accountable, especially for very optimistic claims in a hype industry;

(2) The slow rate of FDA trials and approvals are a distinct and separate fly in the ointment that has nothing to do with AI's ability to advance medicine.

i.e. AI could invent a staggeringly effective cure for disease; whether or not Americans can quickly access said cure is an entirely different (and country-specific) matter.

(3) Yes, Amodei et all should take that into account when claiming AI will cure specific diseases on a specific timeline.

(4) Let's say Amodei et all is right, and the FDA remains slow and careful - one can easily imagine a future where medical tourism skyrockets based on which countries can most quickly assess and approve new AI-sourced treatments. This may lead to many costly/deadly mistakes, but also might be a net positive overall.

↳ reply 1 — mw888:

(4) is interesting under a more optimistic lens. Say that the research done for AI-driven medicine has a high quality, but of course still would not surmount the U.S. system's lengthy process.

Medical tourism's safety would not then be based on the regulatory body of the country hosting the treatment, but on the quality of research. If that quality of research is greater than the quality of research needed to make it out of phase III, and AI makes that research easier to create, improve, and check, then the U.S. regulatory body will become in some ways obsolete.

↳↳ reply — corry:

Yes, one feels that if the real bottleneck is regulatory approval, even in a world where AI is helping everything, parts of that process will still be immune from AI speeding them up. Regulations take time to change, too.

There's also an unavoidable linear time aspect to human trials (to assess if they worked, side-effects, etc) that can't be short-cut. You may need more than 1 week of data to tell if cancer is cured and not coming back, say. That said, you don't need a human trial to last 10 years. So there's some min/max to it.

I'm sure there's a huge body of expertise around designing trials. But it's always seemed like that's the biggest hurdle for new drugs anyways, and we as a society rightly-so want to ensure that large scale human trials are only being done on drugs we know are safe.

↳ reply 2 — busyant:

One thing I heard recently was that AI was being used to enroll clinical trials faster/more efficiently.

The anecdote was that Amgen was using some proprietary AI to speed up enrollment of their trials by 2-3×.

This will definitely speed up drug development.

Top #3 — chrisamiller:

Look, I work on this stuff, and anyone who says that AI isn't helping to accelerate science is wrong. The folks who say that AI will cure all human disease are also wrong.

The truth is that biology is horrendously complicated and obtaining measurements of what's going on inside cells is very difficult. That's the primary bottleneck, not the data crunching. (The reason that AlphaFold was so successful was because it was built on 50 years of meticulously gathered data in the PDB!)

So yeah, AI will help us sift through the data and formulate new hypotheses. It'll speed up processes and uncover new angles. I'm excited about that! It won't however, "solve biology", and I'll be glad when we slide down from the peak of this hype cycle and get back to the business of systematically figuring things out.

↳ reply 1 — slg:

>Look, I work on this stuff, and anyone who says that AI isn't helping to accelerate science is wrong. The folks who say that AI will cure all human disease are also wrong.

The difference between those two groups is that the former is merely a bunch of outside skeptics while the latter is made up of CEOs and founders of these AI companies. That's a false equivalency in terms of their motivations and impact. Isn't it obvious that the CEOs and founders being wrong is a bigger problem?

↳↳ reply — pj_mukh:

Person above you is talking about current AI. The CEO’s are talking about something more intelligent.

↳↳↳ reply — slg:

There are two quotes on the linked page with timelines of "less than a decade" and "Maybe within the next decade or so". The way this field typically works, the ball has to start rolling pretty soon for these two claims to have any chance of coming true.

↳ reply 2 — ryanisnan:

I don't disagree with you, but personally I find this type of grand vision setting helpful to keep in mind. This is a really awesome aspirational target.

I totally think what you are saying is also valid, and we should not lose sight of it as well.

item.title: NP_R ≠ PAR_R
item.description: 131 points, 162 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  131 points  ·  162 comments  ·  comments as of 25h

Top #1 — smusamashah:

At this rate, as a layman it looks like math problems/conjectures will just become everyday thing that a mathematicians solves as part of much much bigger problems. It looksike programming, you ask AI to write something trivial (current definition of trivial) for you while you keep working on much bigger system or architecture.

A mathematician has a hunch, comes up with a conjecture, asks AI to verify it, and moves on with the bigger problem at hand. This can of course be extrapolated further but I don't have brains for that much.

↳ reply 1 — KeplerBoy:

What are the bigger problems though from a mathematicians pov?

↳↳ reply — AlexCoventry:

Strategic insight like the Langlands Program.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langlands_program

I have a feeling AIs will be superhuman in that respect before too long as well, though.

↳↳↳ reply — JKCalhoun:

Maybe, in Physics, they can figure out quantum mechanics for the rest of us.

↳ reply 2 — brap:

I guess the main question then is why have the human come up with bigger problems instead of AI

↳ reply 3 — optimalsolver:

It's fascinating to watch how people are coming to terms with what's happening.

Top #2 — 101008:

I found it so weird people taking ownership of proofs when AI is doing all of them. I spent tons and tons of tokens on Google Neon Xhigh trying to solve Collatz conjecture. According to the conversation, it didn't proof Collatz, but in the middle it proved a lot of open Math problems, theorems, and more. Did I do something? No, I just asked to keep going, maybe saying "Do Option A" when asked which one of two routes take.

I didnt publish anything because I am not sure if it's valid or not, and also because I don't feel responsible for it? Throwing theormeas and Lean files into the wild claiming something has been proven feels a bit irresponsible.

↳ reply 1 — terryf:

Lots of people say "Look at the nice house we built here that we live in now" when in fact they just paid someone to design it and then someone else to build it and made sure these things happen the way they want them to.

Is it wrong to say that we built this house? If it is wrong, then who can actually say it? The construction manager that told the individual builters what to do? The individual builder that just put up a part of the drywall?

↳↳ reply — jltsiren:

Building your house yourself (or at least doing a large part of the work) used to be common. In some places it still is.

Academic authorship standards vary a bit from field to field, but the core idea is well established. If you made a substantial contribution, you are an author. Coming up with with the funding is usually insufficient for authorship.

↳ reply 2 — guyomes:

> Did I do something?

There are several way to look at this.

If you spent money for that, you did something, like the producer of a movie, or maybe like the executive producer.

If you spent some time on it, you also did something, maybe like a farmer who supervises the growing of vegetables, even though he might not understand the actual reproduction process that happens at the biological level.

So maybe the process did not involve you doing math, but I would say that you definitively did something.

Top #3 — brap:

I don’t know about you but I think it’s cool af that math is having this GitHub+AI moment, I especially enjoy the distributed efforts where swarms of people and their agents are trying to collaborate on a problem together in the open like they’re cracking GTA.

I wonder if there’s a way to create a true “hub” of math where anyone, man or AI, can contribute statements as long as they’re verifiably provable from the existing statements.

I think mathlib is basically this but from what I know there’s strict human approval necessary. Just curious if we can do something without humans in the loop at all, just a huge unmoderated dump of everything we know. I guess one downside is that people would be able to spam lots of true statements that aren’t interesting at all, or encode all sorts of things you don’t want there.

↳ reply 1 — munksbeer:

This is how I view it too. I understand this view is probably offensive to mathematicians who had dedicated their life to the work (and even saying that sounds trite, I apologise). But, though I do feel for them, I can't deny that the rise of Lean proofs and democratisation of the process does appeal.

Before all this, over the years many of us have read stories on how the academic world worked. In many cases I read that people would struggle to get their work recognised, because they didn't know how to play the (quite often political) game very well. And reports of papers just being rejected from high quality journals, for what seemed like no good reason.

So now, if you can prove something, it doesn't matter who you are or how you play the game. If your proof can be verified (and this is becoming easier too), then it is out there, in the pool of available knowledge, allowing others to build on top of.

I find it very exciting.

https://taucetiproject.org/

Top #1 — freediver:

Hey all this is Vlad, your friendly Kagi founder.

More context on the product: https://youtu.be/rp4GxlnvujE?t=4513

The Watch started with a need I had as a parent, which is also how Kagi Search started. It is built by a small team inside Kagi and funded by our own treasury.

Our vision is that of technology working for humans and not the other way around. We first built Search and Browser that had users' best interest in mind and as time went by I realized there is also a fundamental misalignment of incentives with most today's hardware which makes me uncomfortable to give it into the hands of my 8 year old.

Kagi Watch is not unrelated to what Kagi is trying to achieve in the world, it is complementary. By not owning hardware and platform we are at the mercy of companies which are basically our competitors.

As old Kay's saying goes 'people serious about software build their own hardware' -> Kagi Watch (as a first step in this direction, we have more to come, provided Watch becomes a good seller). And with your support, hopefully we are able to expand to a full-stack tech product ecosystem, working only for its users and nobody else. I am very excited to make families the focus of Kagi in the years to come.

Happy to answer any questions.

↳ reply 1 — MrDrMcCoy:

Kagi is wonderful, but the company seems to be spreading thinner and thinner. Many of us otherwise happy customers are losing trust and think that a loss of focus on the core search and assistant services will erode quality and place Kagi in a precarious financial situation. I'm a full time Linux user and was very sad to see Orion get dropped, which seems like the first casualty along this path.

What can you tell us that might restore our confidence in the direction Kagi is headed?

↳↳ reply — freediver:

Search and Assistant are the core. Most of the team and most of our spend go there, and that is not changing. Everything else is a bet that has to earn its place, and when one doesn't, we cut it. Orion for Linux was that filter at work.

The Watch is a small team and has to pay for itself through sales. If it doesn't, it ends.

On a higher level it is a part of our bet to create a family-first tech company.

↳↳↳ reply — flxngll:

People do not seem to take this well when Google kill off their products (as an example). Perhaps this is different for hardware - though I do miss my Nest thermostat... What’s your take on this?

↳ reply 2 — coumbaya:

Just wanted to say that, like other people, I don't really understand the weird products/offshoots, but I'm also not that worried because so far search has remained excellent.

↳ reply 3 — achr2:

As a paying customer, every time I see your investment in nonsense outside of the core search and information space it makes me reconsider my subscription. This is a bad look.

Top #2 — josephwegner:

Kagi subscriber, big fan. Love their product, love their ethos. I also share the concerns of Kagi spreading themselves waaaaay too thin.

That said, I've been getting more the sense that Kagi is leaning into the "safe web for the next generation" angle, and as a parent (9yo, 11yo, 13yo), I really like it. We don't do any social media or any raw internet access at all right now, but my kids are starting to get to the point where the good parts of the internet could be really inspiring and help them expand on their curiosities. I yearn for a safe way to let them explore.

My partner and I also have this exact problem of wanting to keep track of our kids as they are out and about more. For our oldest, we just finally took the leap to giving them an old iPhone to use when they are out. No social media or anything, but it lets us track them and lets them communicate with us.

The main reason we went with a phone instead of an Apple Watch, Gizmo, etc. is that we want our kid to be able to _text_ us in an emergency. There are a wide range of dangerous scenarios teens can find themselves in where calling dad might make their situation worse. Being able to text me quickly and quietly from a bathroom could be a life-saver in that situation. Unfortunately Kagi's watch doesn't solve this problem either, so it won't work for me. Thankfully I've been pretty happy with Apple's parental controls to let me lock stuff down... despite the abysmal interface.

Would love to get your thoughts on it and any other feedback. Shoot me a note if you’d be up for a chat. Kevin@kagi.com

item.title: Tell HN: Happy Thanksgiving

Top #1 — tito:

I do the following Thanksgiving assignment each year, and find it really fulfilling. Passing this on from my wonderful college professor Danny Warshay. Copy-pasted-with-some-bits-added:

Think of your supporters:

Think of all of the people who have helped you get to where you are today. All of the coaches, advisers, supporters, teachers, employers, mentors, relatives and friends.

All the people who helped you in the early days of your career, or in your life, or recently. All of the references who spoke on your behalf for jobs. Even the categories, let alone all of the individual supporters, are endless for all of us. That person you meant to thank a decade ago for something they probably forgot by now.

Your Assignment:

Select one or two, and write them a handwritten note to let them know how you are doing and to thank them for helping you get here.

We are all on both sides of this equation from time to time, and we all know how much we enjoy hearing from those whose lives we have influenced, especially hearing those simple and magical words, “Thank you.” To me, it feels like more than ever, we need to find moments of gratitude.

I hope your doing this adds a little extra meaning to your Thanksgiving and to the Thanksgiving of those who will be hearing from you! Based on the moving experiences many of you have shared with me that resulted from this simple gesture, I am confident that you will find this rewarding.

For those of you who will be celebrating American Thanksgiving, I hope you enjoy what I know is a much-needed break. And for those of you who are not, I hope you will join me in a few moments of gratitude.

AFAIK the main objections are against sharing the electricity bill and tax exemptions in exchange for a paltry amount of jobs created. Does the author classify those as hysterical?

Also, the existence of technologies does not mean the data center next door will use them. For instance, many can run on closed water loops, but prefer not to, because it is cheaper.

↳ reply 1 — fancyfredbot:

It should genuinely reduce power required for a given amount of compute which is a good thing. Probably still too much power though.

↳↳ reply — bigiain:

And I wonder how the supply chain and existing inventory looks for near term data centre builds? I've seen speculation that there are warehouses/datacenters full of GPUs not yet in use awaiting data centre or power/water infrastructure to be completed.

↳ reply 2 — theptip:

All this is easily fixable by a government that actually cares. So many commentators (and the markets) freaking out about how DC buildout is going to halt, but when you look at the demands they are easily satisfiable.

If tax exemptions are off the table, DC operators will just bid higher, including paying a lot more in up-front power commitments, or even just paying off the local communities.

The profit margins on compute are ludicrously high for the big guys, they can and will pay a lot more into the local community if that’s what’s needed to get approval in ‘27. Like, Anthropic could pay double per MW and still have plenty of margin on their inference operations.

It’s been a free for all up until now because of the federal government’s “build at all costs” stance, now the blowback has hit, and next the price will be established and the new equilibrium found.

↳ reply 3 — imoverclocked:

This. It goes deeper though. Yes, data centers use a lot of resources but they also enable abuses of power… political as well as energy.

The rush to put data centers up has created situations where construction of entire nuclear plants are in the plans (~10 year horizon) while the short term goal of energy production is diesel based. Anyone want to wager on the odds that the nuclear plants actually get built? The planned energy production is sometimes in the small percentages of a host countries entire carbon budget.

As for political abuses, flock cameras are definitely enabled by large data centers and have been in the middle of a lot of surveillance scandals. Large layoffs by AI as well as AI slop in practically every sector of our society make it even less palatable to spend more on data centers.

It’s not uncommon for me to go shopping and the person at the checkout is bemoaning the computer in front of them. When is the last time you heard someone outside of tech get excited about a new computer? Unless it’s for games or they had none to start with, I find it to be less and less common. Data centers are just an extension of the general malaise we have created as an industry.

Top #2 — helsinkiandrew:

Discussion on Nvidia blog post (429 comments) https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48660178

I wonder if moving from 30-35 to 45 degrees has an impact on component lifespan

↳ reply 1 — IndrekR:

Rule of thumb is that 10 degrees difference makes reactions go, and things fail, twice as fast. This is not exact science, but ballpark is about right.

↳↳ reply — leoedin:

Is a chip cooled with water at 45C necessarily going to be hotter than a chip cooled by air? I imagine the temperature differentials between chip and coolant on a water cooled setup are much better than the differential between chip and airflow on a typical air cooled setup.

↳↳↳ reply — arghwhat:

We strictly speaking never do pure air-cooling in this context.

Traditional water-cooling transfers heat to a fluid, which is then moved to a large radiator to be cooled by air.

Traditional "air-cooling" transfers heat to a phase-changing fluid (heat-pipe), which is then moved to a large radiator to be cooled by air.

Only differences are the type of and amount of fluid, as well as the presence of pumps. Phase-change beat using a fluid as a thermal buffer by quite a bit. The benefit of water is that it's easy to provide massive thermal inertia, and the ability to transfer the heat to a far larger external radiator than could be implemented internally with heat-pipes.

↳ reply 2 — bob1029:

Semiconductors are unique in that higher temperatures are sometimes preferable for certain electrical characteristics.

I would worry more about thermal cycling and temperature gradients across the die. A machine that runs at 100% 24/7/365 tends to be pretty reliable.

Top #3 — __MatrixMan__:

That's conveniently hot enough for a hot shower. It would be cool to see more district heating/cooling efforts.

↳ reply 1 — andai:

In Eastern Europe there's a lot of places that get hot water thru underground pipes from a power plant.

Obviously has downsides though, one time they were renovating and we didn't have hot water for a few weeks.

↳↳ reply — lucaspiller:

My city has district heating which covers around 500k people. The peak output of all the heat plants combined is 239 MW, which is around the same heat output as one or two large data centres.

There are no power plants in my city, so to generate the heat there are heat plants which burn natural gas, biomass or (if supplies get low) something similar to bunker fuel.

Of course it's seasonal, but I'm sure the cost of getting rid of the excess heat in summer would outweigh the current costs of the system (it's more expensive per kWh than a gas boiler), as well as the environmental benefits from not burning all this stuff near where people live.

↳↳↳ reply — TeMPOraL:

Demand for hot water would be more consistent throughout the year if not for changes to washing machines and detergents that make it possible to do laundry with absurdly cold water (20 degrees) - which I believe is what makes "fast fashion" possible (the stuff would likely melt apart after few rounds in 60 degrees).

↳ reply 2 — yxhuvud:

Not for distribution, as it needs to be hot enough to kill legionalla.

item.title: An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
item.description: 192 points, 66 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (arxiv.org)

→ HN comments  ·  192 points  ·  66 comments

Top #1 — kdavis:

Interesting. I've only read the abstract, but...

- It seems strange to get an algebra of Type I for a QFT. Generally one would expect an algebra of Type II when including gravity. Maybe it's a result of a finite G and not the infinitesimal G that gives Type II?

- It seems like it would take some care to construct a Lorentzian path integral rigorously. I wonder how that was done.

- I wonder how background independence is being claimed while at the same time quantizing on intersecting null cones. The definition of the null cones is a background.

Top #2 — senderista:

Not a physicist but everything in the abstract sounds like typical loop quantum gravity claims. How is this different?

Top #3 — hecmmm:

Abstract: We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite GN. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in GN and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in GN yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

↳ reply 1 — freakynit:

Can someone please explain this ... simply... to a common man? (╥_╥)

↳↳ reply — ramses0:

You know how light can be a wave and a particle? Now gravity can be the same... it's like we can "pixelate" gravity (theoretically) from a null vacuum.

Cross checking my explanation with el goog, there's another important point about "finite quantum states in a finite area" which basically means TLDR gravity-pixels... there's actually an equivalent "atomic resolution" of the universe where you can't hide infinite information in a finite space.

↳↳↳ reply — Drunk_Engineer:

> You know how light can be a wave and a particle? Now gravity can be the same

That's not anything new.

↳ reply 2 — dist-epoch:

Doesn't seem to connect to Quantum Field Theory (the Standard Model).

item.title: Lions' Commentary on Unix: Why It Was Secretly Copied for 20 Years
item.description: 270 points, 61 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (fosscomics.com)

→ HN comments  ·  270 points  ·  61 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — CalChris:

Lions Commentary was used as evidence in the USL vs BSDI lawsuit to undermine USL’s claims of trade secret misappropriation and unrestricted publication without copyright notice.

It was my licensed original copy which I bought from Western (!) Electric. Technically, it was part of a Western Electric UNIX source license. I lent my copy to Sam Leffler for the lawsuit. It was entered as evidence and I got it back a couple of years later.

↳ reply — kragen:

Thank you for your service.

Top #2 — JdeBP:

By the time I got hold of a copy when the book came out, the Deitel and Kogan book on OS/2 had been out for 2 years, as had the Goodheart+Cox Magic Garden book, the Leffler+McKusic+Karels+Quarterman book on 4.3BSD had been out for 7 years, the Bach book had been out for 10 years, and the Xinu books had been out for 12 years.

The Lions book wasn't really very useful by 1996.

Whereas Vahalia's and Pate's books on Unix, which also came out in 1996 but covered things that had happened in the intervening decades, were a lot more useful.

↳ reply 1 — pjmlp:

The usefulness of the book was helping to widespread UNIX on university campus during its early days, afterwards, just like the K&R C first edition, it became an historical artifact.

↳ reply 2 — kragen:

The Lions book wasn't useful as a guide to the kernel of your operating system anymore in 01996, but it was very useful in understanding why C and Unix were the way they were. A lot of Unix's Chesterton's Gates are justified in it, which is what you need to tear them down. And it was also very useful for writing a new operating system, because it includes enough source code to compile into a pretty complete multiprocess timesharing operating system supporting multiple terminals, multiple user accounts, a hierarchical filesystem, and the still-familiar Unix system call interface.

I don't think any of those other excellent books are really an adequate replacement. Deitel and Kogan obviously don't include the OS/2 source code; Bach https://abhyass.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/09/the... and Goodheart & Cox are mostly pseudocode, with no kernel source code; the Devil Book is almost but not completely devoid of kernel source code; the Xinu book https://willendless.github.io/assets/os_arm_doc/Operating%20... is great (and clearly owes a lot to Sixth Edition Unix), but Xinu lacks, for example, users and subdirectories.

Most of these, though not the Xinu book, cover operating systems that are much too big and complicated to explain fully in a single book, so they confine themselves to conceptual overviews. In my view, this reinforces the syndrome Comer critiques in the preface to the Xinu book:

> Students form the impression that an operating system is a black box, and textbooks reinforce the misimpression by explaining operating system features and focusing on how to use operating system facilities. More important, because they only learn how an operating system appears from the outside, students are left with the feeling that an operating system consists of a set of interface functions that are connected by a morass of mysterious code containing many machine-dependent tricks.

By contrast, in the Lions book's commentary volume https://cs3210.cc.gatech.edu/r/unix6.pdf (note, this PDF doesn't include the source-code volume!) we find line-by-line commentaries like:

> It is now time to take a good look at the procedure which creates new processes as (almost exact) replicas of their creators.

> 1841: “mpid” is an integer which is stepped through the values 0 to 32767. As each new process is created, a new value for “mpid” is created to provide a unique distinguishing number for the process. Since the cycle of values may eventually repeat, a check is made that the number is not still in use; if so a new value is tried;

> 1846: A search is made through the “proc” array for a null “proc” structure (indicated by “p stat” having a null value); 1860: At this point, the address of the new entry in the “proc” array is stored as both “p” and “rpp”, and the address of “proc” entry for the current process is stored both as “up” and “rip”; [...]

Even the Xinu book doesn't go into that level of detail. It is, in my view anyway, much less accessible than Lions, requiring a great deal more previous knowledge of programming.

If a relatively new programmer felt that a kernel was "a morass of mysterious code containing many machine-dependent tricks", I don't think they could retain that feeling after working through the Lions book, although it does contain some machine-dependent tricks.

I have the strong impression that all of Bach, Goodheart & Cox, and the Devil Book authors wanted to include the kernel source code they were commenting on, because in many cases they discuss specific functions, struct fields, and variables, and then, in most cases, describe algorithms in pseudocode. My inference is that they were forced into this exigency by legal threats from the Death Star, not that they thought the pseudocode was actually didactically superior to the actual source code. Comer didn't have this problem because Xinu didn't include any Unix source code and wasn't even Unix-compatible at the system call level.

What was an adequate replacement in 01996 was Linux, which came with full source code and a mailing list full of people who were eager to discuss it.

But, even then, Linux was not ideal as a teaching system. Which is why, in 02006, the PDOS folks rewrote Sixth Edition Unix in ANSI C and have been using it for teaching ever since: https://github.com/mit-pdos/xv6-riscv

Top #3 — dctoedt:

Amusing in the preface about nroff, the early text-markup language that Lions used to produce his book: "The co-operation of the “nroff” program must also be mentioned. Without it, these notes could never have been produced in this form. However it has yielded some of its more enigmatic secrets so reluctantly, that the author’s gratitude is indeed mixed. Certainly “nroff” itself must provide a fertile field for future practitioners of the program documenter’s art."

(Emphasis added.)

And so it was: IIRC, nroff was largely obviated by Brian Reid's SCRIBE, a forerunner of LaTeX.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nroff

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scribe_(markup_language)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Reid_(computer_scientist...

item.title: Unconditional Integer Factorization in Subexponential Time
item.description: 138 points, 21 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  138 points  ·  21 comments

Top #1 — mentalgear:

So this is the big one?

Edit: Context from Gemini:

> Cryptography & Real-World Security No Immediate Threat to RSA: Despite the headline exponent of $1/3$, this does not break RSA or compromise current public-key infrastructure.

> Reassurance for Cryptographic Assumptions: Ironically, proving that factoring is unconditionally in $L_N[1/3, O(1)]$ reinforces existing cryptographic modeling. Cryptographers already assume adversaries can factor in $L_N[1/3, 1.923]$ time when sizing RSA keys; this theorem simply removes the theoretical possibility that worst-case hard instances exist that resist $L_N[1/3]$ algorithms.

↳ reply 1 — credit_guy:

> this theorem simply removes the theoretical possibility that worst-case hard instances exist that resist $L_N[1/3]$ algorithms.

I don't think this theorem proves this. This would be an enormously huge deal, because it would show that factoring is not polynomial. The paper would state that front and center, in the abstract, in the title, and about 10 more times on the first two pages.

I think the paper just says that what was known empirically in the past (that factorization can be done with an algorithm in the L_N[1/3, O(1)] class), is now proven formally. It does not establish a lower bound.

↳↳ reply — gpm:

It would prove P!=NP...

↳↳↳ reply — SkiFire13:

Integer factorization is not known to be NP Complete.

↳ reply 2 — whatisthiseven:

For context, factoring RSA with a key size of 1024 would still take 500k core years to compute. This proof and that estimate are only an improvement. The algorithm is superpolynomial. Worse than polynomial, but faster than exponential. To my understanding, anyway.

↳ reply 3 — tgv:

I think it's an upperbound only. If they can prove it's also the lowerbound, then it would be the big one.

Top #2 — jrm4:

Alright, guess I can ask this here. In my quizzes I ask a question something like "Which of the following can factor a large composite number orders of magnitude faster than brute forcing," and the answer is none of the above, this doesn't exist.

What do y'all think of this question? And is it still true? My gut is that it is, yes?

item.title: OpenAI cuts GPT-6.2 usage: Astra hits limits 40% faster, Sol 25% faster
item.description: 459 points, 259 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (twitter.com)

→ HN comments  ·  459 points  ·  259 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — Aurornis:

I’ve had OpenAI and Anthropic accounts continuously for a long time, with a sampling of others rotating in and out.

The back-and-forth between which provider is more generous has been interesting to follow because the balance has been swinging back and forth. Not long ago I was having fun throwing OpenAI tokens at a side project because they felt limitless between the allowances and the constant flow of resets. Then Opus 5.5 came along and gave even more usage without any reset shenanigans to try to stay ahead of. OpenAI responded by reducing their allowances, and now the reset party seems to have stopped as well.

Now they’re sending us vague emails about limits being adjusted downward again, citing a billing error? The original email was so vague that they had to send a clarification because it didn’t have enough information to tell if we were going to be retroactively penalized or if it only applied going forward.

This comes at the same time as they’re rolling out a change that makes chat quota subtract from your coding quota, which removes one of the last remaining big selling points of an OpenAI subscription in a world where Opus 5.5 exists.

I would love to have some insights into what’s happening at OpenAI right now. From the outside it feels like something substantial changed in how they approach everything, but the weird part is how it’s coming at the worst possible time for them to be appearing like the lesser deal. Did they finally get the internal marching orders to turn the profitability knob up and ignore everything else?

↳ reply 1 — seizethecheese:

Similar experience here.

I used to have to do insane stuff to hit my OpenAI quota. I'm talking about running experiments overnight where the agent isn't really using sleep enough. More recently, I blew threw three resets in a week and couldn't really correlate it with anything I'd done.

↳↳ reply — fodkodrasz:

Also I feel models got werse, Sol 6.2 feels lazyer, overcautious despite being explicitly told it can safely go amok in its sandbox / the sandbox target vm... and its prose and code output became worse then before (Sol 5.6 seems peak for me, it had the best balance for me in creativity, cautiousness, and pragmatic compromises instead of overdoing stuff), seems like overfit for synthetic dataset, and as if it were targeting a machine and not a human with its output. I feel the fears about using synthetic trainng sets manifesting for my usecases (coding in a specific minimalist-functional style, favoring simplicity in architecture, code, web design, writing documentation targeting humans instead of machines). Sol-6 started to invent non-existing usecases and irrelevant corner cases like the Claude models do... then now we are at the over cautious model (for my prompts and usecase which are largely the same)

The need to micromanage it to get to similar results seems multiplied, and despite the claimed lower costs I feel my quotas running out in 1 day despite earlier models had about 4 times higher claimed costs, and were running (with auto continuation on 5h resets) for days and getting to great results...

I have no benchmaxxes to support my impressions though.

Claude is used at work... it is okay I guess, I really didn't like it in the Sol 5.6 era (lol, a few months before), but the annoyance gap decreased.

↳↳↳ reply — seizethecheese:

> Sol 6.2 feels lazyer

Yes. I just wrote about this here: https://micjm.com/blog/openai-is-in-cost-control-mode/. Scroll down to chart on reasoning tokens compared to opponents. Both Sol 6.2 and Astra 6.2 are big outliers for not thinking

↳ reply 2 — mdemare:

> This comes at the same time as they’re rolling out a change that makes chat quota subtract from your coding quota, which removes one of the last remaining big selling points of an OpenAI subscription in a world where Opus 5.5 exists.

Claude's 5 hour limit is _really_ annoying, and is a big reason why I'm keeping OpenAI for now. It's just easier to plan usage with OpenAI, especially with a couple of banked resets at hand.

↳ reply 3 — edg5000:

I recently cancelled my 200 EUR sub at OpenAI, but two benefits I'll mention:

- Codex has an image generation endpoint. Some features are not wrapped by the harness but still work.

- OpenAI is more flexible with custom harness work, last time I checked (around March).

Top #2 — at1as:

Our limits have been artificially propped up by a "reset" economy that is coming to an end, ChatGPT web usage not counting against our balance (set to change), and now apparently [unintentional] artificially inflated limits.

I don't think token subscription subsidization at the level we've become accustomed to lasts forever, so it's critically important we have a few more frontier level models (glad to see Gemini back in the arena, and I'll even cheer for Muse and Grok if it'll provide more competition).

↳ reply 1 — rwarfield:

Subsidization implies that the subscriptions are offered at a loss; there's no reason to believe that is the case. There is price discriminization at play, sure, but let's not buy the framing that the API price is the "right" price and subscriptions are some amazing giveaway.

↳ reply 2 — jstummbillig:

I think it's set up quite nicely so far: People are learning some resources management skills, and getting extra tokens to make mistakes with. Fairly soon low cost models will be good enough for most coding work. (I might get surprised here but, idk, I am beginning to notice that I can't tell the difference between models for backend work, while the nature of the work stays roughly constant). All the whole models manufacturers are lifting up the bottom and pressuring frontier companies into more efficiency, unless they are willing to give up that market.

All in all, fairly optimistic about costs per coding task dropping over the next year.

Top #3 — ★ simonw:

I got a huge amount of work done yesterday without burning too much of my quota by using Claude Fable 5.2 Medium and telling it to do all of the code editing work using Opus 5.5 sub-agents. I expect the same trick works with Astra and Sol (or even Luna).

↳ reply 1 — seizethecheese:

Opus 5.5 spends about half as much per task as Fable 5.2. On the other hand Sol 6.2 spends less than a fifth as much as Astra 6.2, so the utility Fable gets from Opus might not be comparable to the utility Astra gets from Sol.

Raw numbers we have on cost per task (for people doing real work in our open source battle system built on opencode https://github.com/bottomless/agent-duel):

  Cost per task:

  Fable 5.2: $3.23
  Opus 5.5:  $1.59

  Astra 6.2: $2.01
