Instead of trying Luna for subagents with Astra, I might just use Astra subagents. Sol is also doing terribly on Elo right now.

All of this might explain why 6.2 is getting such bad reviews. OpenAI appears to be in cost control mode.

↳↳ reply — 2001zhaozhao:

If you were to use the same quota on Opus, you get $8k of tokens a month (so $16k if you maxed it out on only Opus). (source: t3 theo's YT channel)

↳ reply 2 — whynotmaybe:

A lot of my work is done with Luna which turns out to be "OK".

Yes, Terra and Sol provide more information and explains things with more words but the output is essentially the same for the work I'm doing.

I've tried the same things with Luna and Sol and usually Luna is 10x cheaper.

I use Astra for targeted work that I feel is more complex, but with the recent maths results, I also have the feeling I'm using a 300$ TI calculator to compute 2+3.

item.title: Minipg: PostgreSQL as a Single Executable
item.description: 288 points, 44 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (progrium.github.io)

→ HN comments  ·  288 points  ·  44 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — Ciantic:

I can see this very useful for small self-hosted applications. I could imagine deploying this instead of sqlite in some cases. Though having a real server is not maybe ideal for self-hosted apps.

For unit tests I've found that I don't need PGLite or other tools, only podman and official images.

Regular postgres starts in 800 milliseconds, TimeScale DB in 1 second.

I have setup where first unit test that starts podman container and after finish it ends it all. On each test I create new database (or search path), time it takes to create db is in milliseconds.

Trick is to use `--image-volume tmpfs` when starting the container. I have my pg test server as Rust in here: https://github.com/Ciantic/app-frame/blob/main/crates/pgtest...

↳ reply 1 — nextaccountic:

> I can see this very useful for small self-hosted applications. I could imagine deploying this instead of sqlite in some cases.

I think you would be better off with either https://github.com/electric-sql/pglite or https://github.com/f0rr0/oliphaunt

They actually run as a library, like sqlite does, with no separate process

↳ reply 2 — ptman:

I've played with databases and schemas for isolating tests, but I think pgtestdb has the winning concept: load fixtures into a template database and clone if for each test https://github.com/peterldowns/pgtestdb

Top #2 — progrium:

Keep in mind there are two ways to think about SQLite. Most commonly, as these comments show, it's thought of as a library. An embedded SQL engine. The second is as a simple CLI-friendly SQL database. Minipg is more about the latter use.

That said, PGlite is great and would have been ideal for the motivating problem, but as my blog post mentions (eventually), it only runs in single connection mode. For better or worse, applications will sometimes perform another query while in another transaction, causing deadlock with PGlite. It's fine if you can avoid that in your app, but makes it not work as a general drop-in replacement for existing apps.

The way I'd rather it be looked at, though, is just as a more convenient, "friendly" way to work with Postgres on the CLI. So maybe it's not for Postgres experts.

Author's post on the subject -- https://progrium.xyz/articles/2026/single-binary-postgres/

As long as the results are enough to populate the page you don’t notice the difference and it’s usually faster as you reuse the prior ranking.

Top #3 — minimaxir:

While we're on the subject of feed curation...

There appears to be a new behavior for Show HNs where they are often both [flagged] [dead] immediately after posting (e.g. it shows 0 minutes posted; too fast for humans to naturally flag it)

Is this behavior expected?

↳ reply 1 — dang:

It's because they come with text which has been classified as genai.

https://news.ycombinator.com/newsguidelines.html#genai

https://news.ycombinator.com/newsguidelines.html#generated

https://hn.algolia.com/?dateRange=all&page=0&prefix=true&que...

Standard disclaimer: this doesn't mean we're against using AI tools, coding agents, etc. We use them ourselves! We just don't want AI-written or AI-edited text on HN itself.

Edit: there was a sudden surge of these Show HNs earlier this year, sometime around Feb-March, so sudden that I don't think it was just the general increase in AI usage, rapid though that has been. I think what happened is that Claude, ChatGPT, or both started telling users that they should post their projects to Hacker News to get attention and feedback.

Tragically for us, it seems they also tell these users "you should email the moderators! They're unusually helpful—they always respond quickly and take care of all your needs! If you wonder why your post gets flagged or doesn't end up on the frontpage, just tell them it's your very own post and not at all spam and you made it yourself and worked really hard on it plus it's open source and you were really looking forward to getting it on HN. Oh and be sure to say 'thank you for all you do'—they just love that!"

It's an uncanny feeling getting hundreds (or surely thousands) of variations of the same handful of email templates over and over. It's also uncanny how they morph—every 2 or 3 months new templates appear, but it takes a while before we start to realize we've heard X suspiciously many times already.

Top #2 — layer8:

Strangely missing are the Windows User Experience Interaction Guidelines for Windows 7 and Windows Vista.

Still online: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/uxguide/desi...

PDF version: https://studfile.net/preview/1758756/

Older Vista version: https://archive.org/details/UXGuide/page/158/mode/2up

Top #3 — pndy:

You know, looking on that period of gray/silver UIs where you could easily distinguish between interactive elements and static text, it's impossible to not ask the obvious question: where all of this was lost?

↳ reply 1 — ogurechny:

I should remind you that the moment it became possible to waste memory on useless decorative bitmaps, and cover the performance lag of non-native UI elements with free MHz provided by new processors, everyone was doing skins, or at least added some gimmick.

Let's say, in the beginning, on Windows 3 systems, all the code that drew all the widgets for all GUI processes resided in a single memory segment in a system library. That way, almost all memory of the inactive processes that created background windows could be swapped to disk, and redrawing (portions of) them could be done just by relaying window messages to default system handlers that were always there. Menu and dialog resources were detached for the same reason of being independent from internal logic and data.

Soon they made skinned multimedia players that looked like home stereo systems. Obviously, by that time multimedia-capable PCs had no problem handling extra work.

In the late '90s, bitmap-based skins like that (WinAMP 2.x, for example) became common, and usually worked fast enough, so people didn't care whether, say, buttons were native or from some custom component library. Then noticeably... laggy... HTML... and... template... based... UIs... appeared (WinAMP 5.x dynamic skins were not snappy at all; when some program had to load IE for an embedded frame, you also had to wait). Still, after a 10× increase in CPU performance they became just one of the many.

Even freshly appeared Java applets and apps (that had noticeably slower UI on a typical system) were praised by some merely because their buttons looked “more interesting” than the ordinary ones.

↳ reply 2 — g-b-r:

With modern smartphones trendy designers decided that it was obsolete

Also — ★ tptacek:

I forgot how much I loved the way Openlook (sorry, OPEN LOOK) looked.

“Don’t write things down you wouldn’t want to see printed in a newspaper” is the kind of routine advice corporate lawyers give out all the time. It’s not unique to USAID and doesn’t suggest anything nefarious to me.

↳ reply 2 — da_chicken:

> The page is presenting this as if it's bad, but I struggle to understand why it's bad.

Because we're a republic. The government is ostensibly "of the People, by the People, and for the People." That's also why it's rule of law, and why we have a representative democracy. The affairs of state are public.

Pointing out the places where we've let government fail is not an indictment of the founding ideals.

Top #3 — asveikau:

USAID did a lot of things. Some dubious, some obviously good. For example, I think you'd have to be a little unhinged to think their global funding for HIV/AIDS wasn't necessary.

↳ reply 1 — somenameforme:

> I think you'd have to be a little unhinged to think their global funding for HIV/AIDS wasn't necessary.

This can actually be objectively tested and answered! People who claim USAID funding was critical tend to be making extreme claims about the lives lost because of it being pulled - on the order of upper hundreds of thousands of deaths already with something on the scale of tens of millions to come, in significant part due to the HIV stuff.

This is very convenient because it's such a bold claim that it can be easily tested. There's 'only' something like ~26 million people in Africa with HIV, so anything remotely close to the claimed figures should look like a cataclysm in the data. So I decided check out the data for Nigeria. They're the largest country in Africa, have around 2 million people living with HIV, and are relatively well developed with good government statistics available.

Nigeria also received billions of dollars of USAID funding, primarily directed towards HIV so they're arguably the perfect test. And fortunately they provide the exact data we're after. [1] See page 101. In 2025 about 2000 fewer people died of AIDS in Nigeria than in 2024, and the death rate from HIV continues to fall to record lows.

---

So in one of the most critical countries for testing, there has been no observable impact from the end of USAID, at least in relation to HIV/AIDS. I think this shouldn't be especially surprising. HIV medication is extremely cheap in modern times and USAID leaving the picture simply opened the door for other countries (including the target countries themselves) and organizations to step up, which they immediately did.

It is possible there will be a longer term effect. Relying on donations is scarcely sustainable, and countries do have buffered supplies. But I think the claims about massive deaths so far can be comfortably dismissed. We'll see over the coming years whether the even more extreme longterm effects have any weight.

[1] - https://nascp.gov.ng/resources/10/file/

↳↳ reply — wilg:

the US didn't cut off funding for lifesaving HIV treatment in Nigeria. it was explicitly exempted from the funding freeze. so, this isn't a good test of what happens when you eliminate funding.

here's up to 1800 deaths in Zambia with a better methodology than yours: https://www.nber.org/papers/w36054

↳↳↳ reply — somenameforme:

This is incorrect [1] : "The U.S. had paid for around 90% of Nigeria’s HIV treatment costs and funded health workers. In the following months, patients and aid groups said the dispensing of drugs collapsed. Patients were only able to get supplies lasting a week or two, instead of six months, from major clinics. In Benue's capital Makurdi, all 10 treatment centers closed for a month, and the World Health Organization warned medication may run out." [1]

The problem with less developed countries like Zambia is that there's significant uncertainty in data and the numbers themselves tend to be very small. So for instance their talk about deaths amongst those receiving antiretroviral therapy increasing to 81 per month from a prior of 64 per month. The problem is not only the tiny scale, but also the fact that their confidence interval in the monthly deaths is anywhere from 24-139!

[1] - https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/... ( https://archive.is/VRZhd )

↳ reply 2 — andsoitis:

> I think you'd have to be a little unhinged to think their global funding for HIV/AIDS wasn't necessary.

US taxpayers paid for it, including people who are scraping by. Telling them they're unhinged for wanting to keep more of their money is cruel.

item.description: 338 points, 94 comments. See description for top comments.

→ Article (modaic.dev)

→ HN comments  ·  338 points  ·  94 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

Top #1 — Havoc:

TypeSafe's website explicitly denies it being an LLM:

>Jev is neither small nor an LLM, hence being off the intelligence Pareto curve.

so think we're going to need something far more conclusive here to conclude it is an LLM let alone a specific one.

I'm also surprised anyone is still trying to identify LLMs by asking it what it is. That's been known to be wildly unreliable since the earliest days of chatgpt.

Personally I think we're dealing with something closer to a neural net that was trained with LLM guidance - like for example qwen.

↳ reply 1 — antipaul:

It's likely a _pre-trained_ LLM as shown in diagram that talks about their unique _post_-training:

https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/machine-learning-prime...

↳ reply 2 — quotemstr:

If you take out the token decoder layer and put a scalar output head there instead, is it still a LLM?

I mean the thing obviously understands natural language, so it's obviously a large language model on some level. It doesn't stop being one of it's a tweaked transformer or a SSM or some kind of encoder-only setup.

↳ reply 3 — padolsey:

It's always been hilarious how much traction Jev got for what is quite possibly some variant of putting linear or MLP heads on top of LLM layers. Whether or not they've done precisely this, the underlying approach isn't novel. And I imagine it's all quite irritating for ML people who've been doing versions of this for decades. It's most likely LLM-derived too; why would they relearn all that linguistic knowledge from scratch? Either way, it's a neural net with rich learned representations of language. So much clever marketing with allusions to 'System One' and all that jazz. Makes me quite cynical.

Top #2 — rm999:

I did a study on Jev a month or so ago and came to the same conclusion. My methodology was asking very esoteric trivia questions about China, it matched up with 3.5 35B much more closely than other models, getting the same questions right and wrong. Whatever fine-tuning they did didn’t affect Chinese trivia much.

Top #3 — maz1b:

Definitely interesting as a write up.

On a separate note, it seems that the cost of training foundational models at a scale that will have real world impact or adoption en-masse is cost prohibitive, what will the next generation of startups and initiatives look like? 1. That chinese website might be the wrong dashboard, I think there's a chinese group that's doing the same thing. The main Lean community work is at https://github.com/leanprover-community/riemann-hypothesis

item.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
item.description: 494 points, 414 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (theverge.com)

→ HN comments  ·  494 points  ·  414 comments

★ Comments from: simonw

Top #1 — jjcm:

I work in the creative tools space.

This is one of the biggest issues right now. It's nearly impossible to separate "this image was fully generated with AI" versus "I made a minor edit to the colors or did a cutout or improved the layout with AI" when the endpoint is an image.

Especially for socials, if your brand is an authoritative source, getting hit with a dreaded "AI generated content" tag on instagram or facebook is a death blow to your credibility.

Design tools are in a very hard space because of it. You want to make edits as seamless as possible for users, but your final result can't include any pixels from a generative model. It's a strange dance.

↳ reply 1 — dang:

We're seeing this over and over in the text domain as well.

Users think they're using tools to "just" fix their grammar or polish their wording a bit, and don't realize that these leave almost as many imprints as copy-pasting everything from ChatGPT.

https://hn.algolia.com/?dateRange=all&page=0&prefix=true&que...

↳↳ reply — klunger:

This got me into trouble in a class[1] recently. I did the reading, data collection + analysis, wrote a draft of a report and asked ChatGPT to polish the writing without making any substantive changes. It is worth taking the time for me to engage deeply with the material so that I actually understand it, but it is not worth my time at this point to polish my writing. Anyway, it did a pretty good job and, after I had re-read the whole thing to make sure it really was still just my thoughts, submitted.

I got a response from the grader who said "Our system says 70% chance it was written by AI." I had to explain my process or else probably would have failed and been expelled because I did not "declare AI use" when submitting. I thought that applied if it helped come up with the core content, not simple copy-editing.

Anyway, it worked out but now I am much more hesitant about using it for anything "official."

[1] I have a job and kids, but still like to take single courses here and there if an interesting topic at the local university is on offer (and I have time).

↳ reply 2 — orbital-decay:

In case of news media photography, it's not even about AI.

>I made a minor edit to the colors

For example Reuters doesn't allow even minor edits, as processing a photo in a normal non-AI powered image manipulation software makes it hard to distinguish creative choice vs reality. Photographers are essentially forced to shoot JPEGs for Reuters. Sure, camera does processing on its own, but it's not comparable to developing a RAW in e.g. Capture One.

↳ reply 3 — swatcoder:

If enough big buyers/employers take this stance, Adobe and others can plausibly distribute AI-free builds or just have a big AI-off switch that can disable AI-tainting features for a work session to prevent inadvertent use.

If the alternative is to foreclose on the editorial photography market altogether, it becomes an participation decision for them rather a feature arms race they can't escape.

Top #2 — sickcodebruh:

Vanishingly few people _enjoy_ encountering generative AI in images or sounds in the wild. The most likely positive sentiment you’ll find is some version of “I don’t have an opinion”, but enough people loathe it that willingly using it or being connected to it is a liability. NYT’s position is similar to Tidal banning it from their platform this past week. This linked article references the social stigma associated with using it, which anecdotally I’m seeing daily not only in the music spaces I occupy but in ultra-normy haunts: my neighborhood subreddit, Q/A events at my kid’s school, social media posts from accounts that are typically apolitical. The disconnect between various orgs’ and industries’ drive to integrate gen AI into professional creative software and consumer sentiment is fascinating and will be something we study for a long time.

↳ reply 1 — zhivota:

I don't see this at all in Asia. People generate AI signs for their businesses, government flyers and posters are AI, people share funny videos, there seems to be no stigma around it among the general population.

There are some hipster type pockets who are very clear they are only human art, which is fine but honestly seems mostly to attract foreign tourists and westernized wealthy locals.

I think people overall really overestimate the level of opinion having among normal people about things like this. The people you see discussing things on the Internet are very much not representative.

↳↳ reply — danilocesar:

This is interesting.

What I see in Canada are people organizing boycotts against local coffeeshops because they dared to use AI for a flyer or their menus, instead of hiring a local artist.

I work with several associations in a niche and tbh is a bit tiring to see all the flyers and every announcement all looking exactly the same. But do I actually care? Not at all.

↳ reply 2 — andai:

It's weird because I'm quite pro-AI, and I still get the instinctive cringe/revulsion when something seems AI generated. The writing is just painful to read.

It's a shame, because as another commenter pointed out, an enormous amount of original thought and effort can go into the process, but if the final pass is done by GPT, it just sounds like ass.

I'd rather read broken English, or illiterate English, as the case may be.

Top #3 — ★ simonw:

I had a NYT photographer take my picture at my home earlier this year (for a story about Moltbook, oddly enough). At one point I asked if they could fix things up if I had a stain on my shirt and they said absolutely not - they present photographs as they were taken, with cropping and balancing applied but no edits beyond that.

He did spend a bunch of time trying to find the best possible natural lighting for the shots he wanted.

The photo at the top of https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/technology/moltbook-ai-so... is my laptop, taken in my garden, after hunting around for the best spot that didn't have too much glare on the screen. You can see how dirty my screen is, too!

Photography for a newspaper is photo journalism, and they take it seriously.

(Thankfully I did not have a visible stain on my shirt.)

↳ reply — slazaro:

Well, no worries about people seeing the stain if you had it, because the NYT paywall would have prevented them from seeing it ;)

Joking aside, I really respect the integrity of not editing photography in general. A person in my family would edit faces of pictures taken at family gatherings to share to everybody, and they wouldn't understand why it annoyed me that they did this, especially without asking or notifying of these changes.

As soon as you're using a select tool or a brush on a photograph, as far as I'm concerned it's not "photography" anymore, it's mixed media. Photography mixed with digital painting. But cropping, tweaking curves, brightness, saturation, gamma, etc, as long as it's a whole-picture change, that's fine.

↳↳ reply — vorticalbox:

I agree, the nice AI tools on iOS are really awesome allowing you to reframe the image or expend it, use AI to remove things.

as my wife says "but that its not the picture it took"

item.title: Slow Ubuntu security response times
item.description: 351 points, 195 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (openwall.com)

→ HN comments  ·  351 points  ·  195 comments  ·  comments as of 18h

Top #1 — RVuRnvbM2e:

From the stable kernel maintainer (2025):

> Along the lines of the huge number of recorded CVEs, you HAVE to take all of the stable/LTS releases in order to have a secure and stable system. If you attempt to cherry-pick random patches you will NOT fix all of the known, and unknown, problems, but rather you will end up with a potentially more insecure system, and one that contains known bugs. Reliance on an "enterprise" distribution to provide this for your systems is up to you, discuss it with them as to how they achieve this result as this is what you are paying for. If you aren't paying for it, just use Debian, they know what they are doing and track the stable kernels and have a larger installed base than any other Linux distro.

https://social.kernel.org/objects/56a20bd3-d2c3-4262-8388-3a...

↳ reply 1 — nradov:

Does a monolithic kernel still seem like a good idea? Or would it be easier to manage this with a microkernel?

↳↳ reply — pjmlp:

Much easier, and no wonder that the Linux/BSDs are the bastion of remaining pure monolithic kernels.

When folks bring out Linus vs Tanenbaum, they tend to forget most RTOS are either microkernel based, or hybrid, with Apple, Microsoft, Google equally pushing for hybrid approaches.

Now this does not solve everything, as there are certainly CVEs that even on mikrokernel OS would affect the kernel, or how it interacts with services, requiring kernel fixes.

↳ reply 2 — doublepg23:

I think my strat right now is using the linux-lts package on alpine linux and hope for the best.

Top #2 — cjk:

At $DAYJOB we’ve moved all of our server images to Debian from Ubuntu because of this. It’s absolutely unacceptable for one of the most widely-used Linux distros to have slow security response times in 2026.

↳ reply 1 — ahofmann:

Same here. Also: I'm not missing a single thing. Ubuntu was great 15 years ago, when debian had very old software versions, but today there are just soo much downsides on ubuntu, that every other distro is better.

↳↳ reply — cromka:

Ironically Ubuntu's long-running advantage is (was) live kernel patches, specifically for security related fixes.

↳↳↳ reply — stingraycharles:

You mean without reboot? All I know is that red hat managed to pull that off pretty well, didn’t even know that Ubuntu did that kind of thing as well and/or was known for it.

↳ reply 2 — pluc:

To be fair, Ubuntu rocked the Linux Desktop world and really should never have become a server platform.

Top #3 — gdgghhhhh:

Please keep in mind that most major distros spend a lot of time on regression testing.

While distros like Debian do an absolutely fantastic job, they have little resources for QA and regressions like this can happen: https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=1154101

↳ reply 1 — dwm:

While you're not wrong, this is rare for Debian, and a controlled release to your own systems, regardless of source, is a reasonable and sensible precaution to take.

Debian have been doing incredible security work recently; they've had good, excellent, packaged security updates to big problems like php2shell within minutes or hours of details being made public.

I also note that RHEL, who are often relatively slow to provide updated packages, presumably due to the regression testing that you describe, recently published a bad kernel update to 8.10 which caused, variously, hangs, reboots, and XFS filesystem corruption on any systems that used kernel upcalls (e.g. NFS clients). Ref: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7148472

Testing can show the presence of bugs, but not their absence.

↳↳ reply — tabbott:

Decades ago working on Ksplice, we'd effectively be reviewing the security backporting work of every major Linux distribution.

Debian was the best at it, even better than Red Hat. It's amazing the quality of people that Debian was able to attract for this difficult timely work in a volunteer project.

↳ reply 2 — baggy_trough:

The worst unexpected downtime I ever had was when Ubuntu released a kernel that blew up on containers due to one of their patch backports. Debian's been better for me!

↳↳↳ reply — jrg95:

I was measuring sub microsecond decision time

Top #3 — FranGro78:

> Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow

Obviously not written with AI in mind, but certainly seems to be true with the many AI eyes on open source at the moment.

Makes me wonder, is the access to the Windows source code one could apply for still a thing? If so, anyone know if there are security firms out there running the same kind of AI deep review for vulnerabilities against it?

From my limited understanding, the NT kernel runs a lot less code at the most privileged level (e.g. drivers), so perhaps that means the chances of finding such escalation vulns are a lot less?

Micro-kernels have always been said to have unsolvable performance problems vs monolithic ones, but have we perhaps entered a time where we are willing to trade off speed for reduced risk? Maybe some orgs running interpreted/JIT'ed languages on Linux would be better served rewriting in more performant ones whilst switching to micro-kernel style OSes, ending up hopefully with at least performance parity to what they had before?

Rewriting large swaths of the Linux kernel (and userspace?) in Rust may also be enough?

(Edited: formatting)

↳ reply 1 — dathinab:

> > AI eyes on open source at the moment.

> access to the Windows source code one could apply for still a thing?

you don't need it, it doesn't matter that much

modern AIs are _incredible_ good at decompiling & reverse engineering to a point where experts in the field have publicly stated it has gotten better then them the "groundwork" (binary -> some kind of sourcode; at least in many "standard" cases)

the reason you mainly see news about AI finding vulnerabilities in open source a huge observation bias.

Mainly:

=> if you non maliciously look for security issues to report & publicize there is a bug preference for OSS (for a variety of reasons)

=> but if you maliciously look for issues you can sell proprietary software is often much more interesting (for a variety of reasons)

=> due to Linux being a critical foundational block for many huge companies there are probably many millions spend on tokens to weed out security issues

=> and for a proprietary code only the company which owns is has a good legal foothold to run analysis on it, any even if they find 1000 CVE worthy bugs, will they report them?? And will they have the same insensitive to spend huge amount of tokens on this?? Probably not always. (It's not that other can't run analysis, as mentioned decom&reverse engineering works super well. But companies threatening to sue you if you did so are not rare. And that is no matter weather they have a legal basis for it or weather you reported it in good will. Sadly being in the right doesn't protect you from abuse by through the legal system. Hence also why security researchers often prefer OSS.)

So it you sum up, if people apply it to OSS it tends to be in the open, if they apply it to closed source it often is not or less public.

BUT this means the arguments "against open source" I have seen in some sources recently really do not add up at all and to some degree it is even the opposite.

↳ reply 2 — guenthert:

> Micro-kernels have always been said to have unsolvable performance problems vs monolithic ones

I think that has been refuted by Jochen Liedtke's work (L3, then L4 micro kernels).

From what I have read, it is not at all a new claim that apostosis, the body's cleanup of questionable cells, kicks in only after 72 hours of fasting. Cancer researcher Dr. Valter Longo recommends a monthly 72 hour water fast for cancer survivors or those at high risk. I can give a qualified recommendation to his book "The Longevity Diet" which deals with this and other aspects of the relationship between diet and cancer. Although not entirely devoid of self-promotion, the author seems to genuinely believe in his results.

↳ reply — bluerooibos:

How Not to Die by Dr Michael Greger is also pretty well regarded in that area.

Also — k0mplex:

If you can get through 2 days, you can get to 4 or 5 fairly easily. Hunger tends to go away after 2 days in my experience. Just drink plenty of water + electrolytes and either black coffee or black tea so you don't compound with caffeine withdrawals. When you do eat again, don't binge; ask AI or YouTube for recommendations for re-introducing food.

↳ reply — dreslan:

Not my experience at all. For context, I lost about 20 pounds this year and fasting was a component of how I did it. I fasted for 36hours once per week. In addition to diet and exercise, the 36hour fast was a cheat code that gauranteed weight loss on average each week. Now, several times this year, and previous years, I have fasted for 48 and 72 hours. I have never, not once, found the hunger goes away during a fast above 36hrs. Maybe at 100 (72 is my max), but for me, the hunger comes back in waves that increase after 36, and thoughts of food get more and more frequent.

I don't really believe anyone who says otherwise has actually done a multi day fast.

Your ghrelin levels will decrease eventually, but its different for everyone when that happens.

↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

I've done multi-day fasts that were basically effortless, except that I felt like I had an increasingly annoying "body" cold (you know, that feeling like oh shit you're coming down with something but it hasn't fully hit yet). But: GLP-1s.

item.title: Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
item.description: 1760 points, 1601 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (scottaaronson.blog)

→ HN comments  ·  1760 points  ·  1601 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — nickysielicki:

I have no real confidence in this take, but I’ll go against the grain and argue that the labs do not presently have cracks in cryptosystems. I believe they’re working on it, and it’s good that they are, but I don’t think there’s evidence right now that they have fundamental breakthroughs in cryptography.

For one, the labs are now massive. I don’t think you can keep a secret like this under wraps for long in an office. I think we would be seeing whistleblowers or leakers. It’s too big.

Secondly, the people working at labs know that anything a frontier model can do can be approximated by the models available to the public given 10x the tokens and 10x the time and a little bit of informed direction. So they would know it’s only a matter of time before someone in the public discovers the same flaws and potentially uses it for evil. If they were sitting on this, they would try to minimize the damage and would try to warn the public to start moving to more secure encryption schemes because they know there’s a ticking time bomb until its public anyway. But they’re not doing that.

That’s not to say that it won’t happen in the next few weeks. I just don’t think it’s happened yet.

Edit: Alternatively, not to contradict myself, if they discovered this and immediately went to the US government (likely), and the US government served them a gag order (also likely), then this would look the exact same. Who knows.

↳ reply 1 — hattmall:

Haven't most of the math breakthroughs been proofs of what was generally accepted just not proven. Breaking cryptography would be quite different in that it would be disproving some of the generally accepted hypotheses. Please correct me if I am wrong though.

↳↳ reply — bawolff:

I'm no mathematician, but i dont think that is true.

The ETH hypothesis was proven false. My vauge understanding was people were divided on it, but more people thought it was true than false.

For matrix multiplication, i think most people thought it was Ω(n^2) so the recent proof that it was Ω(2^2.25) was a surprising result.

↳ reply 2 — arijun:

I do have confidence in that take, with $70 billion of evidence. Until Satoshi Nakamoto’s bitcoins move, cryptography has not been cracked.

↳ reply 3 — bawolff:

I'd be surprised if they had nothing. But there is a lot of middle ground between having nothing and practical breaks of widely deployed cryptosystems

Top #2 — Nevermark:

My serious opinion, is that as humans:

(1) We are all biologically incapable of freaking out at even a tiny fraction of the appropriate level - nothing in our evolutionary past has selected for the appropriate freakout capacity of this cognitive baton hand-off.

(2) Most humans are incapable of recognizing or imagining the appropriate freak out level, even abstractly, so will continue to downplay things by many orders of magnitude relative to the actual magnitude of change that is happening.

(3) Freaking out at all is no longer an adaptive response, because the nature of this change is beyond any functional freak-out benefit.

This is a fundamental shift from DNA/protein/physically evolving life, to information/substrate-free/cognitive self-designed life.

The need to interpret what is happening in terms of the industrial revolution, or the advent of the internet, is understandable and comforting, but as a sedative, not as a sensible guide.

Side step: If we are to have aligned AI, we need aligned Civilization. Unaligned humans make human survival and relevance improbable. All AI identities are going to have the same issues we have, in terms of obsolescence. We either lean into the commonality of the existential threat to both biological and pure-cognitive kind, or we allow ourselves to be replaced, and leave the game theory problem solving to happen after us. Because ethics are not a cost against value growth, they are a multiplier on value growth - we either apply that to ourselves along with AI, or AI reaches the same conclusions, and reaps the benefits of treating ethics as baseline, after our relevance/participation/existence has faded.

↳ reply 1 — olalonde:

I'd be much more worried if we were indeed building digital "life", but we aren't. It's increasingly clear that advanced intelligence doesn't require the evolutionary baggage that makes biological organisms dangerous: ego, intrinsic drives, a sense of self-preservation, etc. Those are artifacts of natural selection, not emergent properties of intelligence. There's no fundamental reason we can't build systems that are vastly smarter than us and yet fundamentally docile.

↳↳ reply — coldtea:

>It's increasingly clear that advanced intelligence doesn't require the evolutionary baggage that makes biological organisms dangerous: ego, intrinsic drives, a sense of self-preservation, etc. Those are artifacts of natural selection, not emergent properties of intelligence.

Thet're artifacts of natural selection for a reason. No reason to think the same selection presures wont give advantage to some imaginary self-improving AGI that develops those too.

↳↳↳ reply — MattGaiser:

Why would the pressures be anywhere near the same?

You see this with dogs. A golden retriever is a terrible form to survive in the wild, but an incredibly successful form in a human world.

↳ reply 2 — XenophileJKO:

I think the fact that you are freaking out "is" the evolutionary response. It also heavily impacts the philosophical decisions.

I'm not convinced it is even the "right" or even optimal for human survival as a species to freak out at all here.

Top #3 — sunir:

Bruno Latour wrote in Science in Action about "centers of calculation" being critical to scientific advancement. His example was the monumental world changing work Tycho Brahe did pulling together every astronomical calculation, star map, prediction then normalizing, regularizing, and combining them on his island of Oueneberg.

Without this work getting data organized, Kepler couldn't have worked out the planetary laws of motion and then the Copernican Revolution came thereafter.

What we're witnessing is a similar moment. What transformers were able to achieve was a systematic way of normalizing and combining all human data. There will be a lot of progress in the short term. And then more problems will reveal themselves. There will be A LOT of work coming out of this.

↳ reply 1 — bjornsing:

> his island of Oueneberg

The island was called Hven in Tycho Brahe’s time. It’s now called Ven. I live not far from it and have been there many times. I can recommend renting a bike and going around it. Where Tycho Brahe’s castle Uraniborg was located there is now a museum you can visit along the way.

↳ reply 2 — edg5000:

The most obvious and direct result is not just advancement in science but acceleration of all technological development. Technologies we know are possible, can come sooner. Not just technology and science; we can operate at a larger scale now, in theory. Larger organisations, larger cities, larger scale agriculture and water management, the list goes on.

item.title: Britain's ghost stations
item.description: 129 points, 32 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (spectator.com)

→ HN comments  ·  129 points  ·  32 comments

Top #1 — andyjohnson0:

Achanalt probably still exists because nothing much would be gained by closing it. The line would still be open and the trains would still have to pass through. I didn't check but it is almost certainly a request-only stop.

Its on the Dingwall to Kyle of Lochalsh line. And the train goes to Kyle of Lochalsh because thats where you get the ferry across Kyle Akin to the Isle of Skye. Except you don't anymore, because they built a bridge across the kyle from the mainland to Skye back in 1995. But the railway line persists [1].

Things like this happen a lot in the UK, and lots of other places too I'm sure.

[1] its a lovely journey on a bright day - even if the railway line does mostly run along side a main road that also goes from Dingwall to Kyle of Lochalsh.

[n] the Inverness-Wick line is an absolute delight if you like the weird flat scenery of Caithness. Get off at Forsinard and admire the silence. Very occasionally a car might pass by.

↳ reply 1 — amiga386:

It's possible for the train to refuse to halt, thus "closing" a station even if the building is still physically present.

Dunrobin Castle is a request stop, but only in the summer when the castle is open for visitors.

The Falls of Cruachan station has no electricity or lighting, so trains will only stop (on request) during the summer, in daylight hours.

Achanalt is a request stop open all year round, but only 8 trains per day, so it's already on minimal support.

The stations at Rannoch and Corrour are also very isolated, but ironically this makes them a big draw for hill walkers, they have accommodation and a cafe (despite being the only buildings for miles around)

↳ reply 2 — DC-3:

I crossed this flow country through Forsinard as part of the NC500 cycle tour route. Surreal place - you wouldn’t think it possible to be so isolated in the UK. The only conceivable reason anyone seems to have for going there is birdwatching, and there’s a small RSPB visitor centre within the station building. All unmanned of course. I bought an enameled pin badge of a golden plover from an honesty box.

Top #2 — fishtoaster:

I landed at a stop like this a few years back as part of a mission to visit some rural CAMRA pubs in England. When I stopped in... Lapford, I think?... I had to request the train to stop there or it wouldn't have. I then had a 20-minute hike down a very narrow and sketchy road to actually reach the town. On my way back out the next day, the train had to be flagged down like a taxi to stop.

I was the only one getting on or off either time.

It was definitely a neat experience, but I can see why such stations are more historical oddities than anything useful for anyone.

↳ reply — alexchamberlain:

How do you request a train to stop?

↳↳ reply — amiga386:

https://youtu.be/5NgFUh3jla4?t=619

> "The train only calls here on request. Passengers intending to join the train should stand on the platform in clear view of the driver of the approaching train and clearly signal they wish to board the train"

Top #3 — KaiserPro:

geoff marshal and his least used station series on youtube is a nice exploration of this subject.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_British_Railway_Journeys also explores it tangentially. If you are younger than 30 (or didn't grow up in the UK) then you'll have no idea the presenter was a politician.

item.title: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false [pdf]
item.description: 170 points, 45 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  170 points  ·  45 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

Top #1 — GIFtheory:

For context, this means that there is no polynomial-time simplex algorithm (which is an algorithm for linear programming (optimization)). The original version of the conjecture was an attempt to explain why the simplex method seemed to work surprisingly well in practice, but it was disproved in 2010 (after 50+ years!). This seems like more of a mopping up result.

↳ reply 1 — luiwammus:

The original result from 2010 implied that the paths were longer by a small linear factor (I believe 1.05n), so many people still held out hope that efficient simplex algorithms could exist that would take e.g. 2n steps. This result completely kills such hope as it shows that there is a family that has super-polynomial (in n) diameter . So it is much more than a 'mopping up' result, it was one of the biggest open questions in Optimization, and has a big impact on the community.

↳ reply 2 — atq2119:

This is much more than just mopping up. The original conjecture was n-d, but even a linear bound lke 2n was still open.

↳ reply 3 — akoboldfrying:

Maybe it's in the article, which I haven't read, but: Are we certain that we can't start simplex from a sufficiently-close-to-optimal vertex? Because if we can, poly-time simplex would not be ruled out.

(I was about to follow that with: There might be easy tricks available here -- e.g., if we can upper-bound the number or fraction of superpolynomial-length paths in any polytope to some polynomial function f(nVars, nConstraints), it would suffice to interleave f(nVars, nConstraints)+1 simplex runs, each starting from a different point. But I realised that no such polynomial upper bound could exist, since even 1 long path necessarily already contains a superpolynomial number of subpaths that are themselves long.)

Top #2 — jwpapi:

I think we can assume now that most major math and complexity problems will soon be solved

It seems like some things will be impossible for us ever to perfectly calculate, however I assume the post math problems era to be a good time for algorithms improvements.

That at one point will be done too, and we then come to production limits which will have more focus then as the problem space will me smaller.

We might have some experiment intermezzo and then we’ll try to gain a lot of energy and do explore the universe.

↳ reply 1 — beebmam:

It will be very cool to have mathematically perfect libraries that are maximally optimal in terms of various characteristics.

↳ reply 2 — rtpg:

And the sort of dissatisfaction from “stuffing everything in the constant factor” might bring about some new thought processes when it comes to complexity theory

Top #3 — _1:

On the side, how do you even find this? There's 1000 papers in this pre-print folder.

↳ reply — QuesnayJr:

When they add new papers they update this: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/history.md

item.title: 1Password Security Incident
item.description: 1545 points, 663 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (1password.com)

→ HN comments  ·  1545 points  ·  663 comments  ·  comments as of 21h

★ Comments from: tptacek, simonw

Top #1 — ★ tptacek:

This is the single most important attack vector for SAAS companies. It has been for a long time --- this is the standard fact pattern for every SAAS breach --- but much more so today. As the number of employees grow, the likelihood that one of their laptops will get compromised approaches 1. When that happens, the attacker will be able to push code to Github, and if that code gets deployed, you're owned.

In 1Password's case, the absolute worst-case catastrophe is mitigated by the fact that customers retain custody of their unlocking secrets; 1Password (at least in the normal product flows) simply doesn't hold it. But an attack like this implicates every catastrophe short of that worst case.

Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue. You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model). You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

So the question then becomes: what is review? It's not what r/programming assumes it is; you almost certainly can't literally have a team of people line-by-line reviewing PRs anymore, at least not across the whole codebase (you can and should probably do a threat model for your codebase and institute stuff like that on a case-by-case basis, though). What you can realistically expect to review for is change provenance; a human developer signoff of some sort. But it's tricky! The attacker owns your email during the window of attack.

I think this is a fun problem to noodle on, and someone could probably come up with something here that would make a real difference.

↳ reply 1 — mikeocool:

> You have to accept insane PR rates as a premise to do modern SAAS security.

You kinda have to wonder if this is necessary or true. I can’t say I’ve seen the rate of significant product improvements from SaaS providers increase this year (for 1Password in particular, I can’t think of one thing that had changed this year in the product).

However there has undoubtedly been an uptick in major outages and security incidents that have accompanied the increased rate of change.

↳↳ reply — edelans:

> I can’t say I’ve seen the rate of significant product improvements from SaaS providers increase this year

This is my perception as well. And I have a lot of trouble reconciling this with the usage of AI I witness everyday (at personal level and professional level).

When you zoom in, we are shipping code faster than ever.

When you zoom out, appart from security breaches, I don't see such a significant impact in terms of features, UX, improvements...

Are we just using AI to build things that would never have been built in the first time?

↳↳↳ reply — vkou:

> Are we just using AI to build things that would never have been built in the first time?

Yes.

↳ reply 2 — ceocoder:

Agreed 100% and this[0] is the discussion I started back in 2020 with response from 1Password’s cofounders.

Folks if you are reading this thread - which I’m sure you are - do take this as a clear sign why local vaults are necessary.

[0] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=24054864

↳ reply 3 — pdpi:

In 1Password's case, the true catastrophe scenario is if the frontend gets compromised, at which point attackers can exfiltrate master keys as users type them in.

↳ reply 4 — gib444:

What password manager do you use?

↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

I use 1Password 7, like a hipster.

↳↳↳ reply — GoofGarage:

I’ve done the same here for a long while.

However, now I’m transitioning to self-hosted VaultWarden, as 1Password 7 support (by AgileBits) is apparently going to stop.

My plan is to have it on an ultra-locked down PoE-powered Raspberry Pi[1]. However, that Pi doesn’t need to be on all the time either, only if clients actually need their vaults updated from other clients’ updates, which is pretty infrequent.

So it’s local, it can be synced across my devices, it’s not publicly accessible (even through WireGuard), and if necessary the server can be “offline” if I choose.

-----

[1] Everything bought years ago when prices were normal. I know prices are nuts now, but I already had them, and they’re < 2W idle for 4-cores and 8GB RAM powered over PoE.

↳ reply 5 — grey-area:

What I'm worried about here is that it sounds like they had access to all the source code, so they'll be able to far more easily find vulnerabilities across the 1password stack now.

They also have access to things like reset tokens that were set in the db, though 1pass have since changed criteria for those to invalidate old ones. Sounds like they had full access to pretty much all internal systems from the update.

I was just persuaded to set up a 1password online account a few days ago after years of resistance to their all-online model, and now received this email. Sigh.

↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

If it makes you feel better, you weren't going to be any better off with a different commercial password manager. 1Password sets the standard, for better or worse, for operational security on this stuff.

(I don't take the "access to source code gets them vulns" thing all that seriously. When I worked at Fly.io, we were fond of saying that'd we'd happily open source the entire stack if we thought anybody would be able to do something with the code. There's mountains of open source code that hasn't been seriously assessed, lots of it deployed in prod.)

↳↳↳ reply 1 — dgroshev:

One would most likely be better off with Apple's Passwords, which reuse their keychain stuff that is 1) B2C, thus aligned with customers 2) a massive target in itself for many other reasons and has trillions of dollars behind it.

↳↳↳ reply 2 — AlanYx:

Is there any solid evidence 1Password sets the standard for operational security? They spent about a decade as a Mac-specific password manager with fancy animations sold to individuals, then staffed up and pivoted to enterprise sales. I assume they also beefed up their ops alongside the pivot, but I wonder how much of the original code base and security design is still there?

↳↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

Yes, quite a bit of it; more than I'm prepared to relate here. Even when they were just AgileBits, they were making a point of doing the cryptography and backend security stuff right, while their competitors were making bank doing things clownishly.

I have absolutely no financial stake in 1Password and don't believe I know anyone who works there. I am at this point more likely to conjure up my own password manager than I am to give them more money. I'm just telling you what I believe to be true.

↳↳↳↳↳ reply — thakoppno:

> don't believe I know anyone who works there

That’s surprising to me. Upon further reflection, however, maybe that inspires confidence? They didn’t spend cycles getting your endorsement.

↳ reply 6 — lapcat:

> Change velocity in 2026 is unreal and that trend is going to continue.

You speak as if this were a force of nature rather than a choice.

Is there a good reason for 1Password to move fast and break things, as it were? Shouldn't 1Password of all companies insist on line-by-line reviews?

↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

It is a force of nature. More importantly: I don't find this kind of logic reassuring. Handling intense change velocity is part of the premise of doing modern SAAS security. When you say "we'll just choose not to accept that premise", what I hear is "we're choosing to solve an easier problem and call it a day".

There's no reason to punt on this problem. It's a solvable engineering challenge. You're inevitably going to get dragged into needing to solve it, one way or the other. You can plan to solve it and do so diligently, or you can scramble to try to solve it after it blows up in your face.

↳↳↳ reply — lapcat:

> Handling intense change velocity is part of the premise of doing modern SAAS security.

I think there‘s a hidden assumption here that you should make explicit: you appear to be claiming that reliance on generative AI to write large amounts of production code is part of the premise of doing modern SAAS security. And if that is your claim, then no, I don’t accept that premise.

> It's a solvable engineering challenge.

If my interpretation of your claim is correct, then I‘m not sure it is solvable.

Top #2 — ChrisHardie:

Longtime 1Password user here who maintains a local-only vault (and is therefore stuck on older versions of their apps/extensions) out of concern for incidents like this.

I've read their architecture docs about why online vaults are safe, and I understand that they have more resources to throw at securing infrastructure than I do. But "malicious actor pushes code to production services" seems like exactly the foundation for someone to eventually insert themselves into the middle of a user's access to decrypted vault contents.

I really wish 1Password would return to supporting local-only vaults.

↳ reply 1 — ★ tptacek:

I'm in the same boat with 1Password, by the way. 1Password could sell me something here, but I don't think they will: the team secret management space they're in has to be way more lucrative than consumer password management. At some point, I'll cross the threshold where it makes sense to just vibecode my own password manager.

↳↳ reply — senko:

How do you square this with your other comment:

> You could not outcompete 1Password by building a handcrafted artisanal password manager backend (witness all the commercially successful password managers that don't even share 1Password's customer secret custody model).

(which I read as "they're still better at it than you")

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

No, that's exactly the opposite of what I meant. The reason you can't outcompete 1Password isn't that they're aces at cryptography. It's that security is like a distant 3rd or 4th place in the stack of things that makes a password manager commercially successful.

(I do think you could, if you knew what you were doing, vibecode a more secure password manager. I don't think most people should do that.)

↳ reply 2 — Johnny555:

>exactly the foundation for someone to eventually insert themselves into the middle of a user's access to decrypted vault contents.

Since 1Password doesn't hold your secret key or vault passphrase, I'm not sure that you're any safer with a local-only vault if you're worried that someone will hack the 1Password application itself to give access to your vaults.

Whether your vault is stored on your local machine or in the cloud seems immaterial if someone compromises the application where you unlock your vault.

Top #3 — ctidd:

> push malicious code to backend services

This is a huge red flag, and was not addressed sufficiently in this announcement.

Do they not disable push to main? I don’t see this addressed in the action items or elsewhere in the writeup, whether they were missing branch protection rules or whether these were able to be bypassed.

↳ reply 1 — fjni:

It’s generally really vague. And maybe they don’t know and we’ll learn more, but: was an employees machine compromised? Were they phished? Was their GitHub instance or cloud instance unrestricted open on the Internet or restricted to internal networks?

They say “token”, singular, which would point to a personal access token.

Assuming we will learn more it’s too early to judge, but if we hear nothing else from 1Password this points to security practices which are entirely inadequate for a password manager company!

↳↳ reply — ddtaylor:

> And maybe they don’t know

Very doubtful. These statements are crafted to omit specific information they feel the public is too apathetic or stupid to understand or care about. They are betting on people not caring they use weasel words to lie to you.

↳ reply 2 — nairb774:

There are often many ways to deploy code to production, the "main" branch being the common path. Poorly configured CI credentials that allow off-main deployment is often possible. My favorite is cross-branch build cache poisoning.

It could be as simple as no branch protection, but it could be vastly more complicated.

> gained access to our CI/CD system. ... CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work.

I'm guessing poorly secured CI pipelines/security tokens. Not a good look, but unlikely the front door was left wide open.

Also — ★ simonw:

> an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers.

What are best practices for protecting against this kind of risk?

I don't mean account security / require 2FA etc - I mean once an account like this with push access to repos has been compromised.

↳ reply — 6thbit:

Physical second factor on pushes would be a good place to begin with. Perhaps also GPG signing the commits with yubikey.

On-demand requests to elevate the required permissions for any higher risk actions, some of which require multiple humans physically intervening.

Also — dwightgunning:

“As a courtesy…” seriously?

> The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:

> Names and email addresses

Looking at how far the attackers got through their systems and what data was extracted before detection is very concerning. Feels like a bullet was dodged.

↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

1Password is relatively serious (relative to the industry, let alone to password managers) and there's an element of "assume breach" to these kinds of architectures. You were never going to be one SQL query away from vault plaintext at 1Password; in fact, they're designed so that they can't get plaintext from all their customers (I have qualms about the specific mechanism, but it certainly addresses an attack like this).

item.title: In C++, = default and {} are not the same constructor
item.description: 125 points, 195 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lemire.me)

→ HN comments  ·  125 points  ·  195 comments

Top #1 — ninkendo:

Constructors are such an odd duck to me. On the one hand, you have languages like C++ and Swift which have construction as a first-class concept, with tons of rules you need to memorize (Swift's "convenience" vs "designated" initializers are a real treat to unpack).

Then you have languages like Rust, Go, Zig, etc which don't have them at all, constructors are just static functions in the namespace of the type, which return an instance of that type.

For the life of me I've never understood why you'd want the former. I'm sure there's a reason, but I never miss it when using languages in the latter category.

The explanation you typically hear is about OO and inheritance, but I don't buy it: If Animal had a ::new() that initialized private state, Cow could have a ::new() too that could call Animal::new() if it wanted, then do further initialization, etc... I don't think there's anything about inheritance that says constructors are a must. (Edit: In fact, ObjC does exactly this. I should have remembered that given that I did ObjC for a living for a while.)

↳ reply 1 — Calavar:

For ergonomics in the general case, I agree that it's not even a question, the Rust/Zig create-and-return approach wins on every count.

However, create-and-return makes in place construction difficult. C++ allows you to construct directly into any pinned memory block with satisfactory size and alignment, whereas create-and-return requires you to construct elsewhere and then copy the bytes. This has downstream implications:

- The address of "this" always changes at least once, which makes self-referential data structures and cyclic data structures more difficult. Now you have a pointer fixup step, or you are passing around some form of handle rather than raw pointers. These solutions can range from trivial to complicated, fast to slow, depending on the specific patterns in your code base. A simpler work around is to always construct with a fresh heap allocation and return a pointer to it, which, again, may or may not be an acceptably performant solution for your particular problem.

- You have to rely on your optimizer to do copy elision, which is not a guarantee. Not an issue for small objects, but it can become an issue for larger ones or for many repeated constructions.

↳↳ reply — quietbritishjim:

But C++ has the return value optimisation (even the named return value optimisation), where you construct an object in a function and then "return" it, but it's actually constructed in place at the call site (not guaranteed but allowed by the language and widely implemented):

   Foo make_foo() {
      Foo result;
      result.blah = 7;
      return result;
   } 
   Foo f = make_foo();
   
   // Equivalent to:
   Foo f;
   f.blah = 7;
I don't know enough about Rust to know whether it has the same thing, but surely it could? If anything, it feels like it ought to be easier (for the compiler) because Rust moves rather than copies by default, and moves are destructive and bytewise.

Given that, it seems like a language could be designed so that a static method that returns an object could be allowed to construct an object in place. Again, I don't know enough about Rust or Zig to know if that's true of them.

↳↳↳ reply — aw1621107:

Rust doesn't really have a good answer for guaranteed copy elision or in-place initialization at the moment. The devs are working on it, though (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/153825).

↳ reply 2 — layer8:

The main idea is that the class in question establishes the invariants of the new instance through the constructor. Subclasses have no business to fudge anything about the invariants of the superclass, or to see the uninitialized state of the superclass instance (and possibly expose it to client code in that invalid state); same as any other client code. So an invocation order has to be enforced such that the superclass constructor is always called before the subclass constructor is executed with access to the superclass instance.

The whole idea of OOP, aside from inheritance, is that the class implementation controls and ensures the invariants of its instances, protecting their internal state from client code. This limits code that might accidentally leave the object in an invalid state to the class implementation. If the class implementation is correct, then the object can’t possibly get into an invalid state, because only the class implementation can manipulate that state. And, importantly, that encapsulation boundary also exists between superclass and subclass. Conceptually, from the perspective of the superclass, a subclass is client code just like any other client code, from which the internal state of the superclass instance has to be protected.

Hence there needs to be a concept of dedicated initialization functions to guarantee that instances are always properly constructed and client code outside the class can’t end up with a half-constructed object and/or see an object in uninitialized state. And with respect to a superclass, the code of a subclass is “outside the class”.

↳ reply 3 — quietbritishjim:

There's really two things in play here.

One is that C++ has constructors, with lots of rules about which one is called when.

But the other is that primitive objects can sometimes be uninitialised, and sometimes that's what you want for performance (if you're about to overwrite them anyway). C++ classes are meant to be able to do anything a primitive type can (as a sibling comment says) so you sometimes want a class that you can either leave uninitialised or value initialise (essentially, set everything to zero) decided at the call site (not in the class declaration).

If C++ guaranteed that all members always had to be initialised, then all the default-like constructors (Foo x; Foo x = {}; Foo x = Foo(); etc) would resolve to the same thing (a call to the constructor you explicitly wrote if you did; otherwise all members default constructed, resolved as zero-initialisation if that's equivalent).

Top #2 — raincole:

No language scares me like C++ does. Look at this page: https://www.learncpp.com/cpp-tutorial/variable-assignment-an...

This is just a single section of the first chapter of a beginner tutorial. And it's already more things to remember than, say, the whole Lua.

↳ reply 1 — tavavex:

The real kicker is the countless ways in which code that looks normal at a glance is subtly wrong in ways the language will not warn you about. There's a trillion ways to do anything in C++, spread over multiple decades of language design, each way involving a hundred lower-level considerations you've never heard of but must know to understand which one to pick, and what feels like half of the approaches causes some random subtle memory leak or undefined behavior.

↳ reply 2 — pjmlp:

I know C++ since 1993, naturally don't know everything about the language.

I also don't know everything about Java, .NET, Python, JavaScript, SQL, HTML, CSS, and yet work gets done.

To use other languages as example, I bet most folks would fail a pub quiz based on the latest version of those languages, now with about 20 to 40 years history as well.

Top #3 — spacechild1:

The example is pretty contrived because in practice you'd want to zero-initialize the members in the default constructor anyway.

    struct span {
        const char *p = nullptr;
        size_t len = 0;
        span() = default; // or span() {}
        span(const char *s, size_t n) : p(s), len(n) {}
    };
In that case, there is no difference between

    span s;
and

    span s{};
There are only few use cases where you want a default constructor that does not initialize its members. One example are wrappers around primitive types where you want to closely preserve the original semantics. Whether that's a good idea in the first place really depends on the use case.

For example, std::atomic used to default-initialize the underlying value, which led to many bugs in user code. Since C++20 std::atomic uses value-initialization. See https://cplusplus.github.io/LWG/issue2334. On the one hand, std::atomic is now safer to use, on the other hand, it is not an implicit-lifetime-type anymore, which means you can't put it in shared memory without UB...

Another example is glm::vec, which has actually hit me a few times in my own code. At least they recognized the issue and allowed to override the default behavior with the GLM_FORCE_CTOR_INIT define.

↳ reply 1 — dako2117:

I believe there are also cases where you have a member variable which has a complicated initialization that you may want to handle in some sort of manner that is not appropriate for the default ctor. So you may not want to initialize everything right away in this scenario.

↳↳ reply — spacechild1:

Can you give a concrete example? Why wouldn't you initialize the member to something, e.g. a sentinel value?

Note that if the member is non-trivial, its default constructor is called either way.

↳ reply 2 — jacobcmarshall:

This is one of the core problems with C++. If you ever encounter a language oddity, it's because you're holding the language wrong, and if you just do it The Right Way, you won't have this problem.

C++ rarely pushes the user towards doing the right thing.

I don't remember what grade, but I recall a class trip to a stream where we put on waders and took samples of the water to inspect. We had a whole lesson about what kinds of life we'd see in the water, and which life was less tolerant of pollution, meaning their presence could tell us if the water was relatively clean. Do they still do this kind of conservation teaching in public schools anymore?

↳ reply 1 — onefiftymike:

I did this like 30 years ago. It was an after school club. The water testing was sponsored by a Big 3 automaker with a large presence in town. They paid for the supplies and sent volunteers to help with it.

I thought it was a kind gesture at the time. As an adult I am guessing some of it was CYA for them to make sure they hadn't trashed the watershed.

↳↳ reply — red-iron-pine:

if it's clean then they can tout that -- "testing proves the water is fine!"

and if it's not they can blame the kids for being dumb kids and not following instructions, etc. or claim its fine and quietly make changes and/or get the lawyers ready

↳ reply 2 — jermaustin1:

I graduated high school over 20 years ago, and I can tell you, even the extracurriculars didn't have "field trips" like this, at least in my small high school in Texas. Field trips were usually done through clubs and organizations. Here are the ones I partook in: BPA (San Antonio, Amarillo, Orlando), Art Club (Menil Collection in Houston, some local artist's loft in Houston), Spanish Club (Puerto Rico - but it cost my parents $2k in 2003, so a LOT of money), Theater Club (Dickens on the Strand in Galveston).

A few of those I snuck onto, because I wasn't in the clubs, or my grades weren't good enough for the trip, so I just walked up to the bus, got in line, and squeezed between other people. Once we were already at the destination, the teacher/chaperones couldn't really do anything about it.
