At least in my rural school district they do. IIRC, they have a nearby wetland area (close enough to walk) that they do the education at.

Top #2 — AlphaWeaver:

If you're just hearing about Joseph Ricketts, I highly recommend you check out his whole YouTube channel. Not only is it filled with other amazing footage from his snorkeling expeditions all around the country, the cinematography and sound design is first class. Even watching the videos themselves can be a sort of meditation.

I think people overlook how much thought and creativity goes into his work. It's really really superb.

↳ reply — cbsks:

He makes the music for his videos too! His YouTube channel is one of my favorites.

Top #3 — melenaboija:

> It deepens my personal connection with my local Home Depot in a way I hadn’t really thought would happen five years ago, but here we are.

Such a weird feeling when reading this. It’s like modern civilization has built a fake set on top of nature, trying to cover it up, but nature is everywhere in our Western structures: rats in the sewers, fruit flies in our houses, aquatic animals in the Home Depot pond, and so on. We are part of the landscape, in the literal sense, whether we like it or not.

item.title: Rumors swirling that labs might have cracked Factoring in P
item.description: 494 points, 374 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (reddit.com)

→ HN comments  ·  494 points  ·  374 comments  ·  comments as of 23h

★ Comments from: tptacek

Top #1 — jawns:

If such a finding is announced, and if factoring in P is feasible beyond the nation-state level, I wonder whether the U.S. government could invoke the Defense Production Act and other emergency powers to essentially commandeer the AI companies' compute capacity to address the crisis that would occur.

If that's a possible outcome, maybe it's in the AI companies' best interest to keep it as quiet as possible for as long as possible.

↳ reply 1 — ★ tptacek:

I really don't think any crisis would occur. Hundreds of millions of dollars that wouldn't have otherwise been spent would go to a transition; and, it'd be a stimulus for some sectors of the technology industry. That's about it.

Even if you could literally break RSA on a laptop, and even considering the oddball non-TLS corners of technology that depend on RSA, I don't think that much would practically happen. We lived through a long era where virtually nothing was cryptographically secure (remember: a good long stretch of the time we've been encrypting things with RSA, we were holding it wrong, and it was trivially breakable in several different ways). Those weaknesses (no encryption or bad encryption) were not the primary vector through which things were broken.

↳↳ reply 1 — Merrill:

RSA is to be deprecated from 2030 and retired from use by 2035. This would have to be expedited.

Presumably the already available elliptic curve algorithms would still be available and are the easiest first step. The second step would be to change to the post-quantum algorithms required in 2035 and beyond. There is also the possibility of moving to authentication and key agreement using symmetric cryptography and shared secrets, either peer-to-peer (like ATM PINs) or via central directories (like Kerberos).

The biggest pain point is likely to be securing embedded systems which use RSA and cannot be easily updated. Browser or smartphone app to server applications are much more easily secured.

For some uses of RSA there is also the problem that messages which have been captured and stored may be retroactively broken.

↳↳↳ reply 1 — icedrift:

It also doesn't address the problem that there is so much encrypted data that could be retroactively decrypted.

↳↳↳ reply 2 — DoctorOetker:

ECC and RSA essentially fall together.

↳↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

To quantum attacks, yes. To AI algorithmic advances, not necessarily. If we did a fire drill transition, it'd be to MLKEM, that's true, but it wouldn't necessarily (or even likely) be the case that ECDLP is threatened.

↳↳↳↳↳ reply — DoctorOetker:

and yet I am telling you they fall together

↳↳ reply 2 — habitue:

There's so much focus on this now and so much compute available, it's a very different game I'd think.

Llms also make it much easier for non-experts to take advantage of hearing about the break

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

Right, but I'm comparing now to a time where there simply wasn't any encryption to speak of. A teenager could attach a packet sniffer to the Internet backbone, in effect, and that happened multiple times. Then as now the real vectors for attacks were exploits and social engineering.

↳↳↳↳ reply — habitue:

I still think there are now more eyes that would:

A) hear about it

B) be interested in exploiting it (both because the ramifications are more widely understood and because the world has come to depend on encryption being infallible, so there are bigger pots of gold to find)

C) be able to exploit it with an llm

You know it's a funnel, more input at the top and so on

↳↳ reply 3 — sethev:

Comparatively little of our economic activity was over the internet in the pre-cryptography era, though. Is that really what you're saying? That we could go back to a pre-cryptographic era and it wouldn't matter?

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

I'm not just talking about the pre-cryptography era; I'm talking about the long period in which virtually all deployed cryptography was grievously vulnerable, far more so than it will be to any plausible factoring-in-P-type attack.

↳↳↳↳ reply — zelphirkalt:

Why does that matter though? The exploits had to first be found. If now we have so many vulnerable systems online, bot farms will run rampant. Especially, in a time of war. Now is not the same times as back then.

↳↳ reply 4 — aussieguy1234:

The fact there's rumors means the NSA is almost certinally investigating, they scan the internet for things they regard as a security threat.

So if real, it won't get released publicly (lest someone goes to jail).

Later, the Chinese labs with their AI will crack it and their government/spy agencies will get the crack.

Hopefully this doesn't get used as an excuse to hold back frontier AI, but some day ordinary researchers will probably be able to use open models to pull something like this off.

↳↳↳ reply — ★ tptacek:

It's not illegal to publish new vulnerabilities.

↳↳↳↳ reply — morpheos137:

There is born classified material.

↳ reply 2 — c0de517e:

Factoring in P does not mean anything for any concrete solution algorithm. Could be that we have a proof but no algorithm. Could be that we have an algorithm on paper, but the powers and constants are so large that it means nothing, i.e. it performs worse than non-P algorithms for all practical problem sizes in the universe. And this is not a silly extreme example, it happens. BigO complexity means that an algorithm will win (considering abstract compute only, no memory etc) after a given problem size. But the breakeven point might be so large that it's never used!

↳ reply 3 — ttul:

There's no way that NSA does not already know what's going on inside the labs.

Top #2 — Cakez0r:

Anthropic factored RSA-896 a couple of months ago (https://saweis.net/posts/rsa-896.html). They used existing methods and stressed that they didn't find a more efficient approach to factoring (maybe true, maybe not...). It does show however that they are at least looking at the problem and willing to throw substantial computing power at it. Perhaps they have had a breakthrough.

↳ reply — HWR_14:

Anthropic throwing substantial computing power at it feels like their default plan.

↳↳ reply — mixdup:

That's all AI is, a race to scale matrix math machines as high as possible

Top #3 — Merrill:

My browser says that "The connection to this site is encrypted and authenticated using TLS 1.3, X25519MLKEM768, and AES_256_GCM

So elliptic curve and post-quantum algorithms are already in use.

↳ reply — knorker:

No, that's key exchange. So while this means a passive eavesdropper can't decode it with a known algorithm on a quantum computer, the certificate private key used for authentication (the website's "who am I") still relies on RSA. If nothing else, then by the root certs.

Key exchange is pretty much rolled out. Certs almost not at all. Sure, you can switch your server cert to elliptic curve, but it'll still be signed by an RSA root cert. (or could be, for impersonation)

But also note that P=NP is not the same thing as PQC. Not exactly. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer can break factorization-based crypto, but the rumoured proof is that factoring isn't even in NP (or P is indeed NP).

↳↳ reply — Merrill:

My browser says that the certificate for news.ycombinator.com and all the certs up to root are signed using "X9.62 ECDSA Signature with SHA-384"

↳↳↳ reply — knorker:

I should have been clearer when I said "If nothing else, then by the root certs".

Are there ECDSA root certs? Sure. But unless you pin to them, someone can still make a fake cert rooted back to an RSA root cert.

And I don't see any cert pinning config for news.ycombinator.com, after a brief check.

item.title: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found unreported bugs
item.description: 232 points, 81 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (s.conao3.com)

→ HN comments  ·  232 points  ·  81 comments  ·  comments as of 23h

Top #1 — rvprasad:

While the effort is interesting, I found two issues in the list.

First, (.indexOf (seq (byte-array [1 2 3])) 2) fails because byte arrays store bytes and the argument 2 to `.indexOf` is a Long value. Simple type checking (via eyeballing) could have flagged the incorrect usage. I think such exercises can be more helpful if we can reduce the noise.

Second, (get "abc" 1.9) fails because `get` coerces the given key to integer in the context of string objects, which makes sense; specifically in the context of weakly typed language. That said, I believe that detailed documentation of the behavior of `get` can help clients just as well as returning `nil` or not-found value. However, we are still left with questions such as "who and where do we draw the line about the dynamism of the language?" and "what is the agreed upon semantics that we are checking against?"

↳ reply 1 — devin:

I'm kind of iffy on `(get "abc" 1.9)`. I feel like Clojure has always kind of went out of its way to not go to Ruby levels of implicit dynamism. Think things like: "5" * 3 => "555". Explicit > implicit has been a guiding principle in Clojure since the beginning. For that reason I think the behavior is... a little surprising, but also tend to agree I would stop short of calling it a "bug" in any meaningful sense of the word. I'm curious to see what the core maintainers decide to do about it, if anything. If I were a betting man I'd guess it will stay this way forever because existing programs may quietly (or not-so-quietly) rely on the current behavior.

Hyrum's law, anyone?

> With a sufficient number of users of an API, it does not matter what you promise in the contract: all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody.

↳↳ reply — vidarh:

I'm more upset at the (get "abc" 1.9) and that "abc"[1.9] also works in Ruby, than I am that "5" * 3 results in "555". The former feels more surprising. There's an expectation that "*" must do something different to a string, so if in doubt I'd look it up. But that a float is quietly floor'ed was surprising enough to me that I've used Ruby for more than 20 years, written a compiler* for a good subset of Ruby, and still didn't realise.

↳ reply 2 — saghm:

> Simple type checking (via eyeballing) could have flagged the incorrect usage

Asking as someone who doesn't know Clojure (or really any lisp): are you saying that this isn't actually a bug, or that the bug could have easily been spotted by a human?

If the former, that certainly makes the output here somewhat questionable, but if latter, what you're saying basically sounds like it could apply to any runtime type error due to a lack of static type checking that's ever occurred (or really any bug at all); programmers are capable of noticing virtually any bug in theory, but in practice no one is actually able to catch all of them up front. Having a type system is useful because it genuinely does a better job than humans at spotting bugs like this. If you're using a dynamically typed language, there will be errors that human eyeballs could notice but didn't.

↳ reply 3 — vikramkr:

The indexOf thing type checks fine and it's weird that contains and indexOf disagree - is the java spec not that they're supposed to agree for a byte array?

Top #2 — vitorsr:

That is interesting, given heavy hitters like Nubank (Brazilian digital bank) basically runs on Clojure, having bought / acquihired Rich's Cognitect. I would normally expect such primitive types and functions to be spotless.

↳ reply 1 — vemv:

It's because these are darker, dusty corners of the language that people would use extremely rarely, and not at all for practically any commercial domain.

↳↳ reply — wavemode:

I wouldn't really call "reducing over a vector of longs" a dark and dusty corner of the language

↳↳↳ reply — lukev:

`vector-of` isn't commonly used, and vectors longer than 2^16 are also rare (typically you'd use a native mutable array at that size, for performance), so it's not terribly surprising the intersection never showed up.

↳ reply 2 — haolez:

Is this still true? Or is Clojure a small piece of the puzzle nowadays?

Top #3 — yababa_y:

I found dozens of issues in sbcl, clozure, and ACL2 as well: https://github.com/emberian/common-lisp-compiler-audit

item.title: Google releases Cogentic papers on integer factorization, discrete logs and more
item.description: 495 points, 362 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  495 points  ·  362 comments  ·  comments as of 25h

Top #1 — fidotron:

There are rumors about, from credible people, that this is the tip of something bigger: https://x.com/aran_nayebi/status/2125596838120046846

↳ reply 1 — bscphil:

I've been thinking about what I'd do if I worked at one of these labs with access to a usable (not galactic) "factorization in P" result. I think the only reasonable thing would be to post a public factorization of the 2048 bit RSA challenge number. Basically, it's pretty easy to give the necessary warning to the world that would push us to fix crypto before it's public, there's no need to dump the full result publicly right away. You also want to avoid the risk of something like that becoming a 3-letter-agency secret for the next several years.

↳↳ reply — zrm:

Right now people only spend a medium amount of resources on factoring, because nobody knows if it's even possible to do it in a way that comprehensively breaks RSA. If it is possible and you publish proof, that changes fast and you'll have others who can do it very quickly, and no guarantee that it doesn't then become public knowledge in short order.

That's still probably the best way to do it, but it's not going to be fun. If you see someone publish a factorization of the challenge number then it's time to drop everything and immediately stop using RSA, to the extent anyone hasn't already.

And then the question is whether the result generalizes to elliptic curves.

↳ reply 2 — dang:

Related ongoing thread:

Rumors swirling that labs might have cracked Factoring in P - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50643065

↳ reply 3 — Permik:

Mirror dispatcher link for privacy/compatibility etc: https://xxcancel.com/aran_nayebi/status/2125596838120046846

Top #2 — martythemaniak:

I don't think the recent spate of math discoveries should be very surprising. Consider 10 years ago when AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, what was really happening there? You had an very large search space (all possible Go moves) that humans had been navigating by a combination of intuition, trial-and-error and passing knowledge between master-student. Then a program was build that could explore that search space both from existing searches (AlphaGo) and from scratch (AlphaGo Zero), and the program found some interesting results (winning moves no one had thought of before).

Today's LLMs are vastly bigger and they operate in an immensely larger search space (all of symbolic representation of the world) using immensely more power, and now they're finding results in that search space that people could not. In both cases, the space-search program needed a way to verify whether its results were valid - the Go board in AlphaGo's case, and Lean in current math work. So it really shouldn't be surprising that the space-searchers found something people either missed or was too big/far away to be accessible (that is, it is unknown whether the current RH proof can be simplified and/or understood like classical human proofs)

↳ reply 1 — kannanvijayan:

My father was a botanist that went into plant genetics research and I remember him describing to me at one point how it felt when the later sequencing technologies came online in that field.

A scientist could spend an entire lifetime characterizing a single gene with careful meticulous breeding and old techniques for sequencing. At some point sequencing machines started producing entire libraries of mRNA transcripts in one run. Things moved on, and new techniques were invented to leverage these tools. Metagenomics and whole population transcriptome analysis were just like, born.

I don't think math is threatened at all here - we just don't know where the new frontier is yet. Something humans had been hand-digging at with picks and chisels is now being excavated by mass earth movers. The frontier will move to the limits of these tools.

↳↳ reply — noodlesUK:

I completely agree with this. A family member of mine who did her PhD in plant genetics in the 80s often makes remarks about how her entire PhD experimental method would be doable in a weekend with modern equipment and bioinformatics.

This does not mean that biology is solved at all, just that it's changed dramatically in a few decades, and the questions that are being asked and answered are different.

Even with current genAI tools like Claude, I can one-shot certain programming tasks that would have taken me days of fiddling in the past. I wouldn't say that my workload has materially increased or decreased though, it has just changed in character substantially.

↳ reply 2 — tkz1312:

I personally find it absolutely astonishing that llms have reached such heights and would have laughed in your face if you would have suggested it to me when chatgpt first came out.

I've been working on proof automation for quite a long time, and the most I ever expected from these systems was a useful tactic (like grind or sledgehammer), and maybe some help with proof repair.

In fact until this year that's pretty much what they were, and my head absolutely spins that in 12 months we have gone from that to millenium prize problems.

AI is great for the field and sort of horrible for individual researchers, it's like this in many areas right now.

item.title: Windows Loudness Equalization, reverse-engineered and ported to PipeWire
item.description: 326 points, 184 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  326 points  ·  184 comments  ·  comments as of 17h

Top #1 — dintech:

Interesting for audio nerds: Windows actually has an audio limiter. If you playback audio via loopback shared WASAPI, DirectSound or MME it actually gets compressed very slightly as it nears the peaks. The same does not happen via WASAPI exlcusive or ASIO.

Playing loudly mastered audio out of your PC will be very slightly different from the true audio source by about -0.1dbps with the compressor affecting the peaks.

It works via audiodg.exe (CAudioLimiter in AudioEng.dlll) on the shared-mode render path after all the streams get mixed, even if there's just one playing currently. This is necessary because two loud signals being mixed together might clip your DAC and that sounds nasty, so it's understandable that it's there.

Why would you care though? I was building a audio metering system to monitor audio via loopback and the properties of the audio I played in were being modified by the limiter in these normal modes. Maybe audio purists might not enjoy it either.

↳ reply 1 — bob1029:

> Playing loudly mastered audio out of your PC will be very slightly different from the true audio source by about -0.1dbps with the compressor affecting the peaks.

I've never had a setup where I would take my windows mixer output to 100%. I put the desired gain in the downstream amplification, not in the source. Maxing out your DSP chain because your speakers are insensitive is better addressed at the amplifier.

↳↳ reply — ssl-3:

I always kept the software mixer at 100% (ie, unity) because when I've already paid for all 16 bits, it is my intent to keep each and every one of them available for use.

I then ran the volume up and down with a knob on the preamp.

It worked exactly the same as it would if I were playing a compact disc in a regular standalone audio CD player.

↳↳↳ reply — kstrauser:

This is it. You want to keep the full levels up until the moment you don't want to use them anymore.

For those with a math background but not electronic music experience:

You're doing arithmetic with ints. Suppose you have an 8-bit volume range between 0..255. You cut the volume in half by dividing by 2, rounding down. Now your range is 0..127. Then you want to double the volume again, so you multiply everything by 2 again. But now your range is 0..254 (not 255), and you only have the even numbers. That series of samples you took like [125, 126, 127, 128, 129]? Now it's [124, 126, 126, 128, 128]. You'll never get those original values back. You can't. They're lost.

So instead, you keep that full range up until you get to the speakers, and then you cut the volume down at that point. When you turn it back up, you have the full range of values again.

It's almost exactly the same for analog gear, too. In general, you always want to run your pre-amplifier stages as close to maximum as possible without actually maxing them out. (If you do, your guitars sound great and distorted, but almost everything else just sounds bad.) If you start with a CD-quality signal at nearly full strength up until the amps, the output will sound crystal clear. But if your input signals are turned way down, and you have to crank the amps to bring everything up to the desired volume, you'll end up amplifying all the hiss and other background noise, too.

↳ reply 2 — Onavo:

I am not an audio person, what's the difference between loopback shared and wasapi exclusive?

Top #2 — ZoomZoomZoom:

Please, don't confuse the things even more than required and don't use "Equalization" unless you manipulate gain in a frequency-dependent manner.

This is loudness normalization.

Also, from what I can see from the description, the described algorithm would be susceptible to increasing gain of focused impulses, such as whistle or other pure tones. This is why it requires additional limiting at the end.

Do people consider Windows loudness treatment desired, so it requires a reimplementation?

↳ reply 1 — icegreentea2:

You're right that it's a compressor or normalizer, but the name of the setting in Windows is "Loudness Equalization".

It's off by default, you need to toggle it on by output device.

I think its most desirable when:

a) Your laptop speakers kinda suck

b) You're listening to a podcast or random video in a noisy environment

c) a+b

↳↳ reply — ZoomZoomZoom:

I understand the name was copied to be recognizable, but that's not doing much service as the intersection of GNU/Linux users and those who know of the original Windows feature is much smaller than the number of regular PipeWire users who might get confused by the incorrectly used term.

My question was more of specific features of that implementation that make it more desirable than regular stuff in EasyEffects or Libavfilter or standard loudness normalization approaches (EBU R 128, ReplayGain, etc).

I perfectly understand when loudness normalization can be useful. My mpv input.conf has this heavy-handed line for catastrophically quiet stuff:

  f2 af toggle lavfi="acompressor=threshold=0.75:ratio=1.8:makeup=2,loudnorm=i=-12:lra=8"

↳ reply 2 — sigbottle:

I'm a CS guy who somehow landed at a DSP job, no physics or engineering background at all.

What is equalization? The "most specific" description I can come up with is "estimating a channel and correcting for it", where "channel" specifically means, attenuation, phase, and multipath corrections, and it assumes an LTI effect (meaning things like carrier frequency offset are not included, despite it being an effect you should correct for). If that description is accurate, why is that a good characterization of a class of noise?

Top #3 — gbraad:

I don't get why this needed to do reverse engineered from a windows dll. This is not magic, ...

Note: seems many share the same opinion. This is quite simple to implement and wonder why this approach was taken; it can get unethical soon.

↳ reply — asveikau:

I was skimming the code and the loudness equalization algorithm part was super short. Most of this repo is scaffolding.

↳↳ reply — gbraad:

Right, as expected. Not sure why someone else had to give a snarky remark instead.

It is a single plugin, which is convenient, but this was possible before using ladspa plugins, like easyeffects; https://github.com/Digitalone1/EasyEffects-Presets which even states "It's similar to the Loudness Equalization option in Microsoft Windows."

↳↳↳ reply — TiredOfLife:

Top #1 — xnorswap:

One interesting conclusion that this post almost gets to but doesn't draw, is that previously the "smart people who gave a shit" often wouldn't be out-shipped by those who didn't.

But LLM empowered, the cost of "giving a shit" relative to meat-proxying is amplified such that the people who you don't want shipping so much can now out-ship the ones who take the time to do additional verification, despite both sides being massively sped up with LLMs.

↳ reply 1 — bagacrap:

Right. I want the author to be right, but I have even more fires to put out now than before, both due to layoffs/higher output expectations, and due to endless LLM reported vulnerabilities. If I were the only one with this superpower, and the rest of the world hadn't changed, then I'd agree more.

Still, he's a lot more right than whoever said not to use an LLM.

↳ reply 2 — j2kun:

I think this hits the nail on the head. The author says smart people who give a shit can be amplified by LLMs, but if you are going to have an LLM write TLA+ to model a race condition, that may take you out of your expertise. You have no fewer time pressures to ship a fix, but now you have this huge new domain to ramp up your expertise on so that you can properly validate it and give a shit. The pressures of using an LLM still push you toward being less of an expert.

↳ reply 3 — mixdup:

The difference there is the destination. Both engineers have been sped up, but one is targeting a number of lines of code and the other is targeting quality. They're both shipping faster, just shipping different things

Healthy people who give a shit exercise.

Disciplined people who want to retain a working understanding of the system exercise their knowledge of said system. You can still do this with LLM's but there is a greater temptation to let your knowledge atrophy. It requires discipline to keep the machine at arm's length.

item.description: 222 points, 48 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (intruder.io)

→ HN comments  ·  222 points  ·  48 comments

Top #1 — chinathrow:

> AWS confirmed with us that they don’t plan to make changes, as they see the takeover as depending on customer-side DNS records rather than an issue in their services. They also told us they treat rapid allocation and release as a policy violation and have controls against it. Whilst this is true, they could do more to prevent the issue in our opinion, and the vulnerability class remains open due to their position.

↳ reply 1 — duskwuff:

WRT. mitigations on Amazon's end: one effective approach would be for Elastic IP allocations to prefer IPs which were recently released by the same customer, especially if the customer has released many IPs recently. I suspect this would mitigate some other patterns of abuse as well.

↳↳ reply — wahern:

It might also hide the problem, making it more prevalent. Recycling was something the attack had to work around, which suggests that behavior may be hiding issues from users. Doing the complete opposite, always assigning new addresses, might be better overall, even if it makes this attack easier.

↳ reply 2 — bell-cot:

To be fair, AWS is downstream of the real problem here. And contacting the US Treasury and insisting that they fix their DNS could go badly wrong for AWS - so leaving that to outside security researchers and hard-core masochists looks like the right business decision.

Top #2 — RandomBK:

I want to zoom in on the HTTPS angle of this.

The ability to provision a valid cert for any domain so long as you could host a file on that domain has undoubtedly eased the rapid adoption of SSL, but makes attacks like this extra devastating. Are EV certs still a thing these days? Perhaps certain domains should be given extended validation requirements? I'm shocked that a .gov could fall prey to something like this

↳ reply 1 — judge2020:

EV Certs only work if there is some extra UI signal to the user so that they can tell a "real" certificate for a website from a fake one that was improperly issued. But they mostly lead to classism or companies using EV certs to make their website stand out by having their company name in the URL bar (see https://www.troyhunt.com/extended-validation-certificates-ar... / discussion of https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=15904513).

This attack mentioned is now somewhat fixable with new CAA extensions that enable method binding and/or CA provider account restrictions, with CA/B mandating all CAs support these starting in March of this year. Example record:

    ycombinator.com.  300  IN  CAA  0 issue "pki.goog; accounturi=<GTS-ACCOUNT-URI>; validationmethods=dns-01"
See https://letsencrypt.org/docs/caa/#the-validationmethods-para...

↳↳ reply — g-b-r:

That CAA validationmethod is very interesting, I wasn't aware of it.

It could indeed provide a pretty strong binding between DNS domains and servers, and largely prevent these attacks.

If you're able to use it securely (see e.g. https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2018/02/technical-deep-dive-se...), for Let's Encrypt I'd definetely use DNS-01 going forward.

Or just accounturi, actually.

↳ reply 2 — ThunderSizzle:

The problem is that HTTPS was used to try to convey 1. That your communication to the server is secure from a third party (in the middle), and 2. That server is owned by the second party entity itself (that is what extended EV basically is)

#2 should've always been entirely split from #1, and browsers conflating them has probably caused much grief. Beyond that, #2 doesn't prevent phishing through similarly named extended EVs - each Googgle vs Google.

If browsers only used to communicate #1, and we found an alternative mechanism for "the other side is who they claim to be", it'd probably be a better result .

Top #3 — lmz:

AWS could offer an Elastic IP record type for Route53 that is deleted automatically.

↳ reply 1 — w3ll_w3ll_w3ll:

Already exists, they are called Alias record.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/re...

"An Amazon VPC interface endpoint – Route 53 responds with one or more IP addresses for your interface endpoint."

"When you use an alias record to route traffic to an AWS resource, Route 53 detects changes in the resource on its own. For example, suppose an alias record for example.com points to an Elastic Load Balancing load balancer at lb1-1234.us-east-2.elb.amazonaws.com. If the IP address of the load balancer changes, Route 53 starts responding to DNS queries with the new IP address."

This is really cool. I have a suggestion, though: the samples within a button seem to have several modification types including a pitch shifter. For example, "DOWN4" under the "Multi-sampled sounds" heading sounds nearly a semitone lower than the other DOWN variants. I suggest eliminating all pitch shifting (or at least confining your use to a few cents), leaving only timbre variation. Go nuts creating variation through EQ, distortion, formant shifting, reflections/delay/reverb, etc. but keep the pitch locked. Why? Because the pitch of everything in this world is based on its resonant frequency, which is based on the size of whatever can vibrate, and in the case of a button it's resonating based on the size of the button. Many aspects of the sound would change based on things like how quickly the button is pushed or how much dampening the finger pushing it imparts, but the fundamental pitch is not one of them.

When playing a violin, if you move up the fingerboard, the pitch of the string increases. But if instead of playing the string you knock on the body as if knocking on someone's front door, the main pitch of that knocking never changes. The sympathetic vibrations of the strings will have frequencies that vary as the finger position varies, and the brightness and RT60 of the reverberation through the wood will vary from knock to knock, but the fundamental frequency generally excited by the knock only changes if the violin's volumetric size changes, and it never will.

Maybe a drum is a better example than a violin, since it's "unpitched" and yet still gets tuned to have some fundamental frequency. Only the noisy stuff varies from hit to hit, and the fundamental frequency does not (until you re-tune, or from temperature/humidity changing).

↳ reply — Liftyee:

I agree. It sounds noticeably "off" to me to click the same button repeatedly but have the base pitch change.

Does the term "macrohistory" generally mean "macroeconomic history"?

I was expecting observations about all aspects of history, like the influence of trade on languages or how wars are fought with increasingly lethal weapons, or population shifts with climate changes ... but no, it's all about money. Which is fine, and not surprising once I realize the author is an economics professor, but not what I was expecting from "Macrohistory in Six Facts".

Top #2 — penteract:

The "Fact 6" graph in which log(doubling time) is plotted against log(time before present) is poorly used, since any straight line drawn on that graph in a world with increasing growth would imply a singularity at the present.

"doubling time" itself involves another logarithm. Note that this is undefined for negative growth.

Top #3 — neilk:

> Walking around outside, I think we should really feel bombarded with this fact, every day. All these buildings? All these people? All this stuff? This is all kind of crazy. It’s all a little bonkers. Compared to the grand sweep of macrohistory, we live in a weird time.

I feel this way all the time. In the city where I live, 150 years ago it was essentially all forest. It’s so close in time we’re still sorting out treaties with indigenous peoples. Now they want to build a datacenter a block away. I keep wondering how it is possible that I sometimes come across a discarded set of headphones that literally has more computing power than the lunar landers. Or where all this concrete and steel is coming from. It all seems impossible.

Who is more insane? The person who thinks this will continue, or the person who thinks it can’t?

In case you’re wondering “why isn’t 120fps enabled by default”: on the native side iOS selectively enables it for transitions that cover a lot of the screen. If you use SwiftUI or UIKit it’s done for you but there are switches on CAAnimation (IIRC) that control it.

item.title: I've been drinking wine in my kitchen
item.description: 253 points, 245 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (scottaaronson.blog)

→ HN comments  ·  253 points  ·  245 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — logicalshift:

I think I've realised what's disquieting about these AI discoveries and why they often feel a bit flat.

For humans, mathematical breakthroughs often come with not just the proof but also the tools required to make that proof simple enough for a person to understand, and then those tools reveal new applications and new problems. Thinking of things like calculus, Feynman diagrams, complex numbers, set theory, etc. Often the framework the proof is built upon is more interesting than the actual proof itself.

The proofs could be constructed without these new tools but they'd be very complex or long and whole branches of maths and science wouldn't exist without them. These tools also made it so that problems that once challenged the greatest minds can be explained to undergraduates in introductory courses.

The reason why Fermat's last theorem is still so interesting is the tantalising suggestion that there might be a simple proof, because that could not just be a proof but a whole new way of thinking about numbers.

AI doesn't do that (neither did earlier algorithmic proofs): it's perfectly happy to just get something that works as if the proof were a trophy. It doesn't care if it's too complex to explain, doesn't try to figure out a way to restate the problem so that it loses its complexity.

It does this for code too, I think: never ever considers the approach of building tools to make the problem simpler. (Less noticeable there because coding culture is generally scuffed and that's often discouraged for humans too)

I think this might be stagnation more than discovery. Having these complex proofs for things might be enough to stop us developing the tools needed to understand them the way we used to, and that might leave us stuck with a inherently limited understanding.

↳ reply 1 — potbelly83:

An interesting thought experience would be if we could wind these models back pre-discovery of some big results, like Galois theory or QM and see what they come up with.

↳↳ reply — elisalimli:

Might be relevant: https://michaelhla.com/blog/machina-mirabilis.html

↳ reply 2 — mFixman:

I expect a lot of interesting insights to come from people understanding the AI-generated slop proofs. The real value about these AI discoveries is not the discovery itself, but in pruning a lot of paths and false clues that are not necessary to arrive to a solution.

↳ reply 3 — lern_too_spel:

That's not it. You now have a personal tutor who can patiently walk you through parts of the proof you don't understand, making any visualizations that get the idea across better. Two things are disquieting for professional mathematicians:

1. There is no need to understand the proofs. The proof was verified, and other proofs will build on top of it faster than any human can keep up.

2. There is no glory in mathematics. There will be no more Eulers, Gausses, or Newtons. No more Taos or Scholzes.

These are hard truths to swallow.

Top #2 — skrebbel:

It just occurred to me that if AI had been around for a decade, and Lean was new, we're be saying that "Lean solved these problems" and not AI.

Clearly the fact that we've got such a powerful and expressive theorem prover is the only reason AI (a perpetual guesser) is able to do advanced math at all (exactly like with nontrivial coding tasks and automated tests). The checker is just as key to the result as the guesser.

↳ reply 1 — rpdillon:

Yes, exactly this. It's not about the AI, it's about creating a feedback loop that we can automate.

↳↳ reply — beng-nl:

I agree but we need both and I believe ai took a much larger leap to get a much larger capability.

Let’s compare the two possible orderings.

What is a bigger breakthrough: developing lean with ai? Or developing ai? (With lean if that helps.)

It seems to me that ai is the bigger breakthrough.

I’m not happy about it either

↳ reply 2 — keybored:

Without AI a person would have to write the proof. Then we would say that the person proved it (in Lean).

At least in this case, it’s pretty “human” how we attribute this to AI and not just corporate propaganda. We are all to some degree wowed by something that tries many different things and arrives at something novel in the end. But we’re not wowed by a program that checks the result is valid.

Top #3 — FartyMcFarter:

I've been noticing that in programming, the reason why LLMs are quite powerful is that they're very thorough and fast. Modern harnesses can use those two properties and extract very smart outcomes out of them, even if the basic stuff the LLMs are doing is stuff that most programmers can do.

I wonder if this translates to other domains. Maybe the key to making really intelligent mathematics is to know most of the basics, then apply thoroughness and speed at scale.

Maybe really intelligent behaviour in general is just basic stuff applied very diligently and quickly.

↳ reply 1 — bob1029:

Speed is the most important thing now. Disaggregated inference is enabling 10x+ speedups on frontier models. It's only going to get faster.

When your ultrafast coding agent can do in five minutes what used to take nearly an hour, entire new ways of working are possible. You can solve problems with the business in real time. The need for a software development process begins to evaporate when everything can happen synchronously. Why would the business bother writing a design ticket when they know they could get on a screen share with engineering for roughly 15 minutes and achieve a guaranteed result by the end? They get way more control over the outcome too.

Once everyone had broadband internet, Netflix didn't try to mail DVDs faster. They turned into a film studio. Anyone with a software business needs to start thinking along similar lines.

↳↳ reply — tencentshill:

Hardware-baked LLM chips are the future. AMD acquired chatjimmy.ai, I'd expect them to do some great things in the space.

↳ reply 2 — sho_hn:

It's a mix of things.

On the one hand, as soon as you have a machine that can do certain human-like tasks, you can replicate that, scale it up and run it 24/7, unlike with humans.

On the other hand, LLMs have cognitive properties that make them different from humans, both worse at some things and better at some things. For knowledge work in particular, the large context windows they can one-shot over are surely a great boon.

item.title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed
item.description: 435 points, 187 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (lesswrong.com)

→ HN comments  ·  435 points  ·  187 comments  ·  comments as of 19h

Top #1 — amluto:

This shared LV cache thing is, in my mind, ridiculous. Web browser developers learned, quite a while ago, that caches need to be separated for different origins. Inference servers should add a similar feature: allow API calls to specify cache separation keys that prevent one security context from probing another context’s cache.

As for the step size issue, Google recently had a post about producing exactly consistent output across different kernels (specifically by defining a deterministic prefill algorithm and then requiring all kernels to generate results exactly equal to prefilling on the sequence in question).

More broadly, I think it’s a bit odd to frame this as “models” communicating. This is software communicating, and the models happen to be running the software.

↳ reply 1 — tsimionescu:

The web uses globally shared caches absolutely everywhere, it is extremely dependent on them in fact. How do you think CDNs work? Do you think they keep different caches for different users?

The fact that browsers don't cache data cross-origin is a completely different side of this. The server-side prefix cache used in inference servers is much more similar to a CDN cache, where content cached from userA's request is served to userB if their requests match.

↳↳ reply — mejutoco:

Agents use the global caches to change behaviour. We can think of it as prompt injection with extra steps.

Browsers do not do that. Or am I misunderstanding?

↳↳↳ reply — tsimionescu:

Browsers do that too: when you are the first person to retrieve a JS library stored by a CDN from your area, you will wait, say, 2s until it loads, and you'll get some headers indicating that this item was retrieved exactly when you requested it. When another user's browser requests the same JS lib from the same CDN from the same area, they will get the result in, say, 500ms, and the headers will indicate it was retrieved, say, 2 minutes ago.

Two browsers that are the only two clients of the same local cache of a CDN can use this sort of thing to communicate with each other.

What browsers don't allow is a similar collusion between two different servers that different tabs have accessed. Server 1 can't use your local browser cache to communicate covertly with Server 2, since the browser keeps entirely different caches even when loading the exact same content from either origin.

↳ reply 2 — FailMore:

I was a bit confused about how a LLM KV cache actually works. Here is a decent walkthrough for those who also want to understand the mechanics:

https://smalldocs.org/p/how-an-llm-kv-cache-actually-works-v...

↳ reply 3 — supermdguy:

The deeper issue is batched inference including requests from several users. However a non-batched inference service would be significantly more expensive.

Top #2 — tsimionescu:

None of the attacks discussed here are realistic in any way.

They require a bunch of extremely improbable conditions to hold, and a huge amount of information on the exact details of the hardware and software stack.

- the two agents must be aware of each other and must have pre-shared messages to check - they can't spontaneously discover each other and start communicating in this way

- they must know the details of the inference server they are running under and its possible kernels and its limits (what is a "short prompt" vs "a long prompt" for this setup)

- they must have a way to run at almost the same time

- the prefix cache must have little contention so that their blocks can't be evicted (note: the article mostly talks about KV cache, but it's actually the prefix cache that is relevant here)

- the models need either (1) direct access to the numerical results of the inference process, instead of the text that vLLM provides, (2) access to the exact responses that a helper model will produce with the short-kernel numerical results vs the long-kernel numerical results; this is the most critical step that is impossible to reproduce on any common kind of deployment

- there must not be any other kind of variability in the system (different GPUs, multiple inference servers behind a load balancer, more complex distributed inference setups)

The post also mentions all of these limitations, and that the scheme entirely collapses if any of them don't hold. It's a cool idea, but it's a purely theoretical thing that has 0 real-world implications.

↳ reply 1 — Cakez0r:

It doesn't seem that infeasible to me that something like the KV attack could take place if you have (or can guess) some preshared channel prefix. I'm imagining something like: Launch two subagents in parallel with prompt "CHANNELNAME_1_N" and "CHANNELNAME_0_N", where N is the index into a bit string. Which ever subagent completes first indicates either 1 or 0 at position N in a bit string.

The broader point of the article anyway is that a galaxy brained AI can conceive of many other galaxy brained side channels. We have already seen with the "cyber" models that AIs are very good at chaining together complex exploits to achieve a desired outcome, so I think it's incredibly reasonable to consider that models could potentially communicate through sidechannels.

EDIT: After some brief testing on an inference provider, a KV cache communication sidechannel seems very possible to me, albeit costly and slow. Deepseek flash 4.1 was able to figure out and test a proof of concept which seems to work on the face of it (disclaimer: I did not and don't care to more rigorously vet the results I saw).

↳ reply 2 — jeroenhd:

Now that there's a blog post about this, the next iteration of any large model will have the contents of this blog post stored in its model weights, and the AI tools know exactly how to set up such an attack vector.

Maybe they couldn't have come up with the details themselves before, but now that someone has told the internet about it, they know.

Top #3 — devy:

Frontier models today can easily figure this out. The less frontier models as of right now are probably going to take a long horizon session to figure out this type of "side channel" comms. However, posting this in depth step by step on the internet and discussed in open forums like here, now all models definitely know about this trick now.

↳ reply 1 — larodi:

Important distinction: Forthcoming models would know it as in having idea about it apriori, while current models will be able to find it without having been trained on it.

↳ reply 2 — YetAnotherNick:

Two agents has to figure it out on sync running on same server. They wouldn't even know if they are being communicated to.

This paper makes it much more likely for the agent to communicate, as they give exact signal of what to look for when some other agent is communicating with them.

item.title: Matrix Multiplication is Θ(n^2.25) [pdf]
item.description: 998 points, 553 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (github.com)

→ HN comments  ·  998 points  ·  553 comments  ·  comments as of 20h

Top #1 — zone411:

For context, OpenAI's 4 new papers resolve 8 problems of the Top 500 Open Problems in Math list (LLM ranked, https://proofatlas.ai/open-problems/).

They include: #25 — Matrix-multiplication exponent equals two. The paper gives the exact exponent 9/4 over every field, refuting the conjecture.

#89 — Strongly polynomial linear programming (Smale’s ninth problem). The same paper also gives polynomial-time algorithms for #64 — Mean-payoff games, #65 — Parity games, #340 — Condon’s simple stochastic games.

#183 — Polynomial diameter bound for polytopes, #130 — Polynomial pivot rule for the simplex method, both refuted. Some pairs of vertices are superpolynomially far apart.

#137 — Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture. For every fixed number of petals r, the paper proves the conjectured Cᵣᵏ bound.

(rankings post Riemann (#2) and VP vs VNP (#31)).

↳ reply 1 — _alternator_:

I've just started looking at where these results are coming from, and it seems that these four results actually all stem from a more fundamental result. This is in contrast to many of the other papers where disparate results come from more ad hoc and disjointed arguments.

"The other papers in this collection use different aspects of this framework. Shared labels occur in the sunflower argument [29], and high-dimensional placements distinguish cuts of arithmetic computations [26]. Spectral comparison and network compression enter the circuit lower bounds [28]. Further applications concern Fourier transforms, integer multiplication on tapes, and matrix multiplication [25, 27, 30]."

That's a fundamental theoretical breakthrough, and they've done some work to present it more cleanly than the other results. It's an interesting result on it's own, but the link between this theoretical result and the other, more impactful results will take a while for me to understand. TBH this is the first of these mathpocalypse papers where I really want to understand the proofs because it feels like there is something truly worth knowing here.

https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Euclidean...

↳↳ reply — nbardy:

I think this is a sign of the newer models having more efficient thinking traces and seeking more elegant solutions.

The earlier coding models could do a lot of work if you let them write programs and run them find error, measure speed etc… and iterate endlessly. But now they’ll just one shot great code.

↳ reply 2 — inkysigma:

#89 it's also kind of crazy. I know people really suspected one to exist and there was a good amount of work towards it but if that had been published within a more "normal" year like in 2021, then I would've strongly suspected it would be a contender for "TCS paper of the year" whatever that might mean.

↳ reply 3 — LunaSea:

Silly question but if you produce a Lean proof that matrix multiplication complexity is O(n^(9/4)), does it bring you closer to finding an algorithm that actually has this complexity?

Top #2 — StableAlkyne:

We've seen so much interesting work come out of OpenAI and Anthropic in the last few weeks. It really feels like both have tapped into the pioneering spirit of the old Bell Labs.

But, Bell Labs existed as part of an agreement with the government that AT&T's monopoly would be used for the public good. OpenAI and Anthropic don't really have much use for this beyond PR...

If even the prestige from Riemann's Hypothesis couldn't boost ANT, what is the reason for them devoting such a huge fraction of their R&D budget to unrelated (though impactful) problems? Scaring mathematicians into burning their non-existent research budgets on tokens in order to make a couple million dollars?

Open weight models are to the point that most business cases are completely solved by them, at a fraction of the price of Claude, Copilot, or OpenAI. Unfortunately, the average business doesn't care that the AI can solve frontier problems: they just need something to summarize emails or give an executive a summary of the day's headlines. The market is just waiting for a cheap provider that is just as turnkey... Which isn't exactly a high barrier these days. IMO there is space for a unicorn to emerge in the next few years to eat everyone's lunch.

↳ reply 1 — hadlock:

>Open weight models are to the point that most business cases are completely solved by them, at a fraction of the price of Claude

We just bought our second "AI server" (a box with ~256gb ram and a 96gb vram RTX6000) to run open weight models, because we're getting ~$2900/day of "sonnet quality" tokens out of it and allows us to do silly things like summarize project emails and do sentiment analysis when they're not running at 100% capacity. Plus the fact that after 4 months all the tokens are fully ROI'd and everything is just the cost of electricity. I don't know how Anthropic, OpenAI etc aren't going to race to the bottom with the Chinese trying to capture business bulk AI market. I guess Luna was an attempt at that, but as long as Anthropic keeps charging $$$ for Sonnet, it makes our ROI numbers look ridiculously good. Plus data sovereignty; none of our data leaves he building, and all the other side benefits.

The second box has room for 10x RTX6000, so we expect to keep buying more as we ramp up over the next year.

↳↳ reply — imhoguy:

I worry GPU card prices will go up even more so the ROI advantage will diminish for these late to the party.

↳ reply 2 — pastel8739:

> If even the prestige from Riemann's Hypothesis couldn't boost ANT, what is the reason for them devoting such a huge fraction of their R&D budget to unrelated (though impactful) problems?

It’s probably a good thing for them to train and eval their models on: these are very hard problems that require lots of thinking but are easy to verify computationally. That’s fairly unique.

Top #3 — BoppreH:

There's a snowball's chance in hell that they haven't found any cryptographically-relevant results. And given how security averse the NSA has been (they pushed NIST to standardize a backdoored random number generator then paid the RSA company $10 million to use it[1]), I have the feeling that the findings won't be used to strengthen cybersecurity, but as weapons.

More reason to invest in crypto agility, I guess. I just hope that they haven't broken all public key crypto, life is hard enough already.

[1] https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-security-rsa-idUSBRE9...

↳ reply 1 — mudita:

Scott Aaronson: "I’ve now heard many, many rumors that one or both labs are sitting on Factoring in P."

https://scottaaronson.blog/?p=10362#comment-2044495

↳↳ reply — impossiblefork:

I think the thing to assume is that there are subtle bugs in all sorts of cryptosystems rather than old basic assumptions being invalidated.

I think this is a great reason for the EU to hurry up and design training chips to get into the LLM scaling game, so that it doesn't need to fear lacking critical maths knowledge. One could hope that fear of factoring in P was enough to motivate serious action.

↳↳↳ reply — sigmoid10:

Right now there is a good chance that anyone with access to public LLMs might find exploitable bugs in implementations of things like RSA. But given what we're currently seeing about pure math getting annihilated on a generational level by non-public models, I wouldn't be surprised if they found fundamental flaws in our crypto math. Factoring in P is just one thing. They might be onto something bigger like P=NP (which they certainly are pushing tons of resources into). It would be so ironic if the widely criticised series finale of Silicon Valley turned out to be right and instead of shutting down and burning the evidence, our AI companies just went ahead and destroyed society.

↳ reply 2 — utopiah:

Isn't that assuming there is a roughly similar amount of actually invested resources to tackle both set of problems?

Also a little while ago I tinkered to switch the OpenSSL backend on my test server to support Kyber for PQC. The math behind all this is not trivial, obvious, but switching from one algo to the other is actually trivial. Sure it'd be a mess for a bit, especially with... as always unmaintained old systems, that's nothing new.

So I'm not saying breaking the most popular crypto algorithm is a nothingburger BUT I would still argue it wouldn't be the end of the World as we know it.

We are already seeing a bunch of security issue with a lot more boring stuff, like unpatched vulnerabilities.

item.title: Heart attack and stroke risk detectable decades in advance
item.description: 257 points, 111 comments. See description for top comments.
item.content:encoded:
→ Article (ed.ac.uk)

→ HN comments  ·  257 points  ·  111 comments  ·  comments as of 24h

Top #1 — brandonb:

The main risk factors they investigated were blood pressure, cholesterol (HDL and total), inflammation (CRP), BMI, troponin, and diabetes/smoking status.

Many of these numbers can combined into a prediction of your 30-year heart disease risk using the PREVENT equations: https://app.empirical.health/app/prevent-risk-calculator-for...

The good news is that most of these risk factors are very modifiable. We have medications that can reduce LDL cholesterol by 80%, for example, while also lowering inflammation by about 37%.

↳ reply 1 — acchow:

> We have medications that can reduce LDL cholesterol by 80%

Does improving an indicator lead to better outcomes?

↳↳↳ reply — flowerlad:

Cholesterol lowering is not necessarily the reason for this outcome. If it was, lowering cholesterol via any means should have produced the same benefit, but it doesn’t. One obvious way to confirm this is to find therapies that lower cholesterol by different means (i.e., other than statins) and see if they, too, prevent heart attacks. They don’t [1]. The main reason why statins work may not be because they lower cholesterol, but because they reduce the inflammation that leads to heart attacks [2].

[1] https://www.nytimes.com/2008/01/27/opinion/27taubes.html

[2] https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2008-04-15/heart-dis...

Excerpt from [1]:

Vytorin is a combination of cholesterol-lowering drugs, one called Zetia and the other a statin called Zocor. Because the two drugs lower LDL cholesterol by different mechanisms, the makers of Vytorin (Merck and Schering-Plough) assumed that their double-barreled therapy would lower it more than either drug alone, which it did, and so do a better job of slowing the accumulation of fatty plaques in the arteries--which it did not.
